questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Predictive maintenance on smart water meters — imbalanced data, metrics and governance
questions.question:
You have been asked to review the proposal before it is deployed. The dataset and model figures are given in the case study.

(a)

Calculate the number of rows the utility will add per year, and the storage this requires in gigabytes if each row occupies 12 bytes. Hence state why a row-oriented operational table is unlikely to be the right home for this data.

[4]

(b)

Describe two preprocessing steps that must be applied to the raw hourly readings before any model is trained, and state the specific problem that each step addresses.

[4]

(c)

Explain why classification accuracy is a misleading measure of this model's performance, and identify the two measures you would report instead, explaining what each one tells the utility.

[4]

(d)

Using the figures given, evaluate whether the proposed model is operationally useful. Your evaluation must include a calculation of the number of false alarms the utility would face.

[5]

(e)

Discuss two ethical or social risks raised by deploying this model, and for each one recommend a specific governance measure that would reduce it.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) The utility adds $90\,000\times24\times365=7.884\times10^{8}$ rows per year. (M1)(A1) At 12 bytes each that is $7.884\times10^8\times12=9.46\times10^{9}$ bytes, so about $9.46$ GB per year and roughly $57$ GB over the six-year history. (A1) An operational row-oriented table is the wrong home for it because the workload is not transactional: nobody retrieves one reading, and the queries the utility needs are aggregations over a meter, a street or a month. A column-oriented warehouse with a meter dimension and a date dimension lets those aggregations read only the columns they need, and keeps the operational billing system — which does need single-row access — free of a table two orders of magnitude larger than anything else in it. (R1)

(b) First, missing and impossible readings must be handled. Smart meters lose connectivity and report gaps, and some report zero for a period when the meter has failed rather than when no water was used; training on those rows teaches the model that a fault looks like normal consumption. The step is to flag gaps explicitly, distinguish a transmitted zero from a missing value, and either interpolate short gaps or mark them as a feature. (M1)(A1) Second, the readings must be aggregated into a fixed-shape window before training, because the model is asked about a meter-week and the raw data is hourly. Features such as the mean night-time flow, the variance of hourly flow, and the ratio of night flow to day flow have to be computed over each window; otherwise the model is given 168 loosely comparable numbers per row and no way to learn what a burst precursor looks like. (M1)(A1)

(c) Over six years the utility has $90\,000\times52\times6=2.808\times10^{7}$ meter-weeks and only 1240 positive cases, so a model that predicts 'no burst' every single time scores $1-\dfrac{1240}{2.808\times10^{7}}=99.996\%$ accuracy while doing nothing at all. (M1)(A1) The two measures to report are recall, the fraction of real bursts the model catches, and precision, the fraction of flagged cases that turn out to be real. (A1) Recall tells the utility how much of the damage it avoids; precision tells it how much of its field capacity it spends on nothing. Neither is visible in the accuracy figure, and at this base rate accuracy cannot distinguish a useful model from a useless one. (R1)

(d) The model flags $0.001\times2.808\times10^{7}=28\,080$ meter-weeks. At 70% recall it catches $0.70\times1240=868$ real bursts, so the number of false alarms is $28\,080-868=27\,212$. (M1)(A1)(A1) Precision is therefore $\dfrac{868}{28\,080}=3.1\%$: roughly thirty false alarms for every real burst found. (A1) With 40 crews the utility can investigate 40 sites a day, so clearing the flagged list occupies about $\dfrac{28\,080}{40}=702$ crew-days, and the list regenerates continuously. Against that, an uncaught burst costs an emergency repair, road closure and water loss that is far more expensive than a planned visit. The model is therefore not useless, but it is not deployable at this flag rate: the correct evaluation is that the utility should either raise the threshold until precision reaches a level its crews can absorb, or use the score to rank rather than to flag, sending out only as many visits per week as capacity allows and accepting lower recall. (R1)

(e) *Risk 1: unequal service by area.* Meter age, pipe material and consumption patterns all correlate with the age and income of the neighbourhood, so a model trained on historical bursts will systematically score poorer areas as riskier, and those areas will receive a disproportionate share of the investigative visits and of the blame. The governance measure is to audit the flag rate and the precision separately by deprivation decile before deployment and at fixed intervals afterwards, and to withhold deployment if the false-alarm rate in any decile is materially worse than the fleet average. (M1)(A1)(A1) *Risk 2: adverse action against customers identified as meter faults.* The same model that finds faulty meters produces a list of households whose consumption looks anomalous, and a faulty meter under-reads as often as it over-reads, so a customer may be presented with a back-bill generated by a statistical score they cannot see or contest. The governance measure is to require a physical meter test before any billing adjustment is made, to prohibit the score from being used as evidence on its own, and to publish the model's error rate on the customer-facing page. (M1)(A1)
questions.explanation: The whole item turns on one number: 1240 positives in 28 million opportunities. Everything the students have been taught about judging a classifier with accuracy collapses at that base rate, and the purpose of (c) is to make that collapse visible rather than to have it asserted. Part (d) then forces the arithmetic that the utility skipped — 868 bursts found at the cost of 27 212 wasted visits and 702 crew-days — and the interesting conclusion is that the model is neither good nor useless but badly thresholded, so the right answer is to change the operating point rather than to accept or reject the proposal. That is a genuinely transferable lesson and it is why the flag rate was fixed at an arbitrary 0.1%. Part (a) and (b) are there to stop the item from being pure metrics: the data does not arrive model-ready, and a candidate who jumps straight to precision and recall has skipped the two steps that decide whether the model can learn anything at all. Part (e) is deliberately weighted towards governance rather than towards naming harms, because every candidate can name bias and almost none can say what to measure. The item is also a test of whether a candidate can hold two criticisms at once. The model is genuinely useful — it finds 868 bursts that would otherwise have been found by a customer ringing up — and it is genuinely undeployable as specified. Accepting one and rejecting the other is the easy route and loses marks; the argument that the threshold, not the model, is what has to change is the one the case study is built to produce, and it generalises to every imbalanced deployment a candidate will meet afterwards.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: Emergency department triage — ADT selection, class design and cost analysis
questions.question:
You are to design the data structure and the classes behind the new triage board. The four required operations and the operating figures are given in the case study.

(a)

Evaluate an unsorted array, an array kept sorted by category, and a binary max-heap as the underlying structure for the waiting list, referring to each of the four required operations in each case.

[5]

(b)

Construct Python class definitions for the two classes you would use to model a patient and the waiting list. Include the attributes, the constructor, and the signatures and a one-line comment for each of the four required operations.

[5]

(c)

A patient who leaves without being seen cannot be removed from a heap directly, because their record may sit in the middle of the array. Justify whether the system should remove such a patient immediately or mark them as departed and skip them when they reach the front of the queue.

[4]

(d)

Using the operating figures, determine the total number of comparisons needed for one day of insertions under the unsorted-array design and under the binary-heap design, and determine which structure you would recommend for this department.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) *Unsorted array.* Adding a patient is $O(1)$, simply appending. (A1) Producing the most urgent patient requires scanning all $n$ entries, so it is $O(n)$; at $n=18$ that is 18 comparisons every time a doctor becomes free. Escalation is $O(n)$ to find the patient and then $O(1)$ to change the category. Removal of a departed patient is $O(n)$ to find and $O(n)$ to close the gap. (A1)

*Sorted array.* Producing the most urgent patient is $O(1)$, taking the head. (A1) Insertion is $O(n)$ because on average $n/2$ entries must be shifted to make room, and escalation is worse still: the patient must be found, removed and reinserted at a new position. The structure optimises exactly the operation that is already cheap and pays for it on the two that are not. (A1)

*Binary max-heap.* Producing the most urgent patient is $O(1)$ at the root and $O(\log n)$ to restore the heap after removal; insertion is $O(\log n)$. (A1) Escalation is $O(\log n)$ if the position of the patient is known, but $O(n)$ if it is not, because a heap offers no search. Removal of a departed patient has the same difficulty. The heap is therefore the best of the three for the two operations that dominate, and its weakness is that it cannot find an arbitrary entry quickly. (R1)

(b)

class Patient:
    """One patient on the triage board."""
    def __init__(self, patient_id, name, category, arrived_at):
        self.patient_id = patient_id      # unique identifier
        self.name = name
        self.category = category          # 1 (most urgent) to 5
        self.arrived_at = arrived_at      # timestamp used to break ties
        self.departed = False             # set when the patient leaves unseen

def __lt__(self, other):
# more urgent first; earlier arrival breaks ties within a category
return (self.category, self.arrived_at) < (other.category, other.arrived_at)

class TriageQueue:
"""Waiting list held in a binary heap with an id-to-index map."""
def __init__(self):
self.heap = [] # list of Patient
self.index = {} # patient_id -> position in heap

def add_patient(self, patient): # O(log n): append then sift up
...

def pop_most_urgent(self): # O(log n): take root, move last up, sift down
...

def escalate(self, patient_id, new_category): # O(log n) using the index
...

def mark_departed(self, patient_id): # O(1): flag only; skipped on pop
...
```

(M1)(A1)(A1) The two classes are related by composition: TriageQueue holds a collection of Patient objects and does not inherit from them. Encapsulation is respected because the heap array and the index map are private to TriageQueue, so no caller can corrupt the invariant that the index map and the array agree. (A1)

(c) Marking and skipping is the right choice. (A1) Immediate removal costs $O(n)$ to locate the patient and then a sift to restore the heap, and it happens eleven times a day, which is not a large cost in absolute terms. (A1) The real argument is not performance but integrity and audit: a patient who has left is still a patient who attended, and the department needs the record for its own statistics and for any later complaint about waiting times. Flagging the record and discarding it when it surfaces at the root removes the patient from clinical consideration immediately, which is what the board is for, while keeping the fact of the attendance. (M1)(A1) The only cost is that the heap retains stale entries, so the occupancy figure shown on the board must be derived by counting non-departed records rather than from the length of the array. (R1)

(d) Under the unsorted-array design each insertion is $O(1)$, so insertion costs essentially nothing; but the design is unusable because producing the most urgent patient costs 18 comparisons each time. (A1) Comparing the insertion work where it differs meaningfully: a sorted array needs on average $\dfrac{n}{2}=9$ shifts per insertion, so $220\times9=1980$ element moves per day. (M1)(A1) A binary heap needs at most $\log_2 18=4.17$ comparisons per insertion, so $220\times4.17\approx917$ comparisons per day, and removals cost at most $2\log_2 18$ each, giving about 1835 comparisons for the day's removals. (A1) I recommend the binary heap with a hash-based index from patient identifier to heap position. The absolute numbers here are small enough that any of the designs would function at this scale, so the recommendation rests on the shape of the growth rather than on today's figures: the heap keeps both insertion and removal logarithmic, and the index reduces escalation from $O(n)$ to $O(\log n)$, which is the operation the department's incident showed it gets wrong. (R1)
questions.explanation: The item is built so that the fashionable answer and the correct answer diverge. A candidate who has memorised that heaps give O(log n) insertion and O(1) access to the maximum will recommend a heap in (a) and stop; the fourth operation, escalation, is the one that discriminates, because a heap has no search and an escalation request therefore costs O(n) unless an auxiliary index is added. Part (d) then removes the usual escape route: at n = 18 all three designs are fast enough, so a recommendation justified only by the arithmetic is worthless, and the candidate has to argue from growth and from which operation the department actually gets wrong. Part (c) is the second discriminator and works in the opposite direction: the performance answer says delete immediately, the engineering answer says flag and skip, because the record still has to exist for audit even though the patient must leave the queue at once. A strong answer notices that the two parts pull against each other and says so. A useful diagnostic while marking is whether the candidate mentions growth at all in (d). At eighteen patients every design is instant, so an answer that recommends a heap purely because 917 is less than 1980 has mistaken the exercise: the department will not shrink, and the incident in the case study was an escalation failure, which is the operation the plain heap handles worst. Candidates who notice that the index is what makes the heap acceptable, rather than the heap itself, have understood the item. Part (b) sits between them and is not decoration: a design that stores the category as a free integer with no tie-break rule will serve two patients with the same category in arrival order only by accident, and the department's incident was precisely about ordering within and between categories.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Distributed monitoring system — architecture, transmission and schema design
questions.question:
The authority has asked your team to design the monitoring and alerting subsystem. The parameters you need are given in the case study.

(a)

Calculate the total volume of data the fleet generates in one operating year, giving your answer in gibibytes, and state what the volume would become if each reading were instead stored as an 80-byte plain-text record.

[4]

(b)

A junior developer proposes that each probe pushes every reading to the central server the moment it is taken, using a separate secure request per reading. Explain why this is a poor design even though the total payload is small, and explain how placing an edge device in each vehicle changes the trade-off.

[4]

(c)

Construct a relational schema, in third normal form, for the part of the system that records vehicles, consignments, probes and excursion alerts. Show the tables with their primary keys, foreign keys and a sensible attribute for each, and state the relationship between consignments and alerts.

[5]

(d)

A second proposal is that each vehicle stores readings locally and uploads the whole day's file once, when it returns to the depot. Evaluate this proposal against the regulatory requirements, considering the alert deadline, the reliability of the evidence trail, and the cost of the system.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Each probe is sampled $\dfrac{10\times3600}{30}=1200$ times per day, so each vehicle produces $4\times1200=4800$ readings per day. (M1)(A1) At 7 bytes each, the fleet produces

$$4800\times7\times140\times300=1.4112\times10^{9}\text{ bytes}$$

per year, which is $\dfrac{1.4112\times10^9}{2^{30}}=1.31$ GiB. (A1) Stored as 80-byte text the same readings occupy

$$4800\times80\times140\times300\div 2^{30}=15.0\text{ GiB},$$

roughly eleven times as much. (A1)

(b) The aggregate payload is only $140\times\dfrac{7}{30}\approx33$ bytes per second, so bandwidth is not the objection. (A1) The objection is per-request cost: each reading would carry its own transport handshake and encryption overhead, so a 7-byte reading could easily be carried inside a request of 800 bytes or more, multiplying the traffic by a factor well over a hundred and adding a fresh handshake every 30 seconds on every vehicle. (M1)(A1) Mobile coverage in a refrigerated vehicle is intermittent, and a per-reading push has no way to buffer across a dropout, so readings would simply be lost when a vehicle passes through a tunnel. (A1) An edge device in the vehicle changes the trade-off decisively: it can buffer readings locally through a coverage gap, batch them into one request every few minutes, evaluate the excursion rule locally so that an alert can be raised within seconds even with no network at all, and forward only alerts plus batched history to the centre. (R1)

(c) Four tables are needed:

VEHICLE(vehicleID PK, registration, depotID FK, commissionedDate)

CONSIGNMENT(consignmentID PK, vehicleID FK, departedAt, returnedAt, productCode)

PROBE(probeID PK, vehicleID FK, positionLabel, calibratedOn)

EXCURSION_ALERT(alertID PK, probeID FK, consignmentID FK, raisedAt, peakTemperature, durationSeconds, acknowledgedBy)

(M1)(A1)(A1) The schema is in third normal form because every non-key attribute depends on the whole of its table's key and on nothing else: probe calibration belongs to the probe, not to the alert, and the depot belongs to the vehicle, not to the consignment. (A1) The relationship between consignments and alerts is one-to-many: one consignment may generate any number of alerts, including none, and each alert belongs to exactly one consignment. (A1)

(d) The depot-upload proposal is cheap and simple, and for the storage requirement alone it would be adequate: the files arrive intact once a day and the six-year archive is straightforward to keep. (A1) It fails the alert deadline outright. A reading taken at the start of a shift would not reach the centre for up to ten hours, against a requirement of 60 seconds, and a spoiled consignment would be delivered before anyone knew. (M1)(A1) It also weakens the evidence trail: a vehicle involved in an accident, or one whose local storage fails, takes the whole day's record with it, and there is no independent copy against which a disputed reading could be checked. (A1) The correct evaluation is therefore that the proposal is acceptable only for the archive tier, not for the alerting tier. A hybrid is justified: the edge device raises alerts immediately over the mobile network, while the full-resolution history is batched opportunistically during the shift and reconciled at the depot. Alerts are small and time-critical; history is large and not. Splitting the two by their deadlines rather than by their size is the whole design. (R1) One further consideration belongs in any real design and is worth raising in an answer: the clock. Timestamps are generated on the vehicle, and if a vehicle's clock drifts then an alert can appear to precede the reading that caused it, which would undermine the evidence trail completely. Synchronising the edge device periodically and recording both the device time and the server receipt time on every alert removes that risk at negligible cost, and a candidate who spots it unprompted is thinking about the system rather than about the question.
questions.explanation: This item is built around a deliberate trap. Every number the student computes in (a) comes out small — 1.31 GiB a year is nothing — and the natural conclusion is that the system is easy. The constraint that actually binds is the 60-second deadline, which has nothing to do with volume, and the six-year evidence requirement, which means the data cannot be thrown away even though it is not needed in real time. The strongest candidates notice that the two requirements point in opposite directions: alerts must leave the vehicle immediately, history must not, and any design that treats them as one stream fails one requirement or the other. Part (b) reinforces the same lesson from the transmission side, where the overhead per request dwarfs the payload. Part (c) then tests whether the student can produce a schema in which metadata is stored once rather than repeated on every alert row, which is the practical consequence of normalisation rather than a definition to be recited. A candidate who finishes (d) by proposing a single tier has missed the point of the whole case study. It is worth marking this item with an eye on whether the candidate ever states which requirement is binding. The volume arithmetic is a decoy that most candidates will do correctly and then use to justify the wrong architecture, and the ones who compute 1.31 GiB and then say 'so the design barely matters' have walked into the trap. The alert deadline and the six-year retention rule are the only two constraints that shape the system, and they pull in opposite directions, which is exactly why the tiering answer in (d) exists rather than a single correct topology.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A2.4 Network security
questions.question:
You have been asked to redesign the protocol. Use the case study to answer all four parts.

(a)

Describe a replay attack against the current protocol. State exactly what the attacker captures, what they transmit, why the lock accepts it, and how long the attack remains available to them.

[4]

(b)

Construct a challenge-response protocol that prevents replay. Your answer must specify what the lock sends, what the phone computes, what the phone returns, and what the lock checks.

[5]

(c)

Explain how your protocol defeats the replay attack, and state clearly one attack it does not defeat. Quantify the probability that an attacker who has captured a million previous exchanges could still succeed by guessing.

[5]

(d)

Evaluate whether the additional cost of your protocol is acceptable for a battery-powered lock. Your answer must include a calculated comparison.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The attacker positions the receiver within range and captures one legitimate frame, which contains the literal text OPEN followed by the 32-bit secret $S$ in hexadecimal. (A1) Because the frame is not encrypted, the attacker reads $S$ directly from the captured bytes; because nothing in the frame varies, no computation is needed at all. (A1)

To unlock later, the attacker retransmits exactly the captured bytes. The lock compares them with its stored $S$, finds them identical, and releases the bolt. (A1)

The attack remains available indefinitely, or until $S$ is changed, because the accepted value never varies and there is no timestamp, counter or expiry. Capturing one frame grants permanent access. (A1)

(b) Protocol:

1. The phone sends a request frame containing HELLO and its device identifier. (A1)
2. The lock generates a fresh 64-bit random value $N$ (a nonce) using its hardware random source, stores it with a short expiry, and transmits CHALLENGE followed by $N$. (A1)(A1)
3. The phone computes $R = H(S \mathbin\| N)$, where $H$ is a keyed hash and $\|$ denotes concatenation, and returns RESPONSE followed by $R$. (A1)
4. The lock computes the same value from its stored $S$ and the $N$ it issued, compares with $R$ using a constant-time comparison, and releases the bolt only if they match and $N$ has not expired or been used before. (A1)

(c) The captured bytes are now useless because each exchange uses a different $N$. A response $R$ valid for one nonce produces a completely different hash for the next, and the phone never transmits $S$ itself, so the attacker who captures a million exchanges has a million $(N_i, R_i)$ pairs but no way to recover $S$ or to compute the response to a nonce they have not seen. (M1)(A1)

It does not defeat an active man-in-the-middle who relays a challenge to the genuine phone and returns the genuine response, because the protocol authenticates the phone to the lock but not the lock to the phone, and it does not defeat physical attacks on the lock or compromise of the phone itself. (A1)

If the attacker instead tries to guess the next nonce, the chance that a 64-bit value repeats one seen before, by the birthday bound after $10^{6}$ exchanges, is approximately (M1)

$$\frac{N^{2}}{2^{65}} = \frac{10^{12}}{3.69\times10^{19}} \approx 2.7\times10^{-8},$$

that is, about one chance in forty million. (A1)

(d) The additional cost is negligible and the protocol is clearly acceptable. (A1) The extra energy per operation is $0.90 - 0.15 = 0.75\ \mathrm{mJ}$ for the hash plus a second transmission of about $0.15\ \mathrm{mJ}$, so about $0.90\ \mathrm{mJ}$ in total. At 25 operations per day that is (M1)

$$0.90\times10^{-3} \times 25 \times 365 = 8.2\ \mathrm{J}\ \text{per year}.$$

The battery stores $2.4\ \mathrm{Ah} \times 3600\ \mathrm{s} \times 3.0\ \mathrm{V} = 25\,920\ \mathrm{J}$, so the extra drain is (A1)

$$\frac{8.2}{25\,920} \times 100\% \approx 0.032\%\ \text{of capacity per year}.$$

On latency, the protocol adds one round trip of $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ to the $250\ \mathrm{ms}$ budget, leaving $210\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the hash and the bolt mechanism against the $4\ \mathrm{ms}$ the hash actually needs. (A1) The conclusion is that the security improvement is effectively free, so there is no engineering justification for shipping the static-token version.
questions.explanation:
The instructive part of this question is that the secret is not weak. A 32-bit value has over four billion possibilities, and if the lock required the attacker to guess it, the attack would fail. The system is broken for a different reason: the same bits are accepted every single time. That makes the problem one of freshness rather than secrecy, and it is why no amount of lengthening the secret would help. A student who diagnoses the flaw as 'the secret is too short' has the wrong model and will propose a longer static token, which is exactly as vulnerable.

The fix follows from the diagnosis. If the value accepted must differ each time, then either the lock or the phone must contribute something new to every exchange, and the lock must be the one to do it, because a nonce chosen by the phone carries no freshness guarantee to the lock. Once the lock issues a random challenge, the phone's response can be a keyed hash over the secret and the challenge, which proves knowledge of $S$ without ever transmitting it. That last property matters more than it first appears: under the original protocol every transmission leaked the secret, so the system was one capture away from total compromise, whereas under the new one an attacker who records a million exchanges learns nothing reusable.

The evaluation in (d) is included because security questions in practice are decided on cost, and because the answer here is unusually clean. The extra energy is about three hundredths of one percent of the battery per year and the added latency is well inside the existing budget, so the secure protocol is effectively free. That removes the usual defence of a weak design, and a candidate who computes it has a much stronger argument than one who merely asserts that security is worth the cost. The part also asks what the protocol does not defeat, because a design that appears to solve everything is usually a design whose limits have not been thought about; here the absence of lock-to-phone authentication leaves a relay attack open, which is a real and documented vulnerability in systems of this kind.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.4 A recursive implementation of a linear recurrence whose call count is exactly twice the answer minus one, where memoisation changes the cost class and the recursion depth sets a separate, independent limit
questions.command_term: Determine, Show that, Determine, Explain, Justify
questions.question:
A service computes terms of a sequence defined by $F(1) = 1$, $F(2) = 1$ and $F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)$ for $n \ge 3$. The implementation currently in production is the following, in a language whose default recursion limit is $1000$ nested calls and whose interpreter executes about $1.0 \times 10^{7}$ function calls per second:
``
FUNCTION term(n)
IF n <= 2 THEN
RETURN 1
ELSE
RETURN term(n - 1) + term(n - 2)
END IF
END FUNCTION
`
A second implementation stores each computed value in a dictionary the first time it is needed and reads it thereafter, so that each index is evaluated once. A third implementation uses a loop and holds only the two most recent values.
Throughout, a *call* means one invocation of term`, including the invocation that answers the original request. The phrase *recursion depth* means the number of invocations that are simultaneously on the call stack at the deepest point of the computation.

(a)

Determine the number of calls made when term(6) is evaluated, by writing down the recurrence satisfied by the call count and evaluating it from the base cases upwards. State the recurrence you used.

[3]

(b)

Let $c(n)$ be the number of calls made in evaluating term(n), and let $F$ denote the sequence itself. Show that $c(n) = 2F(n) - 1$ satisfies the recurrence from part (a) together with its base cases, and hence determine the number of calls made when term(40) is evaluated. Estimate the time this takes at the stated execution rate.

[4]

(c)

The memoised implementation makes exactly $2n - 3$ calls for $n \ge 2$. Determine the number of calls it makes for $n = 40$, determine the factor by which this reduces the work against part (b), and determine the largest value of $n$ for which the unmemoised implementation finishes within one minute.

[3]

(d)

Explain why the memoised implementation still fails when asked for term(2000), even though it is efficient in the number of calls. State the depth of the call stack in each implementation as a function of $n$, and state which implementation is not subject to the failure and why.

[3]

(e)

The service must answer $1.0 \times 10^{4}$ requests per day for values of $n$ up to $1500$, each request arriving independently and needing one term. Justify, with quantitative reasoning, which of the three implementations should be deployed, and state one circumstance in which your recommendation would change.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Evaluating term(n) for n >= 3 invokes term(n - 1) and term(n - 2) as well as being an invocation itself, so the call count satisfies

$$c(n) = 1 + c(n-1) + c(n-2), \qquad c(1) = c(2) = 1 \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

the base cases holding because for n <= 2 the function returns immediately without recursing. Working upwards:

$c(3) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3$, $c(4) = 1 + 3 + 1 = 5$, $c(5) = 1 + 5 + 3 = 9$, $c(6) = 1 + 9 + 5 = 15$ (A1).

So term(6) makes 15 calls to compute the value 8.

(b) Substituting $c(n) = 2F(n) - 1$ into the recurrence, the left-hand side is $2F(n) - 1$ and the right-hand side is

$$1 + \bigl(2F(n-1) - 1\bigr) + \bigl(2F(n-2) - 1\bigr) = 2\bigl(F(n-1) + F(n-2)\bigr) - 1 = 2F(n) - 1 \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

using the definition of $F$ itself. For the base cases, $c(1) = 2(1) - 1 = 1$ and $c(2) = 2(1) - 1 = 1$, both correct (A1). Since a first-order recurrence in two variables with two base conditions has a unique solution, the closed form is established. With $F(40) = 102\,334\,155$,

$$c(40) = 2(102\,334\,155) - 1 = 204\,668\,309 \;\text{(A1)}$$

about $2.0 \times 10^{8}$ calls. At $1.0 \times 10^{7}$ calls per second that is roughly $20$ seconds for one term (A1) — and the cost grows by a factor of about $1.618$ for each increment of $n$, so each extra unit of $n$ adds about $62\%$ to the running time.

(c) For $n = 40$ the memoised version makes $2(40) - 3 = 77$ calls (A1). The reduction factor is

$$\frac{204\,668\,309}{77} \approx 2.66 \times 10^{6} \;\text{(A1)}$$

so roughly two and a half million times less work, taking a few microseconds rather than twenty seconds. For the unmemoised version, one minute allows $6.0 \times 10^{7}$ calls, which requires $2F(n) - 1 \le 6.0 \times 10^{7}$, that is $F(n) \le 3.0 \times 10^{7}$. Since $F(41) = 165\,580\,141$ and $F(42) = 267\,914\,296$ are respectively above and below $3.0 \times 10^{7}$ after dividing by two, checking directly: $c(42) = 535\,828\,591$ calls, which takes $54$ seconds, while $c(43) = 866\,988\,873$ takes $87$ seconds. The largest value computable within a minute is therefore $n = 42$ (A1).

(d) The memoised version is efficient in *calls* but not in *depth*. Each evaluation of term(n) proceeds by calling term(n - 1), which calls term(n - 2), and so on down to the base case, so the deepest point of the computation has about $n - 1$ invocations simultaneously on the stack (M1). Memoisation prevents repeated evaluation of a value; it does not shorten the chain, because the first evaluation of each index still descends the whole way to the base case before anything is stored. At $n = 2000$ the depth is about $1999$, well past the default limit of $1000$, so the interpreter raises a stack-overflow error before the answer is produced (A1). The unmemoised version has the same depth and the same problem, besides being astronomically slow. The iterative version keeps no chain at all: it holds two variables and updates them $n - 2$ times, so its stack use is constant and its depth does not depend on $n$ (A1). It is the only one of the three that is not subject to this failure.

(e) The iterative implementation should be deployed (A1). The reasoning: at $n = 1500$ the naive version needs about $2F(1500) - 1$ calls, and since $F(n) \approx \varphi^{n}/\sqrt{5}$ with $\varphi = 1.618$, $\log_{10} F(1500) \approx 1500 \times 0.2090 - 0.349 = 313$, so on the order of $10^{313}$ calls — beyond any conceivable hardware, and it would also breach the stack limit. The memoised version makes only $2(1500) - 3 = 2997$ calls, which is trivial, but at $n = 1500$ its depth is about $1499$, still beyond the default limit of $1000$, so it would fail at run time for the upper part of the requested range (M1). The iterative version uses about $1500$ loop steps and constant memory per request; at $1.0 \times 10^{4}$ requests per day that is $1.5 \times 10^{7}$ steps per day, a fraction of a second of processor time in total, and it has no stack exposure at all (A1). The recommendation would change if the language runtime guaranteed tail-call elimination or if the recursion limit were raised well above $1500$ — in that case the memoised version, or a plain iterative version with the same cost, would be equally acceptable and the choice could be made on readability alone (A1).
questions.explanation:
There is a pleasing sting in the tail of this one: the number of calls the naive recursion makes is exactly $2F(n) - 1$, which is to say that computing a value costs you about twice that value in calls. The cost is not merely proportional to the answer, it is a fixed multiple of it, and since the answer grows exponentially the cost does too. That identity is worth deriving rather than quoting, and part (b) is built to make candidates do it: substitute the closed form into the recurrence and the definition of $F$ falls out of the other side.

The point of part (c) is that asymptotics alone do not tell you what you can actually run. Two and a half million times less work sounds like an abstraction until it is translated into 'twenty seconds down to a few microseconds', and the one-minute question forces the candidate to sit with the boundary rather than classify the growth. Landing on $n = 42$ requires evaluating both $n = 42$ and $n = 43$ and comparing, and the two answers straddle the budget by a comfortable margin, so guessing is visible.

Part (d) is the real test, and it is the reason the item is claimed at difficulty 5 rather than 4. Having just fixed the exponential blow-up, the natural conclusion is that the problem is solved. It is not, because two different resources are being consumed and only one was measured. Memoisation reduces the number of calls to linear, but the depth of the call stack is set by how the recursion descends, not by how many times it repeats, and that depth is about $n$ in both recursive versions. At $n = 2000$ the fast version fails for exactly the same reason the slow version would have if it had ever got there.

The practical conclusion, in part (e), is that the iterative version is not a micro-optimisation but the only one of the three that is correct over the required range. It also happens to be the cheapest in absolute terms: about $1.5 \times 10^{7}$ loop steps per day is nothing. A candidate who recommends memoisation because it is 'efficient' has optimised one axis and shipped a program that raises an exception on the largest inputs requested.

The general lesson generalises well beyond Fibonacci. Whenever a recursive solution is replaced by a faster recursive solution, the question 'how deep does it go' remains open, and it is usually the one that bites in production, because it manifests as a crash at a specific input size rather than as a gradual slowdown that someone would notice in testing.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A4.3 A model whose reported accuracy of ninety-six per cent is an artefact of splitting a dataset of repeated hospital visits at the scan level rather than at the patient level
questions.question:
A hospital has assembled a dataset of $12\,000$ retinal scans taken from patients attending a diabetic screening clinic, labelled by whether the scan shows signs of the condition. The dataset covers $6\,400$ patients in total: $4\,800$ patients attended once, and the remaining $1\,600$ patients attended three times each, contributing $4\,800$ scans between them. Overall $25\%$ of scans are positive.
A team split the dataset at random by scan, using $80\%$ for training and $20\%$ for testing, trained a convolutional classifier, and reported the following results on the test set of $2\,400$ scans:
| split | true positives | false positives | false negatives | true negatives |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| random, by scan | $560$ | $60$ | $40$ | $1\,740$ |
| grouped, by patient | $360$ | $300$ | $240$ | $1\,500$ |
The second row was produced after a reviewer noticed the problem and repeated the evaluation with a split in which no patient appears on both sides. Both test sets contain $2\,400$ scans and both have the same prevalence of $25\%$ positive.
The hospital intends to use the model to decide which patients are recalled for further examination.

(a)

For the random split, calculate the accuracy, the precision, the recall and the F1 score, giving each to three significant figures. Show the calculation you used for the F1 score.

[3]

(b)

Repeat all four calculations for the grouped split, and determine the percentage by which the F1 score falls between the two.

[3]

(c)

Explain the mechanism by which grouping produces the discrepancy, and determine the expected number of scans in the test set that belong to a patient who also has at least one scan in the training set. State what fraction of the test set this represents.

[3]

(d)

The hospital's administrator notes that the grouped accuracy is still seventy-seven and a half per cent and asks whether the model is therefore useful. Evaluate this claim by comparing the grouped accuracy with the accuracy obtainable by a trivial classifier that predicts 'negative' for every scan, and by considering what the grouped precision and recall mean for a patient who is recalled unnecessarily or missed entirely.

[4]

(e)

Discuss what the team should report to the regulator, given that the ninety-six per cent figure has already appeared in an internal briefing, and state what change to the evaluation protocol should be made before any further claim is published.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) For the random split, with 560 true positives, 60 false positives, 40 false negatives and 1740 true negatives, and a test set of 2400 scans:

$$\text{accuracy} = \frac{560 + 1740}{2400} = \frac{2300}{2400} = 0.958 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$\text{precision} = \frac{560}{560 + 60} = \frac{560}{620} = 0.903 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$\text{recall} = \frac{560}{560 + 40} = \frac{560}{600} = 0.933 \;\text{(A1)}$$

The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall:

$$F_1 = \frac{2 \times 0.903 \times 0.933}{0.903 + 0.933} = \frac{1.686}{1.837} = 0.918 \;\text{(M1)}$$

So the random split reports 95.8 per cent accuracy with an F1 of 0.918.

(b) For the grouped split:

$$\text{accuracy} = \frac{360 + 1500}{2400} = \frac{1860}{2400} = 0.775 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$\text{precision} = \frac{360}{360 + 300} = \frac{360}{660} = 0.545, \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{360}{360 + 240} = \frac{360}{600} = 0.600 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$F_1 = \frac{2 \times 0.545 \times 0.600}{0.545 + 0.600} = \frac{0.655}{1.145} = 0.571 \;\text{(A1)}$$

The F1 score falls from $0.918$ to $0.571$, a fall of

$$\frac{0.918 - 0.571}{0.918} = 0.378 \;\text{(A1)}$$

that is, about 38 per cent of the reported performance was an artefact of the split.

(c) The rows of the dataset are not independent. A patient who attended three times contributes three scans that show the same eyes, taken close together, and almost certainly carry the same label. A random split by scan places some of those scans in training and some in test, so the model is evaluated on scans of patients it was trained on (M1). It can then score well by memorising a particular patient's retina rather than by detecting the condition, and the test set ceases to measure generalisation.

To quantify it, consider one of the $1\,600$ repeat patients with three scans. Each scan independently lands in the test set with probability $0.2$. The expected number of that patient's scans that land in test while at least one sibling lands in training is

$$1 \times \binom{3}{1}(0.2)(0.8)^2 \;+\; 2 \times \binom{3}{2}(0.2)^2(0.8) = 0.384 + 0.192 = 0.576 \;\text{(M1)}$$

the case of all three landing in test contributing nothing, since that patient is then absent from training. Over $1\,600$ such patients the expected number of compromised test scans is

$$1600 \times 0.576 = 922 \;\text{(A1)}$$

out of $2\,400$, which is $38\%$ of the test set. Roughly two in five of the scans the model was judged on belonged to a patient it had already seen.

(d) The administrator's figure is technically correct and clinically misleading. A classifier that always predicts 'negative' would be correct on the $75\%$ of scans that are negative, giving an accuracy of $0.750$ (M1). The grouped accuracy of $0.775$ beats that by $2.5$ percentage points, so in raw accuracy terms the model adds almost nothing over never diagnosing anybody (A1). The metrics that matter are the other two. Grouped recall of $0.600$ means that two in five patients who have the condition are told they do not — a missed diagnosis, which in a screening programme is the failure that costs sight (A1). Grouped precision of $0.545$ means that nearly half of all recalls are of patients who turn out to be clear: each one costs a clinic appointment, and each one also costs the trust of a patient who was told they might be losing their sight. Taken together, an F1 of $0.571$ on a condition with a quarter prevalence is not a deployable screening tool (A1); it is a model that needs substantially more work, and the honest reading is that the ninety-six per cent figure concealed a model that barely beats doing nothing.

(e) The regulator should be told the grouped figures, and told explicitly that the earlier figure was produced by a flawed protocol rather than by a different model (A1). Concretely: the model unchanged reports $0.958$ accuracy and $0.918$ F1 under the scan-level split and $0.775$ accuracy and $0.571$ F1 under the patient-level split, and the difference is entirely attributable to $38\%$ of the test set belonging to patients present in training. Withholding that because the briefing has already circulated would mean the deployment decision is taken on a number the team knows to be wrong, and in a clinical context that is not a presentational matter but a safety one (A1). Before any further claim is published, the evaluation protocol should be changed so that splitting is done by group — all scans from a patient go to exactly one side — and, ideally, so that the whole procedure is repeated by grouped cross-validation, giving a spread of scores rather than a single number, so that the sensitivity of the result to which patients landed where is visible (A1).
questions.explanation:
The technical term is leakage, but the useful way to think about it is that the test set stopped being a test set. Its whole job is to contain examples the model has never seen, so that performance on it estimates performance on new patients. Once a patient's scans are on both sides, that guarantee is gone, and the number produced is a measure of something else entirely — how well the model recognises a retina it has already been shown.

What makes this case nasty is that nothing looks wrong. The split is genuinely random. The metrics are computed correctly. The ninety-six per cent figure is a true statement about the test set. There is no bug to find, and the usual diagnostic instincts — check the split, check the arithmetic, check for overfitting — all come back clean, because the failure is in the assumption that rows are exchangeable, which is not written down anywhere in the pipeline. It is a property of how the data were collected, and it takes knowing that a fifth of the dataset is repeat visits to even suspect it.

The quantification in part (c) is worth doing carefully because it is the difference between 'leakage might be a problem' and 'two in five of your test scans are compromised'. Counting only the test scans whose patient also appears in training, rather than merely the patients who appear on both sides, is the right quantity: a patient with two scans in test and one in training contributes two compromised scans, not one. The all-three-in-test case must be excluded, since that patient is not in training at all. That gives 922 of 2400, and 38 per cent is a number a reviewer can act on.

Part (d) is the part that matters clinically, and the baseline is what makes it bite. Accuracy on a dataset that is 75 per cent negative is a terrible metric, because predicting 'negative' forever scores 75 per cent. The model scores 77.5. Two and a half points above doing nothing is not a screening tool, and no amount of framing makes it one. Precision and recall tell the real story: four in ten true cases missed, and half of all recalls unnecessary. In a screening programme those are the two numbers that determine whether patients are harmed and whether the clinic drowns.

Finally, part (e) is not decoration. The ninety-six per cent figure has already been briefed, and the temptation is to publish the corrected number next to it without saying why it changed. In a regulated clinical setting that is not a presentational choice: a deployment decision taken on a number the team knows to be wrong is a safety failure, and the correction has to be explicit about the cause.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.3 Programming constructs
questions.question:
The readings are stored as a list of integers, one per second. The nightly analysis must finish in a few seconds on the device, and it must report the run lengths exactly.

(a)

Explain, by tracing the loop, what steady_runs returns for the readings [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with the default tolerance of 5.

[3]

(b)

Explain why the developer's claim that the function runs in linear time is unsound. State the property of the input that the claim assumes, and describe the input pattern on which the function performs the greatest number of steps.

[4]

(c)

Construct a Python function that returns exactly the same result as steady_runs but runs in linear time. You may not import any module and you may not use the abs function. A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm, so write the algorithm rather than a demonstration of syntax.

[5]

(d)

A colleague proposes to fix the performance by adding a limit inside the while loop so that it stops after at most 1,000 steps. Evaluate this proposal, using your answers to parts (b) and (c).

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Tracing the loop for readings = [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with tol = 5:

| i | readings[i] | comparisons in the while | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 70 | j = 0, loop does not run | 0 |
| 1 | 72 | $\lvert 72-70 \rvert = 2 \le 5 \rightarrow 1$ | 1 |
| 2 | 71 | $\lvert 71-72 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 71-70 \rvert = 1$ | 2 |
| 3 | 90 | $\lvert 90-71 \rvert = 19 > 5$ | 0 |
| 4 | 89 | $\lvert 89-90 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 89-71 \rvert = 18 > 5$ | 1 |
| 5 | 88 | $1$, then $2$, then $\lvert 88-71 \rvert = 17 > 5$ | 2 |
| 6 | 87 | $1$, then $2$, then $3$, then $\lvert 87-71 \rvert = 16 > 5$ | 3 |

The function returns [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3]. (M1) for tracing the loop as a walk backwards while consecutive differences stay within the tolerance, (A1) for the correct values, (A1) for the list as a whole, including the reset to 0 at index 3 and the growing run at the end.

(b) The claim is unsound because the number of steps the inner loop performs is not a constant — it is the length of the steady run, which is a property of the *data*, not of the code. (M1) The claim assumes that consecutive readings almost always differ by more than the tolerance, so that the loop exits after one or two steps. (A1) That assumption is false for this application: heart rate sampled once a second during steady exercise changes by far less than 5 beats per minute between consecutive samples, so long runs are the normal case and the loop walks back a long way. (A1) The greatest number of steps occurs when every consecutive difference is within tolerance — a constant series, or a slow monotonic drift. For each $i$ the loop then runs all the way back to index 0, giving $0+1+2+\dots+(n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ steps, which is quadratic rather than linear. (A1)

(c)

def steady_runs(readings, tol=5):
    n = len(readings)
    runs = [0] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        step = readings[i] - readings[i - 1]
        if -tol <= step <= tol:
            runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1
    return runs

(M1) for a single pass that keeps no inner loop. (A1) for the observation that makes it work: the steady run ending at i is either empty or it is the run ending at i - 1 extended by exactly one reading, so the answer for i can be read off the answer for i - 1. (A1) for runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1 and (A1) for initialising every entry to 0, which is what makes the run reset after a step larger than the tolerance. (A1) for using no library module and no abs, expressing the tolerance as the two-sided test -tol <= step <= tol.

The work done is $n-1$ comparisons and one assignment per reading, so the time is $O(n)$ and the extra memory is $O(n)$ for the output. A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm; the translation is a for loop over the array indices and the identical recurrence, so the language is irrelevant to the reasoning.

(d) The proposal should be rejected, for three reasons.

First, it does not change the complexity. The inner loop can still run up to 1,000 steps for every reading, so the worst case is still proportional to $1000n$; capping the loop divides the running time by a constant, and a constant factor is not a change of order. (M1) With 86,400 readings a day the uncapped worst case is $86{,}400 \times 86{,}399 / 2 = 3{,}732{,}436{,}800$ inner steps, the capped version still performs up to $86{,}400 \times 1000 = 86{,}400{,}000$, and the linear version performs 86,399. (A1)

Second, and more seriously, the cap makes the result *wrong* precisely where the app matters. A steady run of 1,500 readings would be reported as 1,000, and a run of 4,000 as 1,000; the error is silent, it is always an under-report, and it is concentrated on the longest runs — which are exactly the steady states the app exists to find. (A1)

Third, the trade is unnecessary, because part (c) already gives an exact linear algorithm. Capping the loop trades a correctness guarantee for a constant factor when a change of order was available at the same cost. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question is built around a claim that is easy to believe and easy to falsify: "the inner loop breaks almost immediately, so the function is linear". The claim is not about the code at all; it is about the input. A complexity statement is a statement about *all* inputs, and one input family is enough to destroy it. The family here is a steady recording, and the irony is that steady recordings are exactly what the app is designed to detect. The algorithm is slowest on the data it exists to find.

The mechanism is worth stating in general terms because it recurs everywhere. When a loop's work per iteration depends on the data, the total work is the sum of those per-iteration amounts, and the average tells you nothing about the maximum. Here the per-iteration amount is the run length; if run lengths are bounded by a small constant the total is linear, and if a single run can be as long as the input the total is quadratic. The programmer's sentence — "in a real recording that happens after a step or two" — is the unstated assumption, and it is the whole question. Students are used to reasoning about the *average* case implicitly and calling it the complexity; this item forces them to notice that they have done so.

Part (c) is where the algorithmic insight has to appear. The nested loop is recomputing something that is already known: the run ending at i is the run ending at i - 1, plus one, whenever the last step is small enough. Recognising that the answer for one input can be read off the answer for the previous one — dynamic programming in its smallest form — turns the quadratic scan into a single pass. The two-line recurrence is easy to write once the observation is made, and almost impossible to reach by optimising the loop.

The classic wrong turns are all present. Measuring on one typical recording and concluding "it is fast"; fixing the performance by adding a break or a cap, which corrupts the longest runs; assuming that abs() or function-call overhead is the bottleneck; and confusing the *amortised* case with the worst case. A further subtlety is worth noting for the strongest answers: the linear algorithm is correct only because the run is defined by *consecutive* differences. If the definition were "all earlier readings within the tolerance of the current reading", a running counter would be wrong, and the fix would be a different data structure. The recurrence is not a trick; it depends on the definition, and saying so is part of understanding why it works.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only)
questions.question:
The finance team has asked you to review the pricing code before the catalogue is extended. The reconciliation compares each customer's stored annual_fee with the invoice total.

(a)

Explain what annual_fee holds for SeatPlan(20, 12) and why it is not equal to monthly_fee() * months. Refer to the order in which the statements in SeatPlan.__init__ and Plan.__init__ run.

[3]

(b)

Construct a corrected design in which the annual fee is always computed from the plan's own seat count and no constructor reads a field of an object that is not yet fully initialised. Use composition: a plan must hold a separate pricing object rather than inherit its price. Write the classes and state the annual fee for 20 seats over 12 months.

[5]

(c)

Calculate the annual fee that every SeatPlan caches, the fee that a 20-seat 12-month plan should be charged, and the total annual shortfall across all 900 customers. State how many of those customers are billed incorrectly.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate the two ways of removing the bug - patching the inheritance hierarchy so the field is set before the superclass constructor runs, or replacing the hierarchy with composition - and recommend one for a catalogue that will soon combine seats, usage and region.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) For SeatPlan(20, 12) the attribute annual_fee holds 108. (A1) It is not 2160 because of the order in which the two constructors run. The first statement of SeatPlan.__init__ is super().__init__(months), and inside Plan.__init__ the assignment self.annual_fee = self.monthly_fee() * months calls self.monthly_fee(). (M1) Because monthly_fee is overridden, that call dispatches to SeatPlan.monthly_fee, which reads self.seats. At that moment the instance has only months in its attribute dictionary - the statement self.seats = seats has not run yet - so the lookup falls back to the class attribute seats = 1. The fee is therefore computed for a one-seat plan: $1 \times 9 = 9$ per month and $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year. (A1) Only after the superclass constructor returns is the instance attribute set to 20, and by then annual_fee has already been stored and is never recomputed; a later call to monthly_fee() correctly returns $20 \times 9 = 180$, so the live query and the cached value disagree.

(b) The defect is not that a constructor calls a method. It is that a constructor calls a method on an object that is only partly built, so the method can observe a field that does not exist yet. Composition removes the half-built object by making the pricing rule a separate, fully constructed collaborator:

class SeatPricing:
    PER_SEAT = 9
    def __init__(self, seats):
        self.seats = seats
    def monthly_fee(self):
        return self.seats * self.PER_SEAT

class Plan:
def __init__(self, months, pricing):
self.months = months
self.pricing = pricing
self.annual_fee = pricing.monthly_fee() * months

p = Plan(12, SeatPricing(20))
print(p.annual_fee) # 2160
```

(M1) for giving Plan a pricing collaborator instead of a subclass that overrides a price method. (A1) for constructing that collaborator completely before the plan uses it, so no method ever reads a field that has not been set. (A1) for computing the annual fee from the collaborator's result. (A1) for the correct value, $180 \times 12 = 2160$. (A1) for noting that Plan.__init__ still calls a method, but on a different object that is already finished, which is why the same line is now safe.

Two inheritance-preserving fixes also work and are acceptable. Assigning the subclass field before the superclass constructor runs:

class SeatPlan(Plan):
    def __init__(self, seats, months):
        self.seats = seats        # set first
        super().__init__(months)  # monthly_fee() now sees 20

and passing the already-computed fee up to the base constructor, so the base never calls an overridable method at all:

class Plan:
    def __init__(self, months, monthly_fee):
        self.months = months
        self.annual_fee = monthly_fee * months

All three produce annual_fee == 2160. (A1)

(c) During construction self.seats always falls back to the class attribute 1, so every SeatPlan caches $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year, whatever its seat count. (M1) At an average of 20 seats the correct fee is $20 \times 9 = 180$ per month, which is $180 \times 12 = 2160$ per year. (A1) The undercharge is therefore $2160 - 108 = 2052$ per customer per year. (A1) Across 900 customers the shortfall is $900 \times 2052 = 1{,}846{,}800$, and all 900 are billed incorrectly: a customer is billed correctly only if it happens to have exactly one seat, which the 20-seat average rules out. The cached fee is one twentieth of the true fee at 20 seats, which is why 108 looks like a plausible annual price for a small team rather than an obvious error. (A1)

(d) Both remedies remove the bug, so the choice is about the next change rather than this one. Patching the hierarchy - assign seats before super().__init__, or pass the fee up - is a one- or two-line change with no runtime cost, but it leaves the base constructor calling an overridable method, so the trap stays armed for the next subclass whose fields are set after super(). (M1) The composition design removes the trap: Plan depends on a SeatPricing object, so a subclass cannot observe an unset field. Its cost is one small object per plan - 900 SeatPricing objects of 48 bytes each, about 309,600 bytes once their instance dictionaries are counted, or roughly 0.31 MB - against a shortfall of 1,846,800. (A1) That is a ratio of about six to one between the money and the memory, so the memory argument is irrelevant at this scale. (A1) The decisive argument is growth: the catalogue will combine seats, usage and region, and inheritance multiplies subclasses (three independent pricing features give up to $2^3 = 8$ subclasses, and each new feature doubles that), while composition adds one collaborator per feature. Recommend adopting composition for the extended catalogue. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question hides a value error inside a language feature that students are taught to admire. Polymorphism is presented as the way a subclass customises behaviour; here it is the mechanism that makes the bug invisible. When Plan.__init__ evaluates self.monthly_fee(), the method that runs belongs to SeatPlan, but the object it runs on is only half built. The field the method needs, seats, does not exist yet, and Python's attribute lookup silently supplies the class attribute instead of raising an error. Nothing crashes, no warning is printed, and the object afterwards looks completely correct: p.seats is 20 and p.monthly_fee() is 180. Only p.annual_fee is wrong, and only for plans whose seat count is not 1.

That last detail is what makes the bug survive testing. The author's tests are not careless - they check that seats are recorded and that the monthly fee scales - but each one either calls the method on demand or uses the single-seat case that the class default happens to match. The failing field is the one computed once, early, and then trusted forever. This is the general shape of a constructor bug: a value is computed at the worst possible moment, cached, and never recomputed, so the error is frozen into the object while every live query returns the truth.

The classic wrong turns are worth naming. The first is to look for the fault in monthly_fee, which is correct. The second is to treat the class attribute seats = 1 as a harmless default and conclude that the value is overwritten before use; it is overwritten, but not before monthly_fee reads it. The third is to fix the symptom by recomputing annual_fee after construction, which hides this instance of the bug while leaving the base constructor's virtual call in place for the next subclass. The fourth, and the most expensive, is to assume that because the object constructs without error the design is sound.

The design lesson is the fragile base class. A superclass that calls an overridable method from its constructor hands every future subclass a hidden ordering constraint that is documented nowhere and enforced by nothing. Composition removes the constraint because the collaborator is finished before it is used: the same line, pricing.monthly_fee() * months, is now safe, which is the point the last part tests. Composition is not free - it costs one object per plan - but at 900 plans the cost is a fraction of a megabyte against a shortfall of nearly two million, so the trade is not close. The remaining judgement is about growth: with three independent pricing dimensions inheritance would need up to eight subclasses, and each new dimension would double that.

questions.question:
Evaluate whether the load factor is a reliable predictor of the cost of a lookup in this table. Work in probes, where one probe examines one bucket. Assume the eight keys are inserted in increasing order, that no key is ever deleted, and that the table is empty before the first insert.

(a)

Calculate the bucket index that each of the eight keys hashes to when m = 16, and state the number of probes needed to insert each of those keys.

[3]

(b)

Determine the load factor of the table at m = 16 and at m = 17, and determine how many of the m buckets each table can ever reach with these eight keys. Give both reachable shares as percentages to two decimal places.

[5]

(c)

Determine the number of probes needed to look up the key 128, and the number needed to establish that the key 144 is absent, in each of the m = 16 and m = 17 tables. Explain why the two load factors do not predict the difference you find.

[4]

(d)

Your colleague proposes doubling the table from m = 16 to m = 32. Determine the load factor and the reachable-bucket share at m = 32, and justify whether the proposal addresses the problem you identified in part (c).

[4]
questions.answer:
Part (a). Every key is a multiple of 16, because 16 = 16 x 1, 32 = 16 x 2 and so on up to 128 = 16 x 8. So for every one of the eight keys k mod 16 = 0. (M1) All eight keys hash to bucket 0. (A1)

Linear probing then places them in consecutive buckets starting at 0: the first key finds bucket 0 free and takes it, the second finds it occupied and takes bucket 1, and so on. The probes needed are therefore 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, and the total for the eight inserts is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 36. (A1)

The finished table holds 16 in bucket 0, 32 in bucket 1, 48 in bucket 2, and so on up to 128 in bucket 7. Buckets 8 to 15 are empty.

Part (b). At m = 16 the table holds 8 keys in 16 buckets, so the load factor is 8 / 16 = 0.50. (M1)(A1) At m = 17 it is 8 / 17 = 0.470588..., which is 0.47 to two decimal places. (A1)

The reachable share is a different quantity. At m = 16 only bucket 0 is ever reached, so 1 of the 16 buckets is in play: 1 / 16 = 6.25%. (M1)(A1)

At m = 17 the keys hash to 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10 and 9 — eight distinct buckets, because 17 shares no factor with the key step of 16, so each successive key lands in the bucket before the previous one. So 8 of the 17 buckets are reachable: 8 / 17 = 47.06%. (A1)

It is worth noticing that at m = 17 the reachable share and the load factor are the same number, 47.06%, because every key occupies a bucket of its own. That coincidence does not hold at m = 16, where the two quantities are 0.50 and 0.0625 — a factor of eight apart. The two quantities are equal only when no two keys collide, which is exactly the case in which there is nothing to predict.

Part (c). At m = 16 the key 128 was the eighth key inserted, so it sits at the end of a run of eight occupied buckets that begins at bucket 0. A successful search for 128 examines buckets 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7: eight probes. (M1)(A1)

The key 144 is also 0 mod 16, so it too begins at bucket 0. It must examine all eight occupied buckets and then bucket 8, which is empty, before it can conclude that the key is absent: nine probes. (A1)

At m = 17, 128 mod 17 = 9 and bucket 9 holds 128 alone, so the successful search costs one probe. And 144 mod 17 = 8, and bucket 8 is empty, so the unsuccessful search also costs one probe. (M1)(A1)

The two load factors are 0.50 and 0.47, differing by 0.03, or about 6% of either value. Yet the successful search costs eight times as much in one table as in the other, and the unsuccessful search nine times as much. A quantity that differs by 6% cannot account for a cost that differs by 700%. The load factor describes how full the table is; what governs the cost here is how the keys *distribute*, and with a key step of 16 and a table size of 16 the distribution is degenerate — every key competes for one bucket. The load factor is a correct measure of a real property that happens not to be the property that decides this question.

Part (d). At m = 32 the keys 32, 64, 96 and 128 are all 0 mod 32, and 16, 48, 80 and 112 are all 16 mod 32. So the keys occupy exactly two buckets, 0 and 16, each holding four keys. (M1)(A1)

The load factor is 8 / 32 = 0.25, exactly half of 0.50. (A1) The reachable share is 2 / 32 = 1 / 16 = 6.25%, which is unchanged from m = 16. (A1)

So the proposal does reduce the worst-case successful search from eight probes to four, and the unsuccessful search from nine to five, because each run of colliding keys is now half as long. But it does not address the defect found in part (c). The table can still reach only one sixteenth of its buckets, and it has paid for that with twice as much memory. Doubling the table halves the *consequence* of the clustering while leaving its *cause* untouched, and the cause is that the table size shares a factor with the key step. Changing the size to 17 removes that shared factor; doubling it to 32 does not, and doubling it again to 64 would not either. The general rule is that the number of buckets a key set can reach is m divided by the greatest common divisor of m and the key step, capped by the number of keys — 1 at m = 16, 2 at m = 32, 8 at m = 17.
questions.explanation:
This item is built on a quantity that is correct, standard and useless for the question asked. The load factor is the first thing a prepared candidate computes when a hash table is described, and here it is genuinely informative about one thing — how full the table is — while being almost silent about the thing that matters, which is how long a lookup takes.

The trap is laid by making the two load factors nearly equal in the two tables whose costs are furthest apart. At m = 16 and m = 17 the load factors are 0.50 and 0.47, a difference of 0.03. A candidate who reasons "the load factors are almost the same, so the tables perform almost the same" has done the arithmetic correctly and drawn the wrong conclusion, and nothing in the arithmetic will warn them. The correct answer needs a second quantity — how many buckets the key set can reach — that is not in the standard vocabulary of load factor and probe length.

The reason the two diverge is structural. The keys are 16, 32, ..., 128, so every key is a multiple of 16, and the number of buckets a key set can reach is m divided by the greatest common divisor of m and the key step. At m = 16 that divisor is 16 and the table has one usable bucket; at m = 17 it is 1 and the table has eight, one per key. The load factor cannot see this because it counts keys and buckets, not residues.

Part (d) is where the item earns its label rather than merely stating it. Doubling the table halves the load factor and halves the worst-case probe count, so a candidate who trusted the load factor will find that it *worked* — and will conclude that the proposal is sound. It is not, because the reachable share does not move at all: 2 of 32 buckets is 6.25%, exactly what 1 of 16 was. The load factor improved, the probe length improved, and the underlying defect is untouched. A single measurement that moves in the right direction is not evidence that the cause has been addressed, and the second measurement — the one nobody thinks to take — is what shows it.

questions.question:
Evaluate the design of remove(node). Assume the list is never empty when remove is called, and that no other part of the program holds a reference to the node that is deleted.

(a)

Explain why remove(node) cannot delete node by changing the pointer that currently reaches it.

[4]

(b)

Describe the technique that remove(node) can use instead, stating what it must do to the node's data field and what it must do to its next field.

[4]

(c)

Determine which of the four nodes A, B, C and D a correctly written remove(node) can delete in a list of four nodes, and explain what goes wrong for the node it cannot delete.

[5]

(d)

State the single change to the node's structure that would make every node deletable in a constant number of steps, and state what that change costs.

[3]
questions.answer:
Part (a). In a singly linked list the only pointer that reaches node is the next pointer of the node before it. Deleting node means changing that predecessor's next pointer so that it skips over node and points at node.next. (M1)

The method receives a reference to node itself. From node there is no pointer backwards, so the predecessor cannot be reached from the argument. The only route to the predecessor is to start at head and walk forward until some node's next pointer is node — which costs a traversal of the whole list up to that point, and which would make the reference that was passed in pointless, since the same walk would have found the node by value. (A1)

So the method holds the object that must disappear, while the thing that must change is a field of a different object it has no way to name. (A1)(A1)

Part (b). The technique is to overwrite the node with its successor and then unlink the successor, in two assignments:

node.data = node.next.data
node.next = node.next.next

The first line copies the successor's reading into the node the caller is holding, so that node's value becomes the successor's value. (M1) The second line makes the node point past its successor, so the successor is no longer reachable from anywhere in the list. (A1) The caller's reference stays valid, the list is one node shorter, and the node that is actually released is the successor rather than the node the caller named. (A1)

It is worth being explicit that the *object* the caller holds survives while the *value* it was created with does not. Any other part of the program that kept a reference to the successor is now holding a node that is no longer in the list, and any part that looks for the deleted value will find it in the node it did not nominate. (A1)

Part (c). It works for A, B and C.

For A: A.data becomes B's reading and A.next becomes C, so the list reads (B) -> C -> D. For B: B.data becomes C's reading and B.next becomes D, giving A -> (C) -> D. For C: C.data becomes D's reading and C.next becomes D.next, which is None, giving A -> B -> (D). (M1)(A1)(A1)

It fails for D. D is the last node, so D.next is None, and the first assignment evaluates None.data. In Python that raises AttributeError; in a language without exceptions it would follow a null pointer and the program would be undefined from that point on. (A1)

So three of the four nodes can be deleted and the one that cannot is the one whose successor does not exist. (A1) The failure is not a corner case in the arithmetic sense — it is the ordinary case of deleting the last item, which any logger will reach as soon as it trims its oldest reading. Note also that in a circular list no node has next equal to None, so the technique would appear to work on all four nodes; for the last node it would overwrite the head's data, corrupting the list silently instead of failing loudly, which is worse.

Part (d). Give each node a second pointer to the node before it, making the list doubly linked. (M1) Then the node can be unlinked directly by joining its two neighbours to each other, which is a constant number of pointer assignments for every node including the last one. (A1)

The cost is one extra reference per node. Four nodes need four extra references, so the node structure doubles in size for a list that holds one reading per node. (A1)
questions.explanation:
This item takes a task that sounds routine — delete a node you have been handed — and makes it impossible as stated, for a reason that is invisible in the wording of the task. The candidate is given the object that must disappear; the object that must change is a different one. Nothing in the signature says so, and the failure only appears when the candidate tries to write the assignment.

The trap is that the natural implementation is not merely inefficient, it cannot be written at all. A candidate who has met linked lists will produce "find the node before this one and point it past this one", which is a correct description of deletion and cannot be executed with the argument supplied. The instruction that the method is given nothing else is doing the work: without it, the candidate can quietly assume head is available and never notice the problem.

The workable technique is genuinely surprising, and it is worth noticing how much it gives up. It does not delete the node the caller named; it deletes the node after it and then disguises the survivor. That means the identity of the node object is preserved while its contents are replaced, which is exactly backwards from what a caller expects, and it is the reason the technique is a trap in production code even though it is correct as an algorithm.

Part (c) turns the technique against itself. The trick works on three nodes of four and fails on the last, and the last is not a rare case — it is what happens the first time the logger trims its oldest reading. The failure is a null dereference, which in an exception-free language is silent corruption rather than an error. The circular list makes it worse rather than better: no node has a null next pointer, so the technique never raises, and instead overwrites the head's data. Part (d) is short by design — the answer is one pointer, and the item is testing whether the candidate can name the structural cause rather than patch the symptom.
