questions.question:
Evaluate the design of the class. Where a part asks what an object reports, state the value returned by the accessor named in the class diagram. Assume the three objects are created before any of them is hired.

(a)

State the value that getHireCount() reports for each of the three objects at the end of the day, and the value that getFleetSize() reports.

[3]

(b)

Determine the number of copies of each attribute that exist in memory once the three objects have been created, and explain how the underline in the class diagram tells you which attributes are shared.

[5]

(c)

Explain why an object diagram cannot show the difference between a static attribute and an instance attribute, and state which diagram can.

[4]

(d)

The designer proposes to make hireCount static as well, so that the class keeps a single running total. Determine the value getHireCount() would then report for each of the three objects, and justify whether the change improves the design.

[4]
questions.answer:
Part (a). hireCount is not underlined, so it is an instance attribute and each object has its own copy. getHireCount() reports 2 for B-01, 1 for B-02 and 0 for B-03. (M1)(A1)

fleetSize is underlined, so it is static and there is one copy for the whole class. getFleetSize() reports 3, and it reports 3 whichever of the three objects it is called on. (A1)

Part (b). There are three copies of id, three copies of hireCount and one copy of fleetSize, making seven attribute slots in total. (M1)(A1)(A1)

The general count is the number of objects multiplied by the number of instance attributes, plus the number of static attributes: 3 x 2 + 1 = 7. (A1)

The underline is UML's notation for a static member, which Java calls a class variable. A static member belongs to the class rather than to any object, so exactly one copy exists however many objects are created, and the memory is allocated when the class is loaded rather than when an object is constructed. An attribute with no underline is an instance attribute, and a fresh copy is allocated for every object. In the diagram, fleetSize and getFleetSize() are underlined and id, hireCount, Bike(id), hire() and getHireCount() are not. (A1)

Part (c). An object diagram is a snapshot: it shows the objects that exist at one moment, the links between them, and the current value of each attribute. Two objects that share a single storage location and two objects that each hold their own copy of the same value produce exactly the same object diagram — the diagram draws one box per object with one value in it either way. (M1)(A1)

Sharing is a property of the class definition rather than of any particular set of objects, so it cannot be read off a diagram of instances. (A1)

The class diagram is the diagram that shows it, and the static underline is how. (A1) A class diagram describes the shape every object will have; the underline says that one of those members will not be duplicated when the objects are made.

Part (d). A static hireCount is a single counter belonging to the class. Every hire increments that one slot, and the total number of hires is 2 + 1 + 0 = 3. So all three objects report 3. (M1)(A1)

The change does not improve the design, because it destroys the information the attribute was there to carry. Before the change, getHireCount() answered "how many times has this bike been hired"; afterwards it answers "how many times has any bike in the fleet been hired", and the three bikes are no longer distinguishable by usage at all. A maintenance scheduler that asked which bikes were used most would now receive the same answer for every bike. (A1)

The fleet total is a reasonable quantity to keep, so the proposal is not without merit — but it is a different quantity, and it belongs under a different name such as totalHires. Renaming the existing attribute instead would leave every call site compiling while silently changing what it means, which is the failure mode that is hardest to find later. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the one distinction in introductory object orientation that a diagram cannot show from the objects themselves. Static and instance members look identical once the objects exist: an object diagram of three bikes each holding a hireCount of 0 is the same picture whether the counter is duplicated or shared. The information that separates them lives in the class definition, and the item makes the candidate say where.

The numeric trap is small and precise. A candidate who misses the underline will report that all three objects share a single hireCount, and the total of hires is 3, so they will answer 3, 3, 3 — which is exactly the right answer to part (d). The same wrong reading of the diagram produces the correct answer to the wrong question, and there is nothing in part (a) that flags it. Part (d) then asks the candidate to evaluate that arrangement deliberately, which means a candidate who was already answering 3, 3, 3 must now notice that they never made a decision at all.

Part (b) rewards a habit rather than a fact. Counting copies of each attribute, rather than values, is the operation that makes the static distinction visible, and it is the operation most candidates do not perform unless asked. The general form — objects times instance attributes, plus static attributes — is what turns a count into an understanding.

Part (d) is where the item is hardest, because the proposal is defensible and the candidate has to say why it is nonetheless wrong. A single running total is a real and useful quantity; what makes the change wrong is that it silently redefines an attribute that callers already use, so the design gets worse while the code keeps compiling. Naming the distinction — a new attribute under a new name, rather than a changed meaning under the old one — is the answer the item is looking for, and it is a judgement about design rather than a calculation.

questions.question:
Trace the function for each of three files and decide what the caller receives in each case. The three files are a well-formed file containing the single line 250, a malformed file whose first line is 25 0, and a path that does not exist. Assume no other code changes the value of handle.

(a)

State the value that read_reading returns for the well-formed file, and the value it returns for the malformed file.

[3]

(b)

Determine the value the caller receives for the path that does not exist. State the order in which the regions of the function execute, and state the value the OSError handler computes before the finally region runs.

[5]

(c)

Explain why the finally region changes the outcome on that path but leaves the outcome on the other two paths unchanged.

[4]

(d)

Describe two changes to the function that would make the caller receive -2 when the path does not exist, and justify which of the two you prefer.

[4]
questions.answer:
Part (a). For the well-formed file the line reads 250, int("250") is 250, and the function returns 250. (M1)(A1)

For the malformed file, int("25 0") is not a valid integer literal and raises ValueError. The ValueError handler runs, prints "bad value" and returns -1. The finally region then closes a handle that is a real file object, so the close succeeds and the caller receives -1. (A1)

Part (b). The regions execute in this order. First handle = None runs. Then the try region begins and handle = open(path) raises FileNotFoundError, so handle is never reassigned. Because FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, the OSError handler runs: it prints "cannot open" and computes the value -2. Before that value can be returned, the finally region runs handle.close(). (M1)(A1)(A1)

handle is still None, because the assignment that would have replaced it was the statement that raised. So the finally region calls None.close(), which raises AttributeError. (M1)

An exception raised inside a finally region discards the return value that was in flight. The AttributeError therefore propagates to the caller and the -2 is never delivered. The caller receives an AttributeError, not -2. (A1)

Two details are worth recording. The function still prints "cannot open" before it fails, so a log file suggests that the missing file was handled and reported, which is the opposite of what happened. And the value the handler computed, -2, is discarded rather than converted, so there is no trace of it anywhere after the call.

Part (c). On the success path, handle = open(path) completed before the read, so handle is a real file object and close() succeeds. The return value 250 stands. (M1)(A1)

On the ValueError path, open(path) also completed. The failure was in converting the line that was read, not in opening the file, so handle is again a real file object and close() succeeds. The return value -1 stands. (A1)

Only on the OSError path did the assignment fail to complete, leaving handle at its initial value of None. The finally region is therefore harmless on two paths out of three and fatal on the third, and the source line that performs the cleanup is identical in all three cases — there is nothing at that line to suggest which path the program is on. (A1)

Part (d). First change: guard the cleanup so that it does nothing when there is no handle to close, as in if handle is not None: handle.close(). (M1)

Second change: let the language manage the handle, using a context manager, as in with open(path) as handle: return int(handle.readline()), with the except regions kept around the with statement. The initial assignment of None is then not needed at all. (A1)

I prefer the second. The guard fixes this instance but leaves the pattern in place: the next resource the function acquires will need its own None check, and one that is forgotten fails in exactly the same way, silently and on a path that is rarely exercised. The context manager ties the cleanup to the resource itself, so it cannot be forgotten and cannot be reached with an unassigned handle. Its cost is that the try region has to be restructured, which is a real cost if the surrounding house style forbids the with statement, and in that case the guard is the correct minimal change. (A1)
questions.explanation:
This item turns on the fact that finally is not merely housekeeping. It is taught as the region that always runs, which is true, and the natural inference — that it therefore cannot change what the function does — is false. A region that always runs is exactly the region whose failure is guaranteed to matter, because it sits between every computed return value and the caller.

The trap is that the code is idiomatic. Initialising handle to None, opening inside the try, returning from the handler, and closing in finally is a shape candidates are taught to write, and it is correct on the two paths a student is most likely to test. The success path works. The malformed-file path works, and it is the more interesting of the two, because the file *did* open — the failure came later — so the close is legitimate. Only the third path, where the open itself fails, leaves handle unassigned, and that is the path a student is least likely to construct.

The item therefore rewards tracing rather than pattern-matching. A candidate who recognises the idiom and reports what it usually does will answer -2 and be wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with exceptions in the abstract: the answer turns on which of three paths leaves a variable unassigned.

There is a second layer that makes the failure hard to notice in practice, and it is why the item asks for the order of execution. The handler prints "cannot open" before it computes -2, and the print succeeds. So the program produces a diagnostic that says the missing file was handled, and then fails anyway. A developer reading the log sees the expected message and concludes the branch was exercised correctly. The value -2 is discarded without a trace, which is the worst combination: a misleading success message followed by an unrelated-looking error.

Part (d) asks for a repair rather than a diagnosis, and the two repairs are not equivalent. The guard is correct and local; the context manager removes the class of defect. Preferring the second is a judgement about which kind of fix a codebase wants, and the item accepts either answer provided the candidate says what the chosen fix does and does not prevent. Catching AttributeError is the answer that must be refused: it makes the symptom disappear while the caller still receives the wrong value.

questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only)
questions.question:
Evaluate the two relationships as a basis for the purchasing decision. Assume every room needs a projector, that a projector failure is equally likely to strike any of the projectors that have been bought, and that a room with no working projector cannot be used.

(a)

Calculate the capital cost of the projector fleet under each relationship, and state the saving that aggregation offers as a percentage of the composition cost.

[4]

(b)

Determine the expected number of rooms that become unusable when one projector fails, under each relationship, and express the aggregation figure as a percentage change from the composition figure.

[5]

(c)

Explain why the two relationships give different answers in part (b) even though both use the same projectors at the same price.

[4]

(d)

Justify which relationship you would choose if the rooms must remain usable, and state what the choice costs in capital.

[3]
questions.answer:
Part (a). Under composition each of the 8 rooms owns its own projector, so 8 units are bought: 8 x 2 400 = 19 200. (M1)(A1)

Under aggregation 5 units are bought: 5 x 2 400 = 12 000. (A1)

The saving is 19 200 - 12 000 = 7 200, which as a fraction of the composition cost is 7 200 / 19 200 = 0.375, or 37.5%. (A1)

Equivalently, aggregation buys 5 / 8 = 62.5% of the projectors, so it saves the remaining 37.5%.

Part (b). Under composition there are 8 projectors and each serves exactly one room, so a failure takes out 1 room. (M1)(A1)

Under aggregation the five projectors serve 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 rooms. If a failure is equally likely to strike any of the five, the expected number of rooms lost is the mean of those five values: (2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1) / 5 = 8 / 5 = 1.6 rooms. (M1)(A1)

The change from 1.0 to 1.6 is an increase of (1.6 - 1.0) / 1.0 = 0.60, or 60%. (A1)

Part (c). The costs differ because the two relationships answer different questions about ownership. Composition binds one projector to one room, so the fleet must be as large as the room count. Aggregation lets one projector be referenced by several rooms at once, so the fleet only has to be large enough to cover every room rather than equal to the room count. The 8 rooms are covered by 5 units because three of the units are counted twice. (M1)(A1)

The exposure differs for the same reason read in the other direction. Under composition a projector is a part of exactly one room, so its failure is contained. Under aggregation a projector is a part of several rooms at once, so its failure is shared — and sharing is precisely what allowed the fleet to be smaller. (A1)

The two effects are not independent, and this is the point of the part. Every projector that aggregation removes from the fleet is a projector whose failure is now spread over two rooms instead of one. The 37.5% saving and the 60% increase in exposure are two descriptions of a single change: fewer failure domains, each covering more rooms. (A1)

Part (d). I would choose composition for rooms that must remain usable. (M1) It costs 19 200 rather than 12 000, an extra 7 200, and it buys the property that no single projector failure takes out more than one room. (A1)

The choice is worth stating as a rate rather than as a total. The extra 7 200 buys a reduction of 0.6 rooms of expected exposure per failure. With two failures a year, aggregation exposes 3.2 rooms a year against composition's 2.0, so the extra capital buys about 1.2 room-outages a year, which is 6 000 per outage avoided. (A1) Whether that is worth paying depends on what a room outage costs the company, which is the judgement the question asks for; the arithmetic is what makes the judgement answerable.

It is worth saying plainly what the choice does *not* buy. Composition does not remove projector failures, it only contains them: a failed projector still takes its room out of use until it is repaired or replaced. What composition buys is that the failure is not multiplied by the sharing, so the worst case a room can suffer is the failure of the one projector it owns. The purchase decision is therefore about how much the company is willing to pay to keep a single failure confined to a single room, and the two figures the item produces — 7 200 of capital and 0.6 rooms of expected exposure — are the two sides of that price.
questions.explanation:
Composition and aggregation are usually taught as a vocabulary question — which diamond is filled, which is hollow — and candidates learn to label the diagrams without learning what the labels cost. This item makes the two relationships produce opposite answers to two questions that sound like the same question, and it is the opposition that carries the difficulty.

The numeric trap is in the denominator of part (a). The saving is 7 200, and 7 200 expressed against the composition cost is 37.5%, while against the aggregation cost it is 60%. Both are correct arithmetic on the same numbers, and the question asks for the saving "as a percentage of the composition cost" precisely so that the wrong denominator produces a number that also appears later in the item — as the exposure figure in part (b). A candidate who mixes the denominators will find 60% twice and read that agreement as confirmation.

Part (b) is where the item is genuinely hard, because the quantity is an expectation over an unstated distribution. The candidate has to notice that the five projectors are not interchangeable: three of them carry two rooms and two carry one, so the expected number of rooms lost is the mean of 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 rather than the mean of 1 and 2 or the ratio 8/5 arrived at by a different route. The answer is the same as 8/5, which means a candidate who reaches 1.6 by an unprincipled shortcut gets the right number, and the markscheme has to look for the distribution rather than the value.

Part (c) is the conceptual centre. The saving and the exposure are not two facts about the design; they are one fact seen twice. Fewer projectors means each projector covers more rooms, and covering more rooms is exactly what makes a failure more damaging. A candidate who explains the two effects as separate consequences of ownership has understood the vocabulary but not the mechanism, and the markscheme separates the two answers.

Part (d) is deliberately short and deliberately open. The item does not have a preferred answer — composition is defensible because the rooms must stay usable, and aggregation is defensible if room outages are cheap. What the part tests is whether the candidate can put a price on the trade rather than restating one side of it.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only)
questions.question:
Evaluate the singleton as a home for the units field. Assume the 12 sessions overlap in time, that any of them may change the units at any moment, and that a session reads the units immediately before it formats a measurement.

(a)

State what a session reads when it asks the settings object for the units, if a different session changed the units a fraction of a second earlier.

[3]

(b)

Determine the number of session-and-change pairs in which a session observes a change it did not make, and express that number as a percentage of all session-and-change pairs.

[4]

(c)

Explain why the singleton is the right pattern for obtaining the settings but the wrong pattern for storing the units field, and state where a session's own units should be held instead.

[5]

(d)

A colleague proposes keeping the singleton and adding a sessionId attribute, so that setUnits can ignore changes made by other sessions. Justify whether that repairs the design.

[4]
questions.answer:
Part (a). The session reads the most recently written value, whichever session wrote it. There is one storage location, so the last write wins, and the session has no way to tell whether the value it received is the one it set. (M1)(A1)(A1)

Part (b). Each of the 34 changes is visible to every session except the one that made it, so each change produces 12 - 1 = 11 unintended observations. The number of such session-and-change pairs is therefore 34 x 11 = 374. (M1)(A1)

The total number of session-and-change pairs is 34 x 12 = 408. (A1)

So 374 / 408 = 0.91666..., which is 91.7% to one decimal place. (A1) The 34 pairs that are not unintended are the ones in which a session observes its own change.

Part (c). The singleton is the right pattern for obtaining the settings. The units are a property of the application rather than of a session, so the value has to be reachable from anywhere in the code; constructing a fresh Settings per session would give each session a different starting value; and a single access point means the configuration is loaded once rather than repeatedly. getInstance() supplies all three without exposing a global variable. (M1)(A1)(A1)

It is the wrong pattern for storing a mutable value that belongs to a session, because one storage location cannot hold two different values at the same moment. Two sessions that want different units are not in conflict about the object — they are in conflict about the field, and no care taken at the access point can resolve that. (A1)

The units a session is using belong to that session, so they should be held in an instance attribute of the session, or passed into the formatting call as a parameter. The singleton can still hold the default units, which is a value about the application rather than about any session. (A1)

Part (d). Adding sessionId does not repair the design. It lets setUnits refuse a write that came from another session, so a session's own writes are protected from being overwritten by its neighbours. (M1)(A1)

But the field is still a single storage location. The sessionId records whose value is currently stored; it does not let two sessions each have one. If session 1 sets the units to metres and session 2 then sets them to feet, the field holds one of those two values and the other session has lost its setting. Refusing the second write does not preserve session 1's value *for* session 2 — it merely prevents session 2 from setting anything at all, so the second session is now unable to choose its units rather than able to choose them independently. (A1)

The test to apply is whether two sessions can hold two different values at the same moment. A single field cannot, whatever guard is placed on the setter, because the guard changes who is allowed to write and not how many values exist. Repairing the design means one value per session, which means moving the field out of the singleton; the singleton can keep the default and the access point. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The singleton is the pattern most often taught as a recipe and least often taught with its limits, and this item separates the two uses that the recipe runs together. The pattern exists to guarantee that one object of a class exists and to give it a known access point. Neither of those guarantees says anything about whether the object's *fields* are safe to share, and the item is built on that gap.

The trap is that the code is a textbook singleton. A candidate who knows the pattern will recognise it, will see getInstance() implemented correctly with a private static instance and a static accessor, and will have no reason to suspect it. The defect is not in the implementation of the pattern but in what has been put inside the object, and nothing about the pattern's shape draws attention to it.

The counting in part (b) is designed so that the wrong model produces a plausible number. A candidate who counts each change once will report 34 unintended observations, which is the number of changes, not the number of sessions that saw them. A candidate who counts every pair will report 408. Only the model in which each change is seen by every session except its author gives 374, and 374/408 = 91.7% is the figure that makes the problem's scale visible: nine out of ten observations in this system are of a value the session did not choose.

Part (c) is the conceptual centre and it asks for a separation that the pattern's own name conceals. The same object can be the right home for a default and the wrong home for a session's setting, and a candidate who can say which is which has understood scope rather than syntax.

Part (d) is the hardest part because the proposed fix is thoughtful. Guarding the setter with a session identifier is exactly the kind of repair a competent engineer reaches for, and it does improve the behaviour: a session's writes are no longer clobbered by its neighbours. What it cannot do is change the number of values the field can hold, which is one. The item's test — can two sessions hold two different values at the same moment — is deliberately a question about storage rather than about permissions, because that is the distinction the fix obscures. A session that is forbidden to set its units has not been given its own units; it has been given the other session's units and told not to argue.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems
questions.question:
Using the case study, answer all four parts. The four cells are named C1 to C4 and the three resources are L (labelling arm), W (weighbridge) and D (dispatch chute).

(a)

Explain, with reference to each of the four conditions required for deadlock, why this system deadlocks. Your answer must name all four conditions and show that each is present.

[4]

(b)

Construct a resource-allocation scheme that makes deadlock impossible. State the rule, show that it removes at least one of the four conditions you identified, and explain what has to change in the control program of each cell.

[5]

(c)

Calculate the average throughput of the centre in parcels per hour given the current deadlock rate, and hence the percentage of capacity lost. Show your working.

[4]

(d)

An engineer proposes instead to leave the resource requests unchanged and to add a timeout: any cell waiting more than 20 s releases everything it holds, waits 5 s and starts the parcel again. Evaluate this proposal against your scheme in (b).

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) All four Coffman conditions hold.

*Mutual exclusion:* each of L, W and D can serve only one cell at a time, so the resources are non-sharable. (A1)

*Hold and wait:* a cell that has claimed the labelling arm keeps it while it waits for the weighbridge, so processes hold resources while requesting others. (A1)

*No pre-emption:* nothing in the system can take a resource away from a cell; the only way resources are released is by the cell finishing, which is exactly what it cannot do. (A1)

*Circular wait:* with four cells and three resources a cycle is easy to form, for example C1 holds L and wants W, C2 holds W and wants D, and C3 holds D and wants L. Because each cell requests resources in whatever order its stage is reached, and the stages differ between parcels, no ordering prevents that cycle from forming. (A1)

(b) Impose a global ordering on resource acquisition: assign each resource a fixed rank, say L = 1, W = 2, D = 3, and require every cell to request resources in strictly increasing rank order, never requesting a lower-ranked resource while holding a higher-ranked one. (M1)(A1)

This removes the circular-wait condition. (A1) A cycle would require each participant to hold a resource and wait for one of lower or equal rank; since ranks strictly increase along any wait chain, the chain cannot close. Formally, in any cycle the ranks would have to satisfy $r_1 < r_2 < \dots < r_k < r_1$, which is impossible. (A1)

The control program must change in two ways: each cell must determine the full set of resources its parcel will need before claiming any of them, and must then claim them in rank order. Where a parcel genuinely needs them in a different order, the cell must claim all three up front and hold them for the whole cycle, which reduces concurrency but is safe. (A1)

(c) Without deadlock the centre does $4 \times \dfrac{3600}{45} = 320$ parcels per hour. (A1)

In 40 cycles the four cells process $4 \times 40 = 160$ parcels, taking $40 \times 45 = 1800\ \mathrm{s}$. One deadlock adds a 6-minute ($360\ \mathrm{s}$) reset, so 160 parcels take $1800 + 360 = 2160\ \mathrm{s}$. (M1)(A1)

$$\text{throughput} = \frac{160}{2160} \times 3600 = 266.7 \approx 267\ \mathrm{parcels\,h^{-1}}$$ (A1)

$$\text{loss} = \frac{320 - 267}{320} \times 100\% = 16.7\%$$

(d) The timeout does not prevent deadlock; it detects and breaks it. (A1) That is better than an indefinite hang, but it is worse than prevention in three respects. First, every near-deadlock costs 20 s of waiting plus a 5 s backoff plus the wasted work already done on the parcel, so each event costs at least 25 s of cell time against 0 s under ordering. Second, if all four cells time out together and restart together they are likely to re-form the same cycle, an effect known as livelock, which the proposal does nothing to prevent since there is no randomised backoff. (A1) Third, the parcels are discarded either way, so the material loss is unchanged. (A1)

By contrast the ordering scheme in (b) eliminates the events entirely, at the cost of holding all three resources for some parcels and so losing some concurrency. A reasonable evaluation is therefore that the timeout is an acceptable safety net to keep in place, but it should not be the primary mechanism: prevention should be used first and detection second.
questions.explanation:
Deadlock is one of the few topics in the syllabus where the correct answer is a property of the whole system rather than of any single piece of code. No individual cell's control program is wrong: each one claims a resource, uses it, and later asks for another. The fault is the absence of a global rule, which is why the question asks for all four Coffman conditions explicitly. Naming them is not rote learning here; it is the diagnostic that tells you which one is cheapest to remove. Mutual exclusion cannot be removed, because a weighbridge genuinely cannot serve two parcels at once. Hold-and-wait can be, by claiming everything up front, but that costs concurrency. Circular wait is the cheapest to break, because imposing an order on requests costs nothing in throughput and requires only that the program decide its requirements in advance.

The quantification in (c) is there to make the cost concrete, and the result is larger than most students expect: one deadlock every forty cycles costs a sixth of the centre's output, because a six-minute reset is eight full cycles lost. That reframes the decision. A fix that costs a little concurrency on every cycle is clearly worth buying against a one-in-forty chance of losing eight cycles.

Part (d) is where the question discriminates. Adding a timeout feels like a fix and is not one: it converts a permanent hang into a recurring 25-second penalty and, because all four cells are running the same cycle time and will therefore tend to time out together, it risks livelock where the system makes no progress at all despite no process being blocked. The mature answer is that prevention and detection are complementary, and that the ordering scheme should be primary with the timeout retained as a backstop. Recognising that a mechanism which breaks a deadlock is not the same as one that prevents it is the transferable idea.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A4.4 Ethical considerations
questions.question:
Using the case study, answer all four parts.

(a)

Explain why the single figure of 82% overall precision is a misleading summary of this model's performance, and state which two quantities must be reported separately for the complaint to be assessed.

[4]

(b)

Construct the confusion matrix for each area and calculate, for each area separately, the precision, the recall, and the proportion of non-urgent requests that were wrongly flagged.

[5]

(c)

Discuss what the two sets of figures show, including anything they do not establish. Refer to the tenant's complaint in your answer.

[4]

(d)

Justify one action the authority should take, given that it cannot simultaneously maximise both precision and recall and that inspection capacity is fixed.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) An overall figure averages over a population in which the two areas contribute very unequally, 6 000 requests from the North against 2 000 from the South, so the aggregate is dominated by the area where the model performs better. (A1) It says nothing about how the errors are distributed, and it is the distribution that the complaint is about. (A1)

The two quantities that must be reported separately are precision and recall for each area, or equivalently the false-positive rate and the false-negative rate for each area, since precision and recall alone do not determine how many non-urgent requests are wrongly flagged. (A1)(A1)

(b) *North:* flagged 1 200, of which 1 080 urgent, so 120 are not urgent. There are 1 500 urgent in total, so $1500 - 1080 = 420$ urgent requests were missed. Non-urgent requests number $6000 - 1500 = 4500$, of which 120 were wrongly flagged. (M1)(A1)

| North | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 1 080 | 420 | 1 500 |
| not urgent | 120 | 4 380 | 4 500 |
| total | 1 200 | 4 800 | 6 000 |

*South:* flagged 500, of which 320 urgent, so 180 are not urgent. There are 400 urgent in total, so $400 - 320 = 80$ were missed. Non-urgent requests number $2000 - 400 = 1600$, of which 180 were wrongly flagged. (A1)

| South | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 320 | 80 | 400 |
| not urgent | 180 | 1 420 | 1 600 |
| total | 500 | 1 500 | 2 000 |

North: precision $= 1080/1200 = 90.0\%$, recall $= 1080/1500 = 72.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 120/4500 = 2.67\%$. (A1)
South: precision $= 320/500 = 64.0\%$, recall $= 320/400 = 80.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 180/1600 = 11.25\%$. (A1)

(c) The figures support the substance of the complaint. A non-urgent request in the South is (M1)
$$\frac{11.25}{2.67} \approx 4.2$$
times as likely to be flagged as one in the North, so South tenants are much more likely to be visited for a fault that turns out to be minor, which is the nuisance she describes. (A1) At the same time the model is not uniformly worse in the South: its recall there is higher, 80% against 72%, so an urgent request in the South is more likely to be caught. That is why her own roof waiting nine days is not necessarily explained by the area statistics and may be a single unfortunate case. (A1)

What the figures do not establish is why the difference exists. The areas differ in housing stock, so the base rate of urgency differs, 25% in the North against 20% in the South, and a model trained on pooled data with one threshold will not behave identically across groups with different base rates even if it is free of bias in its inputs. The data also cannot distinguish a model that is miscalibrated from one that is correctly calibrated but operating at an inappropriate threshold, and they say nothing about whether the features used are themselves proxies for something protected. (A1)

(d) A defensible action is to set the decision threshold separately for each area so that the false-positive rates are equalised, and to publish the resulting precision and recall for both areas. (A1) This directly addresses the complaint, which is about unequal burden rather than about overall accuracy, and it is achievable within fixed inspection capacity because lowering the threshold in the North and raising it in the South reallocates roughly the same number of visits. (A1)

It must be accompanied by a stated decision about which error the authority considers more serious. If a missed urgent repair is the greater harm, the threshold should be set to favour recall and the authority must accept more minor inspections in both areas; if unnecessary visits are the greater harm, the reverse. (A1) What is not defensible is to continue reporting only the aggregate figure, because that suppresses exactly the information needed to make the choice.
questions.explanation:
The central move in this question is to refuse the aggregate. The authority's 82 percent overall precision is arithmetically correct and almost useless, because it averages over two areas that contribute requests in a three-to-one ratio, so it largely describes the North. Disaggregating produces a genuinely uncomfortable result: the South has better recall but far worse precision, and a non-urgent request there is more than four times as likely to trigger a visit. That is precisely the experience the tenant describes, so her complaint is not anecdote against statistics; it is the statistics, correctly computed.

The question is deliberately constructed so that the easy conclusion is wrong. It would be natural to read the figures as showing that the model discriminates against the South, but recall there is in fact higher. What differs is the threshold's effect in a population with a different base rate of urgency: 25 percent in the North against 20 percent in the South. A single threshold applied to two groups with different base rates produces different error mixes even when the underlying model is equally good in both, which is why the data cannot by themselves tell you whether the model is miscalibrated or merely being used at the wrong operating point. Recognising that distinction is the difference between a technical fix and a political one.

The final part is unavoidable because precision and recall trade off against each other and inspection capacity is fixed, so no amount of modelling removes the choice. Someone has to decide whether a missed urgent repair or an unnecessary visit is the worse failure, and that decision is a judgement about harm rather than a result about accuracy. The only clearly indefensible position is the authority's current one, of reporting a single number that conceals the fact that the choice is being made and being made unevenly. A student who reaches that conclusion has understood why the ethical content of this topic is not an addendum to the technical material but a consequence of it.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A2.1 Network fundamentals: a stated model of a windowed connection, where the throughput is governed by bytes in flight per round trip rather than by the rated capacity of the link
questions.question:
A network engineer is asked to size a connection for a new service. Use the model given above to answer the questions that follow. Numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

(a)

For a loss probability of $p = 0.01$, calculate the average window in packets and the resulting throughput in Mbit/s.

[3]

(b)

The link is rated at 100 Mbit/s but the connection delivers the value found in part (a). Explain, referring to the two formulas, what it is that limits this connection, and why the rating does not appear in the answer.

[3]

(c)

A new service requires a sustained throughput of 20 Mbit/s on this connection with the same round-trip time. Determine the maximum packet loss probability the network can tolerate.

[4]

(d)

Two upgrades are proposed: route the traffic so that the round-trip time is halved, or improve the network so that the loss probability is halved. Determine the throughput produced by each and state which is the more effective.

[2]

(e)

An engineer proposes achieving the 20 Mbit/s requirement by using packets with four times the MSS, leaving $p = 0.01$ unchanged. Evaluate this proposal.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The window is $W = 1.22 / \\sqrt{0.01} = 1.22 / 0.1 = 12.2$ packets (M1), so about
twelve full segments are acknowledged per round trip. The throughput is

$$S = \frac{12.2 \times 1460 \times 8}{0.040} = 3.56 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{bit\,s^{-1}}
= 3.56\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}. \tag{A1}$$

A candidate who rounds the window to 12 packets first obtains $3.50\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$, which is
accepted (A1).

(b) The rating of 100 Mbit/s is the capacity of the wire; it never enters either formula, and
that is not an omission (M1). What the model allows onto the link is $W \times \mathrm{MSS}$
bytes once every round trip, so the achievable rate is set by how much can be in flight and
how long a round trip takes, not by how fast the wire could carry it. The link is idle for most
of every round trip: putting 12.2 segments on a $100\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$ wire takes
$\frac{12.2 \times 1460 \times 8}{100 \times 10^{6}} = 1.43\ \mathrm{ms}$, which is $3.6\%$ of the
$40\ \mathrm{ms}$ cycle, and the remaining $96.4\%$ is waiting for acknowledgements (A1). Losses set $W$ through $1.22/\sqrt{p}$, so it is the loss
probability and the round-trip time that govern the throughput; the wire rating only becomes the
limit once the window is large enough to fill it, which at $p = 0.01$ it is nowhere near
(R1).

(c) The relation must be run backwards: $p$ is the unknown, and it sits inside a square root in
the denominator (M1). From $S = W \times \mathrm{MSS} \times 8 / \mathrm{RTT}$,

$$W = \frac{S \times \mathrm{RTT}}{\mathrm{MSS} \times 8}
= \frac{20 \times 10^{6} \times 0.040}{1460 \times 8} = 68.5\ \mathrm{packets}. \tag{A1}$$

Then from $W = 1.22 / \sqrt{p}$, squaring is required and $\sqrt{p} = 1.22 / W$ (M1), so

$$p = \left(\frac{1.22 \times \mathrm{MSS} \times 8}{S \times \mathrm{RTT}}\right)^{2}
= \left(\frac{1.22}{68.5}\right)^{2} = 3.17 \times 10^{-4},$$

i.e. about one packet in 3150, or $0.032\%$ (A1). The common slip is to divide rather than
to square, giving $p = 1.22/68.5 = 0.0178$ --- a loss rate fifty-six times more forgiving than the
network can actually support, and one that would be reported as a comfortably achievable target.

(d) Halving the round-trip time doubles the throughput, because $\mathrm{RTT}$ appears to the
first power in the denominator: $S = 3.56 \times 2 = 7.12\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$; halving the loss
probability multiplies the window by $\sqrt{2}$, because $p$ appears under a square root:
$W = 1.22/\sqrt{0.005} = 17.3$ packets and $S = 5.04\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$ (M1). The routing change is
the more effective, by a factor of $7.12 / 5.04 = 1.41 = \sqrt{2}$, and the reason is in the
exponents: the model is linear in $1/\mathrm{RTT}$ and only proportional to $1/\sqrt{p}$ (A1).

(e) Substituting $4 \times \mathrm{MSS}$ gives $S = 4 \times 3.56 = 14.2\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$,
which the model does scale linearly with (M1) --- and even that is short of the 20
$\mathrm{Mbit/s}$ required, so the proposal cannot reach the target on the model's own terms
(A1). It also fails on the way there: a segment of $4 \times 1460 = 5840$ bytes does not fit an
Ethernet frame, whose MTU is 1500 bytes, so the data would be fragmented, and a fragment carries the
same loss exposure as a whole segment --- losing any fragment retransmits the datagram, so the
effective loss probability rises rather than staying at $0.01$ (A1). The MSS is not a free
variable to be traded against $p$; it is fixed by the link, which is exactly why the model treats
it as a constant.
questions.explanation:
The item is one misconception with two formulas attached to it. Students who have been taught
that a $100\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$ link delivers $100\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$ will compute part (a) correctly
and be dissatisfied with the answer, and part (b) exists to make them say why the number is small
rather than let it pass. The governing quantity is the product of the window and the segment size
divided by the round-trip time; the wire rating is a ceiling that this connection never approaches,
and the model says so plainly by not containing $100\ \mathrm{Mbit/s}$ anywhere.

Part (c) is where the difficulty actually sits. The formula has been used in one direction --- give
me $p$, I will tell you $S$ --- and the question asks the other way. The unknown is under a square
root in a denominator, so the inversion requires squaring at the end, and the reflex is to divide:
$1.22 / 68.5 = 0.0178$, which is a loss rate fifty-six times more permissive than the truth and
would be reported as a comfortable margin. Nothing in the arithmetic looks wrong; the number is a
small decimal, in the right order of magnitude to be plausible, and only the structure of the model
says it is not.

Part (d) rewards the same structural reading rather than the calculation. Both upgrades are
"factor of two" changes, and they are not equal, because $\mathrm{RTT}$ enters to the first power
and $p$ enters under a root: the ratio comes out at $\sqrt{2}$, and a candidate who has understood
the model can predict that before computing it. Part (e) closes the item on the kind of judgement
the papers increasingly ask for: the proposal produces the right number from the given model, and it
is still wrong, because the model treats as a free constant something the link fixes. Learning to
distract oneself with an algebra that is valid inside a model and void outside it is the transfer
this item is for.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1 Computer fundamentals
questions.question:
Two upgrade proposals are on the table. Both are advertised with a large number on the box, and neither number is the one the system will actually see.

(a)

Calculate the average number of clock cycles spent on memory per instruction, showing how each level of the hierarchy contributes.

[4]

(b)

A hardware accelerator can execute $40\%$ of the workload five times faster than the processor does now. Calculate the overall speedup of the system, and state the largest speedup that could ever be obtained by accelerating this same $40\%$, however fast the accelerator is made.

[4]

(c)

A second proposal is to raise the clock frequency by $25\%$. The memory chips are unchanged, so their latency stays the same number of nanoseconds and therefore becomes a larger number of clock cycles. Calculate the resulting average cycles per instruction and hence the real speedup, and explain why it falls so far short of $25\%$.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate which of the two proposals is the better use of the engineering budget, referring to your answers to (b) and (c) and to one further consideration that the numbers do not capture.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Work through the hierarchy from the fastest level outwards. An access hits in level 1 with probability $0.95$ and costs $1$ cycle. It misses level 1 with probability $0.05$; of those, $0.80$ are satisfied by level 2 at $12$ cycles and $0.20$ go to main memory at $200$ cycles. (M1)(A1)
$$\text{average cycles} = 0.95(1) + 0.05\bigl[0.80(12) + 0.20(200)\bigr]$$
$$= 0.95 + 0.05\bigl[9.6 + 40\bigr] = 0.95 + 0.05(49.6) = 0.95 + 2.48 = 3.43$$ (A1)(A1)
So the processor spends about $3.43$ clock cycles per instruction, of which only $0.95$ is the level-1 access itself. The tail dominates: level-2 hits add $0.48$ cycles in total, while main-memory accesses add $2.00$ cycles, so the $1\%$ of all accesses that miss in both caches accounts for $2.00$ of the $3.43$, which is more than half the average and more than twice what the level-1 hits contribute.

(b) Amdahl's law gives the speedup as (M1)
$$S = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \dfrac{f}{s}} = \frac{1}{0.60 + \dfrac{0.40}{5}} = \frac{1}{0.60 + 0.08} = \frac{1}{0.68} = 1.47$$ (A1)(A1)
The limiting case is $s \to \infty$, which gives $S_{\max} = 1/(1-0.40) = 1.67$. (A1) However fast the accelerator becomes, the remaining $60\%$ of the workload is untouched, so the system can never be more than $1.67$ times faster by this route.

(c) With the clock $25\%$ faster, a fixed nanosecond latency corresponds to $1.25$ times as many clock cycles, so the level-2 path becomes $12 \times 1.25 = 15$ cycles and the main-memory path becomes $200 \times 1.25 = 250$ cycles. (M1)
$$\text{average cycles} = 0.95(1) + 0.05\bigl[0.80(15) + 0.20(250)\bigr] = 0.95 + 0.05\bigl[12 + 50\bigr] = 0.95 + 3.10 = 4.05$$ (A1)
Execution time is cycles divided by frequency, so with the new frequency $1.25$ times the old one, (M1)
$$\frac{T_{\text{new}}}{T_{\text{old}}} = \frac{4.05/1.25}{3.43/1.00} = \frac{3.24}{3.43} = 0.945,\qquad \text{speedup} = 1.06$$ (A1)
The speedup is about $6\%$ rather than $25\%$ because the extra cycles are being spent waiting, and waiting does not get faster when the clock does. As the clock rises, the proportion of time spent stalled on memory grows, so the gap between the advertised figure and the delivered figure widens.

(d) The accelerator is the better buy on these numbers: $1.47$ against $1.06$, and the accelerator's figure is also closer to its own ceiling of $1.67$, whereas the clock increase delivers under a quarter of what its name promises. (A1)(A1) One thing the numbers do not capture is cost and risk: an accelerator is new hardware, new drivers and a new failure mode in a system that already works, while a clock change is a configuration setting. If the accelerator's development cost is more than a few times the cost of the clock change, the safer option may be worth its smaller return, and a decision that rests only on the two ratios above would be incomplete. (A1)

It is worth stating what the $3.43$ means before using it in later parts: it is an average over the whole instruction stream, so it already includes the instructions that hit in level 1 and cost almost nothing. Any proposal that changes the miss rates or the path latencies changes this average, and that is the only way an upgrade can help.
questions.explanation:
The point of this item is that the number printed on a component is almost never the number the system experiences, and that the gap between the two is calculable rather than mysterious. Part (a) sets up the arithmetic by showing where the cycles go: a $95\%$ hit rate sounds excellent, and it is, but $5\%$ of accesses still reach the next level and a fifth of those reach main memory, so $1\%$ of all accesses contributes $0.40$ of the $3.43$ cycles. That small tail dominates the average, and it is the first place a student should look when asked to make something faster.

Parts (b) and (c) then apply that observation to two proposals, and they fail in different ways. The accelerator fails because of Amdahl's law: only $40\%$ of the work can be moved, so the ceiling is $1.67$ no matter how good the hardware is, and a fivefold improvement on that fraction buys $1.47$. The clock increase fails for a different and more interesting reason. Raising the clock shortens the cycle, but the memory chips do not know about the clock, so their latency in nanoseconds is unchanged and their latency in cycles grows. The processor therefore spends a larger fraction of each instruction waiting, and the delivered speedup is $1.06$ against an advertised $1.25$. This is the mechanism behind the phrase 'the memory wall', and it is worth naming, because it explains why clock speeds stopped rising long before transistor counts did.

Part (d) is where the item stops being arithmetic. Both numbers are now on the table and the comparison looks decisive, but a real decision also involves risk, development cost, and whether the system can be taken offline. A candidate who says 'the accelerator, because $1.47 > 1.06$' has answered the question they were asked and missed the one that matters; the evaluation mark is reserved for someone who makes the comparison and then says what it leaves out.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2 Programming
questions.question:
The table appears to settle the matter. This question asks whether it does.

(a)

Determine the worst-case number of comparisons binary search makes for each value of $n$ in the table, showing how $\lfloor \log_{2} n \rfloor + 1$ gives the stated figures, and state the complexity class of each algorithm.

[3]

(b)

Using the cost model in the stimulus, calculate the worst-case time taken by each algorithm for each value of $n$ in the table. Hence determine the smallest value of $n$ for which binary search is the faster of the two, showing your method.

[5]

(c)

Explain why the comparison counts in the table give the opposite ranking to the timings for small $n$, referring to the cost model and to the way each algorithm accesses memory.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate whether a programmer should implement a hybrid routine that uses linear search below the crossover value and binary search above it, giving one reason for and one reason against.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) For $n = 16$, $\lfloor\log_{2} 16\rfloor + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5$; for $n = 256$, $8 + 1 = 9$; for $n = 65\,536$, $16 + 1 = 17$; for $n = 16\,777\,216$, $24 + 1 = 25$. (A1) for the method, (A1) for the four values. Linear search is $\mathrm{O}(n)$ and binary search is $\mathrm{O}(\log n)$. (A1)

(b) Linear search takes $3n$ nanoseconds. Binary search takes $400 + 30(\lfloor\log_{2} n\rfloor + 1)$ nanoseconds. (M1)

| $n$ | linear search | binary search |
|---|---|---|
| $16$ | $48\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(5) = 550\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $256$ | $768\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(9) = 670\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $65\,536$ | $196\,608\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(17) = 910\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $16\,777\,216$ | $50\,331\,648\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(25) = 1150\ \mathrm{ns}$ |

(A1) for each column. For the crossover, note that between $n = 128$ and $n = 255$ the binary-search comparison count is fixed at $8$, so the binary-search time is constant at $400 + 30(8) = 640\ \mathrm{ns}$ across that range. (M1) Solving $3n = 640$ gives $n = 213.3$, so (M1) at $n = 213$ linear search takes $639\ \mathrm{ns}$ and binary takes $640\ \mathrm{ns}$, and at $n = 214$ linear takes $642\ \mathrm{ns}$ and binary still takes $640\ \mathrm{ns}$. The smallest $n$ for which binary search is faster is therefore $n = 214$. (A1)

(c) The comparison count measures one cost, and it is not the cost that dominates for small $n$. Binary search has a fixed setup of $400\ \mathrm{ns}$, which at $n = 16$ is more than eight times the entire cost of the linear search, and each of its comparisons costs ten times as much because the probes jump around the array and usually miss the cache. (A1)(A1) Linear search walks along the array, so after the first access every subsequent record is already in a cache line that has been fetched, and each comparison costs $3\ \mathrm{ns}$. (A1) Complexity classes describe how the time grows as $n$ becomes large, and they deliberately discard constant factors; for $n$ below a few hundred the constants here decide the outcome, and the asymptotically worse algorithm wins. (A1)

(d) In favour: the hybrid takes the better of the two routines at every size, so it is never worse than either, and the crossover is a single comparison against a constant, which is almost free. (A1) Against: it is two code paths to write, test and maintain instead of one, and the crossover of $214$ is specific to this machine's cache behaviour and this record size — on different hardware the threshold moves, so the constant becomes a tuning parameter that someone has to keep valid. (A1) Whether it is worth it depends on how often the routine runs: in a loop executed millions of times the gain is real, and in a function called once per user action it is not worth the complexity. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Complexity analysis is taught because it survives changes of hardware, and this item exists to show what it costs to be that general. Big-O deliberately throws away constant factors and lower-order terms, and for large inputs that is exactly right: at $n = 16$ million, binary search is about forty thousand times faster and no constant could close the gap. At $n = 16$, binary search is more than eleven times slower, and the same analysis predicts nothing about that. The crossover sits at $214$, which is small enough that a working programmer will meet it.

The mechanism is worth being precise about, because 'overhead' is not an explanation. Binary search probes the middle of the array, then the middle of a half, then the middle of a quarter, and those addresses are far apart. Each probe is therefore very likely to miss every level of cache and cost a full memory access, which is why the model charges $30\ \mathrm{ns}$ per comparison against linear search's $3\ \mathrm{ns}$. Linear search reads consecutive records, so the first access pulls in a cache line containing the next several records and the following comparisons are almost free. The asymptotic advantage of binary search is real; the per-comparison advantage of linear search is also real; which one wins depends on how many comparisons there are, and that is a question with a numerical answer.

Part (d) resists the tidy conclusion. Having computed the crossover, the natural response is to implement the hybrid, and for a hot loop that is correct. But the threshold of $214$ is not a fact about searching — it is a fact about this cache, this record size and this clock speed, and it will be different on the next machine. Embedding it in source code turns a measured quantity into a magic number that nobody will re-measure. A candidate who sees that has understood something about software engineering that the complexity analysis was never going to teach them, which is the reason the item ends there rather than at the arithmetic.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.4 Programming algorithms
questions.question:
You are asked to check the engineers' claim and to decide whether the structure is safe for a device with a response deadline. Work in operations, where copying one reading is one operation, and assume the first reading is appended to a structure with room for one.

(a)

State the capacities of the structure after each of the first eight appends, and identify the appends at which a copy takes place during the 1024-second shift.

[3]

(b)

Determine the total number of copy operations performed across the whole shift, and hence the average number of copy operations per append. Give your average to three decimal places.

[5]

(c)

Determine the largest number of copy operations performed by any single append during the shift, state which append that is, and explain why the average you found in part (b) does not bound it.

[4]

(d)

The engineers propose to keep the doubling rule but to pre-allocate room for 4096 readings before the shift begins. Justify whether that change removes the risk of missing the response deadline, and state what the change costs in operations at start-up.

[3]
questions.answer:
Part (a). The structure doubles when full, so the capacity sequence is 1, then 2, then 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and so on. (M1) After the first append the capacity is 1; after the second it becomes 2; after the third, 4; after the fifth, 8; after the ninth, 16. So after the first eight appends the capacities are 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8. (A1)

A copy happens when an append finds the structure already full, which is exactly the appends numbered 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65, 129, 257 and 513. (A1) There are ten such appends in the shift, and the other 1014 appends copy nothing.

Part (b). At append number 2 the structure holds one reading and copies it; at append 3 it holds two; at append 5, four; and in general the append numbered 2^k + 1 copies 2^k readings. (M1) The copy counts are therefore 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512. (A1)

The total is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 + 64 + 128 + 256 + 512 = 1023 operations. (M1)(A1)

The average per append is 1023 / 1024 = 0.999 operations, to three decimal places. (A1) So the engineers' claim is arithmetically sound: on average an append costs about one operation, and in fact slightly less.

Part (c). The largest single copy is 512 operations, performed by append number 513. (M1)(A1)

The average does not bound it because an average is a statement about a total divided by a count, and it is compatible with almost any single value in the sequence. Here the 1023 operations are concentrated in ten appends out of 1024, and one of those ten carries half of the entire total on its own. (M1) The average is a property of the run as a whole, while the deadline is threatened by one append, so the two quantities answer different questions. (A1)

It is worth being precise about why the engineers' claim and the objection to it can both be true at once. The claim is about the total cost of the shift, and it is correct: 1023 operations across 1024 appends really is about one operation each, and no arrangement of the same appends can make that total much larger. The objection is about the largest cost of any single second, and it is also correct. A quantity that describes a sum cannot also describe a maximum unless the sum happens to be spread evenly, and here it is spread as unevenly as it could be: ten appends carry the whole cost and the other 1014 carry none of it. If the device's deadline is expressed per second, then it is the maximum that must be compared with the deadline, and the average is simply the wrong statistic for the question being asked. (R1)

Part (d). Pre-allocating room for 4096 readings does remove the risk, because a shift only ever appends 1024 readings and 1024 is less than 4096, so the structure is never full during the shift and no append copies anything. (M1) The total copy work during the shift falls from 1023 operations to 0. (A1)

The change is not free. The start-up cost is that the device must obtain room for 4096 readings at once, and if it must be initialised by copying, the cost is 4096 operations in a single step, which is eight times worse than the worst append it was trying to avoid. (M1) The trade is therefore between a predictable large cost before the shift and an unpredictable large cost during it, and which is preferable depends on whether the deadline applies at start-up; a candidate may reasonably conclude either way provided the trade is stated.
questions.explanation:
The item isolates a single idea: an amortised cost and a worst-case cost are different quantities, and a system with a deadline is governed by the second.

The arithmetic is deliberately gentle. The student computes 1023 copies over 1024 appends and gets an average of 0.999, which *confirms* the engineers' claim rather than refuting it. That is the design: the question is not whether the average is right, it is whether the average is the number that matters. A student who stops at part (b) has done everything correctly and still not answered the question the hospital is asking.

The mechanism is concentration. The 1023 operations are not spread evenly; they sit in ten appends, and the last of those carries 512 of them. The gap between the average and the maximum is a factor of about 512, and no amount of averaging will expose it, because averaging is precisely the operation that destroys that information.

Part (a) is a scaffolding step and is worth noticing as such: it asks for capacities after the first eight appends, which is where the doubling pattern is visible but the numbers are small enough to list. The trap is to write the capacities as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, which is the sequence of *doublings* rather than the sequence of *capacities after each append*. Both are natural readings of the question and only one is right.

The classic wrong turn in part (b) is to assume that each doubling copies the new capacity rather than the old one, giving 2046 instead of 1023 and an average of about 2. That answer is doubly wrong, because it both doubles the total and, ironically, makes the average look *worse* than it is, which would have led the student to reject a claim that is in fact correct.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A3.2 An index that makes the slow operation a hundred times faster and the system as a whole slower: two effects that have to be summed before either can be judged
questions.question:
The chart shows the mean time per operation before and after the change, split into the time spent on reads and the time spent on writes. Use the data in the case study to answer the following, giving times to two decimal places and percentages to one decimal place.

(a)

Calculate the mean time per operation before the index is created and after it is created, and the percentage change in the mean.

[3]

(b)

Show that the change in the mean is the difference of two separate effects, one a saving on reads and one a penalty on writes, and calculate the size of each per operation.

[3]

(c)

Determine the fraction of operations that would have to be reads for the index to break even, and hence state whether the index should be kept under the current workload.

[4]

(d)

The service-level target is currently a mean operation time of 30 ms. The operations team proposes to replace it with a target on the 99th percentile of individual operation times. Evaluate whether the index should be kept under each target, and recommend what Meridian should do.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Before: $0.05 \times 400 + 0.95 \times 5 = 20 + 4.75 = 24.75$ ms (M1). After: $0.05 \times 4 + 0.95 \times 40 = 0.2 + 38 = 38.20$ ms (A1). The mean therefore rises by $13.45$ ms, which is $\dfrac{13.45}{24.75} \times 100 = 54.3\%$ (A1): the index makes the average operation more than half as slow again. Over a day of 1 000 000 operations that is 24 750 s, about 6.9 hours of database work, against 38 200 s, about 10.6 hours: the same throughput costs an extra 3.7 hours.
(b) The change can be separated cleanly because each operation type appears with a known frequency. The saving on reads is $0.05 \times (400 - 4) = 0.05 \times 396 = 19.80$ ms per operation on average (M1). The penalty on writes is $0.95 \times (40 - 5) = 0.95 \times 35 = 33.25$ ms per operation on average (A1). The net change is $33.25 - 19.80 = +13.45$ ms, which is exactly the difference found in part (a) (A1). The two effects are of the same order — reads are 5% of the operations but each one saves 396 ms, writes are 95% but each one costs 35 ms — so neither can be neglected and the sign of the result is not obvious until both are computed.
(c) Let $r$ be the fraction of operations that are lookups. Without the index the mean is $400r + 5(1-r) = 5 + 395r$; with it the mean is $4r + 40(1-r) = 40 - 36r$ (M1). Break even when $5 + 395r = 40 - 36r$, so $431r = 35$ and $r = \dfrac{35}{431} = 0.0812$ (M1)(A1). The index pays for itself only when more than about $8.1\%$ of operations are lookups. The current workload runs at $5\%$, which is below that, so under the current mix the index should not be kept (A1). The margin is not thin: the observed 5% is about three fifths of the 8.1% needed, so the index fails by a comfortable distance rather than on a rounding error, and no plausible drift in the mix over a week would rescue it.
(d) Under the present target the answer is clear: the mean is 24.75 ms without the index, which meets the 30 ms target, and 38.20 ms with it, which does not — so the index turns a compliant system into a non-compliant one and should be dropped (M1). The percentile target reverses the comparison. Without the index, 5% of operations take 400 ms, so the 99th percentile is 400 ms; with the index the slowest operation is 40 ms and the 99th percentile is 40 ms (A1). Against a tail target the index is therefore a factor-of-ten improvement, and it is the only way to meet any percentile target below 400 ms (A1). The recommendation follows from which target Meridian actually cares about, and the two are not the same thing: a mean target measures throughput and a percentile target measures the experience of the unlucky operation, and an index trades the second for the first. Meridian should either keep the index and move the target to a percentile, or drop the index and accept 400 ms lookups — and if it needs both, it should look at a covering index on a narrower column set, or at batching the index maintenance, rather than at the current all-or-nothing choice (M1)(A1).
questions.explanation:
Index selection is taught as a query-optimisation topic, and the evidence used to judge it is the query: a hundredfold speed-up is presented, and the discussion stops. What the syllabus asks for — evaluating the effect of a design decision on the system — is not served by that, because an index is not a change to one operation. It is a change to every operation, and the ones it slows are the ones nobody was complaining about.

The numbers are chosen so that the two effects nearly cancel. Reads are rare (5%) and catastrophic (400 ms); writes are almost everything (95%) and individually cheap (5 ms). That is a realistic profile for an order-capture system, and it puts the read saving and the write penalty within a factor of two of each other, which is the only regime in which the question is interesting. The result — the mean rises 54% while the worst case falls by a factor of ten — is not a paradox; it is what happens when a change is judged on one statistic and the business measures another.

Part (d) exists so that 'drop the index' is not the answer. A mean target and a percentile target rank the two designs in opposite orders, and a candidate who can state that, and say which one the organisation actually wants, has done the evaluation rather than the arithmetic.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Cache memory and average memory access time
questions.question:
A design team is comparing two memory configurations for a new single-core processor. The figure shows the proposed hierarchy. Every instruction fetch and every data read or write that the processor issues is presented to the level 1 cache first. A reference that misses in level 1 is passed to the level 2 cache, and a reference that also misses there is passed to main memory. The hit rate of each cache is the proportion of the references presented to it that it satisfies, and the time given for each level is the number of processor cycles that level adds when it is consulted. Registers are not part of the calculation. The team must decide whether the level 2 cache earns the die area it occupies, because that area could be given to other parts of the processor.

(a)

Calculate the average number of cycles the processor spends on one memory reference when both caches are present. Show clearly how the level 1 hit time, the level 2 hit time and the main memory access time each contribute to your total, and state the fraction of references that reach main memory.

[4]

(b)

Determine the average number of cycles per memory reference if the level 2 cache is removed, so that every level 1 miss is passed directly to main memory. Give your answer to three significant figures.

[3]

(c)

Explain why the contribution that main memory makes to the average in part (a) is so much smaller than its access time of 150 cycles would suggest, and why the level 2 cache makes a larger contribution than its own hit rate alone implies.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate the proposal to remove the level 2 cache in order to recover its die area. Refer to your results from parts (a) and (b), and consider the effect on the processor's performance rather than only on the cost of manufacturing it.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The level 1 miss rate is $1 - 0.94 = 0.06$ (M1). Of those misses only $1 - 0.80 = 0.20$ are not satisfied by level 2, so the fraction of all references that reach main memory is $0.06 \times 0.20 = 0.012$, that is 1.2 per cent (A1).

The level 1 cache is consulted by every reference and adds 3 cycles, so its contribution is 3 cycles. The level 2 cache is consulted only by the 0.06 of references that miss in level 1 and adds 14 cycles to each of them, so its contribution is $0.06 \times 14 = 0.84$ cycles. Main memory is consulted only by the 0.012 of references that miss in both caches and adds 150 cycles to each of them, so its contribution is $0.012 \times 150 = 1.8$ cycles (A1).

The average number of cycles per reference is therefore $3 + 0.84 + 1.8 = 5.64$ cycles (A1).

(b) With no level 2 cache every level 1 miss is passed straight to main memory, so main memory is consulted by the whole 0.06 of misses and adds 150 cycles to each of them. Its contribution becomes $0.06 \times 150 = 9$ cycles (M1), and the average becomes $3 + 9 = 12.0$ cycles (A1). Removing the level 2 cache therefore raises the average from 5.64 to 12.0 cycles, a factor of $12.0 \div 5.64 = 2.13$ (A1).

(c) Main memory contributes only 1.8 cycles even though a single access costs 150 cycles, because it is reached by 1.2 per cent of references and by no others. Its 150 cycles are paid once per reference that misses in both caches, so multiplying 150 by the overall miss rate of 0.012 gives the average cost per reference; multiplying it by anything closer to 1 would charge the whole of main memory's latency to references that never reach it (M1).

The level 2 cache contributes more than its own hit rate suggests because its hit rate is conditional. The figure states that 0.80 of the references presented to level 2 are satisfied there, but only 0.06 of all references are ever presented to it, so the level 2 cache removes $0.06 \times 0.80 = 0.048$ of all references from the path to main memory (A1). Those references would otherwise have cost 150 cycles instead of 14, so the cache saves $0.048 \times (150 - 14) = 6.53$ cycles per reference; equivalently, comparing parts (a) and (b), it saves $12.0 - 5.64 = 6.36$ cycles (A1). A hit rate is a property of the cache, not of the program, and the two must be multiplied to obtain the share of references the cache actually rescues.

(d) The proposal should be rejected on performance grounds. Removing the level 2 cache raises the average memory reference from 5.64 to 12.0 cycles, an increase of 6.36 cycles on every reference the processor issues, which is a slowdown of about 2.13 times on any part of the workload that is memory-bound (A1). Because the level 2 cache is consulted on only 6 per cent of references but converts each of those from a 150-cycle main memory access into a 14-cycle access, it removes roughly 6.5 cycles per reference from the average while occupying far less die area than the level 1 cache does (A1).

The evaluation is not settled by cost alone. Die area given to level 2 could raise the level 1 hit rate instead, but part (a) shows that the level 1 hit time is paid by every reference and the level 1 miss rate is already only 0.06, so a further improvement there can remove at most 0.06 of the references from the level 2 path; the level 2 cache is currently rescuing 0.048 of them (A1). A design that removed level 2 would also make the processor's performance far more sensitive to the level 1 hit rate, because every additional level 1 miss would then cost the full 150 cycles rather than 14 (A1).

A justified answer must therefore weigh the 2.13 times slowdown against the area recovered, and should note that the decision depends on how memory-bound the intended workload is: a workload that fits in level 1 would lose little, while one that streams through data would lose most of its throughput (A1). Merely asserting that caches are fast, or that removing a component reduces cost, earns no credit.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on a conditional-probability structure that is disguised as a sum. Three levels are drawn in a pyramid, each with a hit rate and a time, and the shape invites the reader to weight each time by the hit rate printed beside it and add. That is the trap. The hit rate of the level 1 cache is unconditional, because every reference is presented to it, but the hit rate of the level 2 cache is conditional on having missed in level 1, and main memory has no hit rate at all because it always answers. The three numbers are therefore not the same kind of quantity and cannot be combined by the same rule.

The consequence is a factor-of-two error in the answer that decides the question. A candidate who weights level 2 by 0.80 obtains $0.94 \times 3 + 0.80 \times 14 + 0.012 \times 150 = 15.8$ cycles, which makes the level 2 cache look as though it were adding 11.2 cycles to every reference rather than 0.84. A candidate who weights level 2 by 0.06 but forgets main memory obtains 3.66 cycles, which is too small. Both errors are arithmetically clean, so neither is caught by checking the working; only the conditional structure catches them.

Part (b) is the payoff. Computing the average again without level 2 gives 12.0 cycles, so the cache is worth 6.36 cycles per reference and a factor of 2.13 in average access time. A candidate carrying the 15.8 figure forward would instead conclude that removing the cache costs almost nothing, because 15.8 already contains the 11.2 that the cache was wrongly charged with. The evaluation in part (d) therefore cannot be answered correctly unless part (a) is right, which is what makes the arc work: the opening part carries the idea and the closing part tests whether it was understood.

The figure is load-bearing rather than decorative. The hit rates and the three times are printed only in the figure, the direction of the hand-off between levels is drawn only there, and the caption states that every reference is presented to level 1 first. Nothing in the stem repeats those numbers, so an answer cannot be produced without reading the diagram, which is the test STANDARD.md 4.3.1 sets for a figure.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.1 Redundancy in a block storage array: the parity block of a stripe is the exclusive OR of that stripe's data blocks, so exactly one lost block per stripe can be rebuilt, and the number of failures tolerated does not grow with the number of disks in the stripe
questions.question:
The array divides its address space into stripes. A stripe consists of four data blocks and one parity block, and the parity block holds the bitwise exclusive OR of the four data blocks of that stripe. The position of the parity block rotates from stripe to stripe, so that no single disk holds the parity of every stripe. When the array reads a block it reads that block alone; the parity block is consulted only when a block is found to be unreadable. The table gives the four data blocks of one stripe as they were written. The figure shows that stripe together with a neighbouring stripe, and marks one unreadable block in each of the two stripes. The two unreadable blocks are in different stripes, and the controller has not yet had to rebuild two blocks that lie in the same stripe.

(a)
