Calculate the parity block of the stripe given in the table, and state the fraction of the array's total block capacity that remains available for data when every stripe carries one parity block for four data blocks.

[3]

(b)

Show that the value of the block D3 can be rebuilt from the parity block and the three surviving data blocks of the stripe, and determine the value that is rebuilt.

[4]

(c)

Explain why the array can rebuild the two unreadable blocks marked in the figure at the same time, even though it could not rebuild two unreadable blocks that lay in the same stripe.

[3]

(d)

Determine how many simultaneous block failures the array can survive within a single stripe, and state what a second parity block in every stripe would change.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The parity block is the exclusive OR of the four data blocks, so it is computed by combining them two at a time.

0x5A XOR 0x3C = 0x66
0x66 XOR 0xF0 = 0x96
0x96 XOR 0x27 = 0xB1

The parity block is 0xB1. The exclusive OR is associative and commutative, so the order in which the four blocks are combined does not matter.

A stripe that holds four data blocks and one parity block occupies five blocks in order to store four blocks of data. The fraction of the array's capacity available for data is therefore 4/5 = 0.80, that is eighty per cent. The remaining twenty per cent is the cost of the redundancy: one block in every five is spent on the parity and holds no data of its own.

(b) When the block D3 is unreadable, the array knows the parity block 0xB1 and the three surviving data blocks 0x5A, 0x3C and 0x27. The parity block was formed as the exclusive OR of all four data blocks, and the exclusive OR is its own inverse: a value exclusive ORed with itself gives zero, and a value exclusive ORed with zero is unchanged. Combining the parity block with the three surviving blocks therefore cancels those three and leaves the missing one.

0xB1 XOR 0x5A = 0xEB
0xEB XOR 0x3C = 0xD7
0xD7 XOR 0x27 = 0xF0

The rebuilt value is 0xF0, which is the value the table records for D3. The same computation works whichever of the four blocks is lost, because the parity block is symmetric in the four of them; a rebuild of D1 would combine 0xB1 with 0x3C, 0xF0 and 0x27 and return 0x5A.

(c) Each stripe contributes exactly one equation. For the stripe in the table the equation is D1 XOR D2 XOR D3 XOR D4 = P, in which the only unknown is the one block that has been lost, so the equation can be solved. The two unreadable blocks marked in the figure lie in different stripes, so each of the two stripes supplies its own equation, and each of those equations contains one unknown. The two equations are independent of one another, because the stripes are computed separately when the data is written, so they can be solved at the same time and the two blocks can both be rebuilt.

If two blocks of the same stripe were lost, that stripe would supply one equation containing two unknowns, and one equation in two unknowns does not determine either unknown. Every assignment of values to the two missing blocks that keeps the exclusive OR equal to the parity block would satisfy the equation equally well, so the array would have no way to tell which assignment was the original. The stripe's single equation is one constraint, and one constraint removes one unknown.

(d) A stripe with one parity block carries one equation and can therefore absorb exactly one lost block. That number does not depend on how many data blocks the stripe holds: a stripe of four data blocks and a stripe of twelve data blocks each carry one equation and each tolerate exactly one failure. Widening the stripe raises the fraction of the array available for data, since the parity overhead falls from one block in five to one block in thirteen, but it does not raise the tolerance at all. The tolerance is set by the number of parity blocks in the stripe and not by the number of disks in it, which is the point that a candidate who reasons by analogy with the disk count will miss.

A second parity block in every stripe would give each stripe two equations instead of one. Two equations in two unknowns can be solved, so such an array would tolerate two simultaneous block failures within the same stripe, and it would also be able to rebuild a block even when the parity block itself is one of the two failures. The cost is a second block of overhead: a stripe of four data blocks would then occupy six blocks, so the fraction available for data would fall from 4/5 to 4/6, that is from eighty per cent to about sixty-seven per cent.
questions.explanation:
This item is about the difference between a local fact and a property of an aggregate, and the two are separated deliberately. The local fact is that a parity block can be computed and that one lost block can be rebuilt; almost every treatment of RAID gets this far. The aggregate property is that a stripe tolerates one failure no matter how many data blocks it holds, and that the array tolerates as many failures as there are stripes that have lost a block, provided no stripe has lost two.

The four parts walk the candidate from the local to the aggregate. Part (a) is a computation and can be done by anyone who can apply the exclusive OR. Part (b) adds the inverse property, which is the reason the scheme works at all. Part (c) is the first part that cannot be answered by computing anything, because the question is why two failures in different stripes are simultaneously solvable, and the answer is that the stripes are separate systems of equations. Part (d) generalises and asks for the number, which is one, and for the reason, which is that the number of parity blocks and not the number of disks sets the tolerance.

The belief the item is aimed at is common and reasonable-sounding: that a bigger array with more disks is more redundant. It is false in the sense that matters. A twelve-disk array with one parity block per stripe survives exactly as many simultaneous failures within a stripe as a four-disk array does, and in practice it is less safe, because the rebuild of a large array takes longer and the array is at its most vulnerable while it runs. The final part's second half asks for the second parity block, which is the design that does raise the tolerance, and which pays for it with capacity.

The marking is arranged so that the local computation in (a) and (b) cannot carry the item. A candidate can take full marks on those two parts and still score nothing on (d), and that is the intended discrimination.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.2 A weighted check digit modulo a prime detects every interchange of two digits, because the change it makes to the total is a product of two factors each smaller than the modulus; an unweighted digit sum detects none, because the change is zero
questions.question:
The nine identifying digits of record R-4471 are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5, and the check digit is the final 2, so the code as the publisher printed it is 0306406152. The code held in the catalogue is 0306406512: the eighth and ninth digits have been interchanged somewhere between the publisher's list and the catalogue's keyboard. The catalogue's routine accepted the code, and the record has stood in the catalogue for two years. The correct rule for a ten-digit ISBN weights the first digit by ten, the second by nine, and so on down to the tenth digit weighted by one, and requires the weighted total to be a multiple of eleven. A rival scheme weights each digit by its own position, counting the first digit as position one, and requires the total to be a multiple of ten. The catalogue's routine is a third scheme again: it weights every digit by one.

(a)

Calculate the check digit that the weighted rule requires for the nine identifying digits 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5, and hence state whether the code held in the catalogue satisfies the rule.

[3]

(b)

Determine the weighted total of the code held in the catalogue, and state what its remainder on division by eleven shows about the interchange of the two digits.

[3]

(c)

Explain why the catalogue's routine accepted a code that the weighted rule rejects, referring to the effect that interchanging two digits has on the sum of those digits.

[3]

(d)

The rival scheme that weights each digit by its position and works modulo ten is not equivalent to the weighted rule. Deduce, from the change that interchanging two digits makes to a weighted total, one interchange that the rival scheme fails to detect, and explain why the weighted rule modulo eleven cannot fail to detect any interchange of two digits.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The weighted rule weights the digits from ten down to one. For the nine identifying digits 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5 the weights are 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2, so the weighted total of the identifying digits is

10(0) + 9(3) + 8(0) + 7(6) + 6(4) + 5(0) + 4(6) + 3(1) + 2(5)
= 0 + 27 + 0 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 24 + 3 + 10
= 130.

The check digit carries weight one, so it must satisfy 130 + d = 0 (mod 11). Now 130 = 11 x 11 + 9, so 130 is 9 more than a multiple of eleven, and the check digit must make up the difference: d = 11 - 9 = 2. The check digit is 2, which agrees with the final digit of the publisher's code 0306406152.

The code held in the catalogue is 0306406512, which has the same ten digits in a different order. Its weighted total is 136, and 136 = 11 x 12 + 4, so the total is 4 more than a multiple of eleven. The code held in the catalogue therefore does not satisfy the rule, and the check digit it carries, 2, is not the check digit for the nine digits that precede it in that order.

(b) The weighted total of the code held in the catalogue is

10(0) + 9(3) + 8(0) + 7(6) + 6(4) + 5(0) + 4(6) + 3(5) + 2(1) + 1(2)
= 0 + 27 + 0 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 24 + 15 + 2 + 2
= 136.

The remainder on division by eleven is 4, and a valid code would leave a remainder of zero. The remainder is not zero, so the interchange is detected: the code held in the catalogue is not a valid ISBN under the weighted rule, and the nonzero remainder is the evidence. Comparing the two totals, the publisher's code gives 132 and the catalogue's code gives 136, so interchanging the eighth and ninth digits raised the total by 4. That increase is not an accident of these particular digits; it is the difference between the two weights, 3 and 2, multiplied by the difference between the two digits, 1 and 5.

(c) The catalogue's routine adds the ten digits together and tests whether the total is a multiple of ten. The ten digits of the publisher's code are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1, 5 and 2, which add to 27. The ten digits of the catalogue's code are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 5, 1 and 2, which also add to 27. Addition does not care about the order of its terms, so interchanging two digits leaves the sum of the digits exactly as it was. The routine therefore computes the same total for both codes, finds 27 in each case, and accepts both, because 27 has the same remainder on division by ten, namely 7, as itself.

The routine is not merely weaker than the weighted rule; it is blind to the whole class of errors to which keyboard entry is most prone. Interchanging two adjacent digits is the commonest mistake made when a long number is copied by hand, and the routine's weighting, which is to say a weight of one on every position, makes every interchange invisible. A check that cannot see the commonest error is not a check that has been weakened; it is a check that is not doing the job it was written for.

(d) Consider a weighted total in which the digit at position i carries weight w_i. Interchanging the digits at positions i and j replaces the contribution w_i d_i + w_j d_j with w_i d_j + w_j d_i, so the total changes by

(w_i d_j + w_j d_i) - (w_i d_i + w_j d_j) = (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i).

For the rival scheme the weight of a digit is its position, so w_i = i and w_j = j, and the change is (i - j)(d_j - d_i). The rival scheme accepts the corrupted code when this product is a multiple of ten. Take the digits at positions 1 and 3, and suppose they are 0 and 5. Then i - j is 1 - 3 = -2 and d_j - d_i is 5 - 0 = 5, so the change is -2 x 5 = -10, which is a multiple of ten, and the rival scheme does not notice the interchange. The interchange of a 0 and a 5 two positions apart is therefore one that the rival scheme misses. The reason the miss is possible is that ten is not prime: the factor of five that the digit difference supplies can be paired with the factor of two that the position difference supplies to make a multiple of ten.

For the weighted rule the weights are ten, nine, eight and so on down to one, and the change made by an interchange is (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i). The digits are between 0 and 9, so d_j - d_i lies between -9 and 9, and the positions are between 1 and 10, so w_i - w_j also lies between -9 and 9. Neither factor can be a multiple of eleven, because eleven is larger than nine, and neither factor is zero when the digits differ and the positions differ. Since eleven is prime, a product is a multiple of eleven only if one of its factors is, and neither factor is. The change is therefore never a multiple of eleven, so the total of a code with two digits interchanged can never be a multiple of eleven, and the interchange is always detected. Choosing a prime modulus larger than the largest possible value of either factor is what makes the guarantee hold.
questions.explanation:
Check digits are usually taught as a procedure: multiply by the weights, add, take the remainder. The procedure is easy to learn and teaches nothing about why it works, and the commonest student belief is that any check digit scheme is roughly as good as any other. This item is built to make that belief fail on contact with a specific error.

The error is planted rather than described. The catalogue holds a code whose digits are the publisher's digits in the wrong order, and the catalogue's routine, which sums the digits, reports the code as valid. The candidate is not asked to find the error by brute force; the error is given in the question. What is asked is why the routine cannot see it, and the answer is an invariance: the sum of a set of digits does not depend on their order, so a scheme that weights every digit equally is blind to every interchange. The reasoning is short but it is a genuine argument about a property of the scheme rather than a computation.

The final part raises the question that the invariance argument invites. If equal weights see nothing and distinct weights see something, which distinct weights see everything? The answer is that the change made by an interchange is a product of two small factors, so it suffices that the modulus be prime and larger than both. Eleven is prime and larger than nine, and both factors are bounded by nine, so no interchange escapes. The rival scheme modulo ten fails because ten is composite: a digit difference of five and a position difference of two can supply the factors of five and two separately. The candidate is asked to exhibit such an interchange, which cannot be done by testing codes at random and requires the product to have been understood.

The item also carries a small piece of professional judgement. The catalogue's routine was written by someone who had a rule of thumb, and it passed every test the writer thought to apply, because the writer tested codes rather than interchanges. The item's third part asks for the reason the routine is blind, which is the same kind of question a candidate should learn to ask about any validation they write themselves.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Two's complement overflow and exclusive OR checksums
questions.question:
A sensor network transmits each measurement as a three-byte frame. The first byte is the reading and the second is a calibration offset, and both are 8-bit two's complement values; the third byte is a checksum. Two frames captured from the network are shown in the figure, together with the 8-bit sum that the receiver's adder produced for each of them and the carry-out bit that the same adder produced. The receiver must reject any frame whose two signed values cannot be added without the result being misrepresented, and the engineer who wrote the receiver used the carry-out bit to make that decision.

(a)

Determine the signed decimal value of the reading and of the offset in frame A, and state the true arithmetic sum of those two values. Show how the first bit of each byte is used in your decoding.

[3]

(b)

Deduce the signed decimal value that the 8-bit sum in frame B represents, and state with a reason whether the addition of the two signed values in frame B has overflowed.

[3]

(c)

Calculate the checksum of each frame from its first two bytes, and state whether each of the two checksums in the figure is correct.

[3]

(d)

Explain why the carry-out bit cannot be used to decide whether a signed addition has overflowed. Your answer should refer to both frames and should state the condition that does detect overflow.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) In frame A the first byte is 0x7A, which in binary is 0111 1010. Its leading bit is 0, so the value is positive and the remaining bits give $64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 122$ (A1). The second byte is 0x9C, which is 1001 1100. Its leading bit is 1, so it is negative, and its magnitude is found by taking the two's complement: $1001\,1100 \to 0110\,0011 \to 0110\,0100$, which is $64 + 32 + 4 = 100$ (A1). The offset is therefore $-100$.

The true arithmetic sum of the two signed values is $122 + (-100) = 22$ (A1). Because the two values have opposite signs, the sum lies between them and no overflow is possible.

(b) In frame B the first byte is 0x6F, which is 0110 1111 with a leading bit of 0, so the reading is $+111$. The second byte is 0x32, which is 0011 0010 with a leading bit of 0, so the offset is $+50$ (M1). Their true sum is $111 + 50 = 161$, which is greater than the largest value an 8-bit two's complement number can hold, namely $+127$ (A1).

The 8-bit sum shown in the figure is 0xA1, which is 1010 0001. Its leading bit is 1, so it represents a negative number, and its magnitude is $0101\,1110 + 1 = 0101\,1111 = 95$, giving $-95$ (A1). Adding two positive values has produced a negative result, so the addition has overflowed.

(c) The checksum is the exclusive OR of the first two bytes. For frame A, $0111\,1010$ XOR $1001\,1100 = 1110\,0110$, which is 0xE6 (M1) (A1). The figure shows 0xE6, so the checksum of frame A is correct (A1).

For frame B, $0110\,1111$ XOR $0011\,0010 = 0101\,1101$, which is 0x5D (M1). The figure shows 0x5D, so the checksum of frame B is also correct (A1). This matters: the frame that overflows is not corrupt, and a receiver that relied on the checksum alone would accept it.

(d) The carry-out is the bit that leaves the most significant position of the adder, and it reports whether the unsigned sum of the two bit patterns exceeded 255. That is not the same question as whether the signed sum exceeded 127 or fell below $-128$, because the same bit patterns mean different things under the two interpretations (A1).

Frame A shows the first failure. Its bytes are 0x7A and 0x9C, whose unsigned values are 122 and 156. Their unsigned sum is 278, which exceeds 255, so the adder produces a carry-out of 1. The signed values, however, are 122 and $-100$, whose sum is 22 and fits comfortably; the carry-out is 1 while there is no overflow (A1). A receiver that rejected on the carry-out would discard a good frame.

Frame B shows the opposite failure. Its bytes are 0x6F and 0x32, whose unsigned values are 111 and 50. Their unsigned sum is 161, which does not exceed 255, so the carry-out is 0. The signed values are $+111$ and $+50$, whose sum of 161 exceeds 127, so the result stored is $-95$ and the addition has overflowed (A1). A receiver that accepted on the carry-out would accept a frame whose value is wrong by 256.

Overflow for signed addition is detected from the signs of the operands and the sign of the result, not from the carry-out: overflow occurs when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the opposite sign (A1). Equivalently, it is the exclusive OR of the carry into the most significant position and the carry out of it. In frame A the signs are opposite, so no overflow is possible whatever the carry-out is; in frame B both operands are positive and the result is negative, so overflow has occurred whatever the carry-out is (A1).
questions.explanation:
The item separates two things that share a name. The carry-out bit and signed overflow are both described informally as the addition having gone past the end, and on many textbook examples they coincide, which is exactly why the carry-out is such a persistent error. The two frames here are chosen to break the coincidence in both directions, so the rule cannot be salvaged by adjusting it.

Frame A is the false-rejection case. Its two bytes are 0x7A and 0x9C. As unsigned patterns these are 122 and 156, summing to 278, so a carry-out is produced. As signed patterns they are 122 and $-100$, summing to 22, so nothing is wrong. The carry-out is 1 and there is no overflow. Frame B is the false-acceptance case. Its bytes are 0x6F and 0x32, which are 111 and 50 unsigned and also $+111$ and $+50$ signed. The unsigned sum is 161, which fits in eight bits, so there is no carry-out; the signed sum is 161, which does not fit, so the stored result of 0xA1 reads back as $-95$. The carry-out is 0 and there is an overflow.

Because the same hardware bit is wrong in both directions on the same item, a candidate who guesses cannot pass part (d) by pattern-matching on the first frame. The correct rule is stated in terms of the signs: overflow occurs when two operands share a sign and the result does not. It can also be expressed as the exclusive OR of the carry into and the carry out of the sign position, which is the form a hardware designer would use and which is why the single visible carry-out is not enough.

The checksum is a deliberate second layer. Both frames have correct checksums, so the third byte offers no help in detecting the overflow and a candidate who looks for corruption there finds none. This forces the answer back onto the interpretation of the two signed bytes, which is the point of the item.

The figure carries every value the answer needs, including the carry-out that the receiver's engineer relied on, so the trap is presented as data rather than described in the stem. The two frames are decoded from the same two's complement function in the generator that the markscheme uses, so the picture and the answer cannot drift apart.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Choosing a translation strategy from a three-way cost model, where the compiler and the interpreter cross at a value of N that is never on the cheapest frontier
questions.question:
A laboratory writes a data-reduction tool that has to run on the three operating systems its collaborators use. The team can distribute the tool in any of three forms. In form A the source is compiled ahead of time into a native executable, and one executable has to be built and tested for each of the three systems. In form B the source is shipped as it stands and translated every time the tool is run. In form C the source is compiled once, on the laboratory's own machine, into bytecode, and that single bytecode build is shipped to all three systems and executed there by a bytecode interpreter.

The figure gives the total cost of each form, in arbitrary cost units, as a function of N, the number of times the tool is executed in total across all three systems. A dashed line marks the number of executions the team currently expects. The costs are the whole cost of owning each form: translation, distribution and execution.

(a)

Determine the value of N at which forms B and C have the same total cost, and state which of the two forms is cheaper immediately below that value and which is cheaper immediately above it. Show the equation you solved.

[3]

(b)

Determine the value of N at which forms C and A have the same total cost. Hence state, for each of the three forms, the range of N over which that form is the cheapest of the three. Where a boundary of your range is a tie rather than a strict win, say so.

[4]

(c)

The team's current estimate is the value of N marked on the figure. Determine the total cost of each of the three forms at that estimate, and state the saving the cheapest form makes against the next cheapest. A colleague recommends form A for every project because it has the lowest cost per execution. Explain why a comparison of forms A and B on their own would have supported that recommendation at this estimate, and state the smallest number of executions at which the recommendation would actually change. Reach a judgement on which form the team should ship.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The figure gives the three cost models directly: form A is $1200 + 4N$, form B is $20N$, and form C is $240 + 8N$, all in the same cost units. Forms B and C are equal when $20N = 240 + 8N$, so $12N = 240$ and $N = 20$ (M1). At that value both cost $400$ (A1). Immediately below 20 the coefficient of $N$ is smaller for B than for C, so B is cheaper: at $N = 19$, B costs $380$ and C costs $392$. Immediately above 20, C is cheaper: at $N = 21$, B costs $420$ and C costs $408$ (A1).

(b) Forms C and A are equal when $240 + 8N = 1200 + 4N$, so $4N = 960$ and $N = 240$ (M1). At that value both cost $2160$ (A1).

The three ranges are found by taking the lower of the three costs at each N, not by listing the pairwise crossovers.

  • Form B is the cheapest for $N \leq 19$. At $N = 20$ B and C are tied at $400$.
  • Form C is the cheapest for $21 \leq N \leq 239$. At $N = 240$ C and A are tied at $2160$.
  • Form A is the cheapest for $N \geq 241$. At $N = 241$, A costs $2164$ and C costs $2168$ (A1).

Two of the three boundaries are therefore ties rather than wins (A1).

(c) At the estimate marked on the figure, $N = 100$. Form A costs $1200 + 400 = 1600$; form B costs $2000$; form C costs $240 + 800 = 1040$ (M1). Form C is the cheapest, and the saving against the next cheapest, which is form A, is $1600 - 1040 = 560$ cost units (A1).

The colleague's recommendation is not unreasonable when only A and B are considered. Forms A and B are equal when $1200 + 4N = 20N$, so $N = 75$, and A is cheaper than B for every $N$ above 75 (M1). At an estimate of 100, which is above 75, a comparison of those two forms alone therefore recommends A, and the recommendation is supported by the arithmetic of that comparison. It is still the wrong recommendation, because the question is not which of A and B is cheaper but which of the three is cheapest. At $N = 75$ form A and form B both cost $1500$, while form C costs $840$ (A1). The crossover at 75 is a genuine crossover, and it is not on the cheapest frontier: at every value of N the frontier passes through, form C is below both of the strategies that cross there. Reporting the crossover at 75 as a boundary of the answer puts a segment into the frontier that does not exist, and it does so in the direction that looks most plausible, because A really is cheaper than B above 75 (A1).

The recommendation changes at $N = 241$, which is the smallest number of executions for which form A is the cheapest of the three (A1). Below that, form C is cheaper. So the estimate would have to be wrong by more than a factor of two, in the direction of more executions, before the colleague's recommendation became the right one.

The judgement is that the team should ship form C at the current estimate (A1). Form C costs $1040$ against $1600$ for form A, a saving of $560$ cost units, or thirty-five per cent of form A's total. It also keeps the property that made form A attractive in the first place, since a single bytecode build is produced once and then runs on all three systems, so no per-system build or test effort is needed. The judgement is not unconditional: it holds while the estimate stays below 241 executions. If the tool is later executed far more often than expected, the per-execution cost of $8$ for form C against $4$ for form A becomes decisive, and form A becomes the cheaper choice. A recommendation that is not attached to the estimate it was made for is not a recommendation, it is a preference (A1).
questions.explanation:
This item is about the difference between a comparison and an optimisation. Any two linear cost models cross once, so there are three crossovers among three forms: A and B at 75, B and C at 20, and A and C at 240. Each is real arithmetic and each can be found by setting the two expressions equal. The cheapest form at a given N, however, is the minimum of the three, and a crossover between two strategies is only a boundary of that minimum if neither of them is beaten by the third at that value. At $N = 75$ the third form costs $840$ while the two that cross both cost $1500$, so the boundary at 75 is not a boundary of the minimum at all.

The A and B crossover is the trap because it is the one a candidate is most likely to compute. The colleague's claim in part (c) is written to invite exactly that computation: 'the lowest cost per execution' is true of form A, the comparison with form B is the one the claim invites, and at an estimate of 100 the comparison gives the colleague the right answer. Everything the candidate is told points at A, and the figure contradicts it.

The item also carries the two tie points, at $N = 20$ and $N = 240$, where two forms cost exactly the same. They matter because they fix the boundaries of the ranges: C is cheapest from 21 and not from 20, and A is cheapest from 241 and not from 240. A candidate who writes the boundaries as strict inequalities in the wrong direction creates a gap or an overlap at each tie, and part (b) asks for the ties to be named so that this is visible in the answer rather than hidden in it.

Finally, the item is an evaluation rather than a calculation because the arithmetic does not by itself say which form to ship. Form C is cheaper at the estimate and it preserves the single-build property that form A was chosen for; form A is cheaper per execution and wins if the estimate is badly wrong. The judgement mark is for attaching the recommendation to the estimate it was made for, which is the same discipline the guide asks for when it requires the use-cases of each translation approach to be considered.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Two transfers that interleave so that the second reads the balance before the first commits, and the committed value is short by exactly the first transfer
questions.question:
A savings account holds a balance of 500. Two transfers into the account are submitted at almost the same moment: one adds 100 and one adds 50. Each transfer is written as a transaction that reads the balance, computes the new balance from the value it read, writes that value back, and commits. The application does not use a lock, and the database engine is running at an isolation level that permits the two transactions to interleave.

The figure shows what the engine actually did, as an ordered list of operations. Each operation is labelled with the transaction that issued it and the moment it was issued. Nothing in the figure has been simplified: this is the whole of both transactions, and both of them commit.

(a)

Using the timeline, state the balance that each of the two transactions reads and the balance that each of them writes. Determine the balance that is left in the account once both transactions have committed, and state which of the two COMMIT statements fixes that value.

[3]

(b)

Determine the balance that would remain if the two transfers had run one after the other, and show that both possible orders give the same result. State the amount by which the interleaved execution has lost. Name the ACID property whose role this interleaving has defeated, and name one of the other three properties that this same interleaving has not defeated, justifying each of your two answers.

[4]

(c)

A developer proposes to change nothing in the application, to rely on ROLLBACK to undo any damage, and to allow both transactions to run for longer so that they overlap more often. Evaluate that proposal. Your answer should state what ROLLBACK can and cannot recover in this timeline, identify the smallest change to the timeline that removes the loss, and reach a judgement on whether this anomaly can be prevented using transaction control commands alone.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The first SELECT is issued by the first transaction at t1 and returns 500. The second SELECT is issued by the second transaction at t3 and also returns 500, because the first transaction has not yet written anything at that moment (A1). The first transaction writes $500 + 100 = 600$ at t4, and the second writes $500 + 50 = 550$ at t6 (A1). The last COMMIT is the second transaction's, at t7, and it fixes the stored balance at 550 (A1). The first transaction's 600 is not in the database any more: the second transaction wrote over it.

(b) Run in either serial order, the arithmetic gives the same answer. First then second: the first reads 500 and writes 600, then the second reads 600 and writes $600 + 50 = 650$. Second then first: the second reads 500 and writes 550, then the first reads 550 and writes $550 + 100 = 650$ (M1). Both orders give 650, which is what makes 650 the correct result rather than merely one possible result (A1).

The interleaved execution has left 550, so the loss is $650 - 550 = 100$ (A1). That is exactly the amount the first transaction added, which is what a lost update looks like: one transaction's write is entirely overwritten by another's, and the update that is lost is the earlier one.

The property whose role has been defeated is isolation (A1). Isolation is what guarantees that the result of running transactions concurrently is the same as the result of running them in some serial order, and here the concurrent result of 550 matches neither serial order.

Atomicity has not been defeated. Each transaction did what atomicity requires: the first transaction's read and write both took effect and it committed as a unit, and the second's did the same. Atomicity is about a transaction not being half-applied, and neither transaction was half-applied; the first was applied in full and then overwritten in full by a later transaction, which is an ordering fault and not a failure of atomicity. Durability has not been defeated either: both COMMIT statements were honoured and both transactions' effects were persisted, and the persisted value is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with losing committed data. Either answer earns the mark, provided the candidate distinguishes it from isolation.

(c) ROLLBACK undoes the writes of the transaction that issues it, and only while that transaction has not yet committed. In this timeline there is nothing left for it to undo (A1). By t7 both transactions have committed, so neither can be rolled back: a rollback of the first transaction is refused because it has already committed, and a rollback of the second would remove the 550 and leave the account at 500, which is worse, not better. The value the first transaction computed, 600, was overwritten inside the second transaction's write and is no longer held anywhere the database can reach. ROLLBACK recovers a transaction that has failed; it cannot recover a value that a later committed transaction has already replaced.

Making the transactions run for longer, so that they overlap more often, makes the anomaly more likely rather than less. The loss happened because the second transaction's read fell between the first transaction's read and its COMMIT. Widening the interval between a transaction's read and its commit widens exactly the window in which another transaction can read the old value, so the proposal increases the frequency of the fault it is offered as a defence against (A1).

The smallest change to the timeline is to move the second transaction's read so that it happens after the first transaction's COMMIT, that is from t3 to after t5 (A1). If the second transaction reads after t5 it reads 600, and it then writes $600 + 50 = 650$, which is the correct result. Nothing else needs to change: both transactions keep their structure, both still commit, and no statement is rewritten. The change is a change of ordering, and it corresponds to a real mechanism, which is to make the second transaction wait until the first has finished, whether by taking a lock on the row before reading it or by raising the isolation level so that the engine takes one on the transaction's behalf (A1).

The judgement is that this anomaly cannot be prevented using transaction control commands alone (A1). The commands the guide lists are BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK, and between them they let a candidate start a transaction, finish it successfully, or abandon it. None of them constrains when another transaction may read. The fault is in the interleaving, and the interleaving is controlled by locking and by the isolation level, which are properties of how the transaction is declared and of how the engine schedules it rather than commands that a developer issues. A candidate who answers that ROLLBACK can be used to detect and retry the second transaction should be credited for the retry idea, but must also be asked to say what triggers the rollback, since nothing in this timeline fails and so nothing raises an error for the application to catch.
questions.explanation:
This is the classic lost update, and it is worth being precise about why it is hard. The two transactions are individually correct. Each reads the balance, each computes a new balance from what it read, each writes, each commits. There is no statement a reviewer could point at and call wrong. The defect is entirely in the ordering: the second transaction's read falls after the first transaction's read and before the first transaction's COMMIT, which is the one interval in which the value it reads is about to be superseded.

That is why the figure is given as an ordered list rather than as a description. The candidate cannot answer by pattern-matching the word 'transaction' to a list of ACID properties; the properties have to be used to predict an outcome, and then checked against the arithmetic. The item is a harder route to exactly the content the guide names, which is the role of isolation in maintaining integrity.

The loss is exactly 100, the first transaction's increment, and that is not a coincidence of the numbers chosen. When one transaction overwrites another's write with a value computed from a stale read, the surviving value is the later transaction's read plus the later transaction's increment, so the difference from the correct serial result is the earlier transaction's increment in full. A candidate who notices this has understood the mechanism rather than the example, and the answer says so.

Part (c) is written so that the two plausible remedies are both wrong. ROLLBACK cannot help because by the time anyone notices, both transactions have committed, and rolling back the second would discard a correct 50 to remove a wrong 100. Making the transactions longer makes the window wider and the fault commoner. What actually fixes it is a change of ordering, which is to say a lock or an isolation level, and the judgement the part asks for is that the transaction control commands the guide lists do not reach that far. That is a real and examinable point: BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK delimit a transaction, and they do not schedule it.

The item deliberately avoids the terms 'dirty read' and 'non-repeatable read', which belong to a finer-grained taxonomy than the guide asks for. Everything the candidate needs is in the timeline and in the four properties named by A3.3.6.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Reading an append-only load table whose rows supersede one another, where the two natural wrong totals err in opposite directions
questions.question:
A retail group loads its sales data into a warehouse every night. The warehouse never updates a row and never deletes one: each night's load appends new rows, and the table's whole history is still present. The same product can appear in more than one night's load, and more than one source system can report on the same product in the same night.

Two rules govern how the table is read. A row supersedes any earlier row that carries the same product and the same source, so only the newest row for a given product and source is current. Rows from different sources are not alternatives to one another and are added together, because they describe different parts of the same sale. The table is shown in the figure, together with the night on which each row was written.

The operations director has asked for the current total units and the current total revenue, and has been given two different answers by two analysts.

(a)

State the number of rows the table holds, the number of distinct products it holds, and the number of distinct combinations of product and source. Hence state how many of the rows have been superseded, and explain why an append-only table holds more rows than it holds current facts.

[3]

(b)

Determine the current total units and the current total revenue, applying the reading rules given above. State how many of the four rows contribute to your total, and explain for each row that does not contribute why it does not.

[4]

(c)

One analyst adds units and revenue over every row in the table. The other finds the greatest load date in the table and adds only the rows that carry it. Calculate the units and revenue that each analyst reports, and state the direction and the size of the error in each against the correct total. Explain why the correct total is neither of the two answers nor the average of them. Then reach a judgement on which of the two errors the warehouse's own design makes easier to detect, and why.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The table holds four rows. It holds two distinct products, P1 and P2, and three distinct combinations of product and source: P1 from the till, P1 from adjustments, and P2 from the till (A1). One of the four rows has therefore been superseded, since four rows describe three current facts (A1).

An append-only table holds more rows than current facts because it never overwrites. When a source restates its figures for a product, the correction is written as a new row rather than applied to the old one, so both the superseded row and the row that supersedes it remain in the table (A1). This is the property the guide calls time-variant: the table records what was believed at each point in time, not only what is believed now, and the earlier belief is preserved rather than erased.

(b) The current rows are found by taking, for each combination of product and source, the row with the greatest load date.

  • For P1 from the till there are two rows. The row written on 1 April carries 100 units and 2000 revenue, and the row written on 8 April carries 90 units and 1800 revenue. The later row is current, so the April 1 row does not contribute (M1).
  • For P1 from adjustments there is one row, written on 1 April, carrying 50 units and 1000 revenue. Nothing supersedes it, so it is current and it contributes (A1).
  • For P2 from the till there is one row, written on 8 April, carrying 40 units and 800 revenue. It is current and it contributes (A1).

The current totals are therefore $90 + 50 + 40 = 180$ units and $1800 + 1000 + 800 = 3600$ revenue (A1). Three of the four rows contribute. The row that does not is the 1 April row for P1 from the till, and it does not because the 8 April row from the same source for the same product supersedes it.

(c) Adding every row gives $100 + 50 + 90 + 40 = 280$ units and $2000 + 1000 + 1800 + 800 = 5600$ revenue (M1). The error is an over-statement of 100 units and 2000 revenue, and it is exactly the superseded row counted as though it were still current (A1).

Taking the greatest load date, which is 8 April, and adding only the rows that carry it gives $90 + 40 = 130$ units and $1800 + 800 = 2600$ revenue (M1). The error here is an under-statement of 50 units and 1000 revenue, and it is caused by dropping the P1 adjustments row, which was written on 1 April and has never been superseded (A1).

The correct total is 180 units and 3600 revenue, so it is neither 280 and 5600 nor 130 and 2600. It is also not the average of the two revenue figures, which would be $(2600 + 5600)/2 = 4100$ (A1). The two errors do not offset each other because they are not errors of the same kind. The first counts a row that should be excluded; the second excludes a row that should be counted. They happen to be different rows of different sizes, so nothing makes their effects equal and nothing makes them cancel. Treating two wrong answers as bracketing the right one is only sound when the errors are known to be symmetric, and nothing here establishes that (A1).

The judgement is that the warehouse's design makes the first error the easier of the two to detect (A1). The over-statement is caused by a row that is still physically present and still carries its original load date, so the row that should have been excluded can be found by comparing load dates within a product and source: wherever two rows share a product and a source, the older one is superseded, and the table itself supplies the evidence. The under-statement is caused by a row that has been silently omitted. Nothing in the data records the omission, because the row that was left out is indistinguishable from the rows that were correctly left out, and the query that produced the figure returns a smaller number with no indication that anything is missing (A1). An append-only design therefore makes the error of counting too much self-diagnosing and the error of counting too little invisible, which is the reason the reading rule has to be stated explicitly rather than inferred from the data.
questions.explanation:
An append-only table is a log of what was reported, not a picture of what is true. That is its strength and it is also the reason it cannot be summed naively. Every aggregate over such a table has to be paired with a rule that says which rows are current, and the rule has to be applied at the grain of the thing that can be restated. Here the grain is the pair of product and source, because the till and the adjustments ledger report on the same product independently and neither supersedes the other.

The two wrong answers are the two ways of getting the grain wrong. Summing every row applies no rule at all. Filtering on the greatest load date applies a rule at the wrong grain: it treats a load as the unit that supersedes, so a source that did not report on the most recent night disappears from the total. The second error is the more interesting one because the query looks principled. It contains a deliberate filter, it produces a smaller and therefore apparently safer number, and it is wrong because the thing being superseded is a row and not a night.

The two errors run in opposite directions, which is what makes the item a test of reasoning rather than of arithmetic. A candidate who computes both and finds one high and one low may be tempted to conclude that the truth lies between them, and the average of 4100 is not the truth. Bracket-and-average is only valid when the two errors are known to be of comparable size and opposite sign, and here they are 2000 and 1000 in opposite directions, which is a ratio of two to one and not a symmetry.

The final judgement is about the design rather than the query. Because the warehouse never deletes, the superseded row is still there and can be found by a rule that the table itself supports; the error of counting it is therefore a rule that can be checked against the data. The error of dropping a row leaves the data consistent with the wrong answer, so no amount of inspection of the table will reveal it. That asymmetry is the practical reason a warehouse specification states the currency rule rather than leaving it to be inferred, and it is the point the part is asking the candidate to reach.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A rule-based packet filter in which one rule is unreachable because a broader rule with the same destination pattern is evaluated first
questions.question:
A small research institute has three networks. Its staff work from the internet, its system administrators work from an administration subnet at 10.0.9.0/24, and its servers sit in a server subnet at 10.0.5.0/24. The boundary is a stateless packet filter that holds an ordered list of rules. The filter compares a flow against the rules from the top of the list downwards, and the first rule whose source, destination and port all match the flow decides the action; no later rule is consulted, whether the action was ALLOW or DENY. The last rule in the list is the catch-all.

The administrator has been asked to allow the system administrators to reach the servers over SSH from the administration subnet, while denying every other flow that enters the server subnet. The rules currently in the filter, and two flows that were captured at the boundary, are shown in the figure. The server subnet holds the host 10.0.5.20, which runs the public web service, and the host 10.0.5.31, which the administrators manage.

(a)

Using the rule table, determine the action the filter takes for each of the two flows in the figure, and name the number of the rule that decides each one. For each flow, show why every rule above the deciding rule fails to match it.

[3]

(b)

Explain why rule 3 never decides the action for any flow at all, whatever its source address and whatever port it carries. Your answer must refer to the destination pattern in rule 3, to the destination pattern in the rule above it, and to the position of that rule in the list, and must state the property of the two patterns that makes the outcome unavoidable.

[4]

(c)

State the smallest change to the table that restores the administrator's intention, and evaluate one security consequence of making that change. Your answer should state how many hosts in the server subnet the restored rule would reach, explain what the rule grants to every device on the administration subnet, and state whether rule 4 should be kept.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Flow 1 runs from 203.0.113.7 to 10.0.5.20 on port 443. Rule 1 has a destination of exactly 10.0.5.20 and a port of 443, and its source is a wildcard, so it matches and the action is ALLOW (A1). Rule 2 is never consulted, because the filter stops at the first match and rule 1 sits above it.

Flow 2 runs from 10.0.9.14 to 10.0.5.31 on port 22. Rule 1 does not match it: the destination 10.0.5.31 is a different host from 10.0.5.20, and the port 22 is a different port from 443 (A1). Rule 2 has a destination of 10.0.5.0/24 and a port wildcard, so it matches any host in the server subnet on any port. The address 10.0.5.31 lies in 10.0.5.0/24, so rule 2 matches and the action is DENY (A1). Rule 3 is not consulted, even though its source, destination and port all describe flow 2 exactly.

(b) Rule 3 requires a destination in 10.0.5.0/24 and a port of 22, from a source in 10.0.9.0/24. Rule 2 requires a destination in 10.0.5.0/24, and its source and port are both wildcards (A1). Every flow that can match rule 3 therefore also matches rule 2: the set of destinations rule 3 accepts is the whole server subnet, and that is exactly the set of destinations rule 2 accepts, so rule 3 adds no destination that rule 2 does not already cover (A1).

Rule 2 also accepts every source and every port, so it cannot fail on a flow that rule 3 would have accepted. Since rule 2 sits above rule 3 in the list, the filter reaches rule 2 first for every such flow, matches it, and stops (A1). The property that makes this unavoidable is that rule 2's match set is a superset of rule 3's, and a superset earlier in a first-match list makes the rule below it unreachable. It is not a configuration error that a validation check would catch by looking at rule 3 alone: rule 3 is well formed, and it is only the pair of rules and their order that makes it dead (A1).

(c) The smallest change is to exchange the positions of rule 2 and rule 3, so that the SSH allowance is evaluated before the blanket denial (A1). After the exchange, flow 2 is matched by rule 3 and is ALLOWed, while flow 1 is still matched by rule 1 and unaffected, and a flow into the server subnet from anywhere other than the administration subnet still falls through to rule 2 and is denied (A1).

The security consequence is that the restored rule is written over a subnet, not over a host. Its destination is 10.0.5.0/24, which is 254 usable addresses, and its source is 10.0.9.0/24, which is another 254 (A1). The administrator wanted the system administrators to manage 10.0.5.31; the rule as written grants SSH access from every device on the administration subnet to every host in the server subnet, including the public web host at 10.0.5.20. One compromised workstation on the administration network therefore has an SSH path to the whole server estate, and the workstation does not need any privilege beyond an address in the subnet. Narrowing rule 3's destination to the hosts that actually need managing, or pairing it with multifactor authentication, would keep the intent while removing the reach (A1).

Rule 4 should be kept. It is the default deny, and it is the reason the table fails closed: anything that matches no earlier rule is dropped. Removing it would leave unmatched traffic with no decision, which in most implementations means it is permitted, so the table would move from denying by default to allowing by default and every flow the other rules do not name would be admitted. The correct reading of rule 4 is that it is not redundant with rule 2; rule 2 denies the server subnet, and rule 4 denies everything else, including flows to the rest of the estate (A1).
questions.explanation:
A stateless packet filter is an ordered list, and its semantics are first-match. Two consequences follow that are easy to state and easy to get wrong. The first is that the order carries meaning that no individual rule expresses: the same four rules in a different order are a different filter. The second is that a rule can be well formed, correct in its own fields, and still never decide anything, because a rule above it matches everything it would have matched. That condition is called shadowing, and it is the reason a firewall audit compares rules in pairs rather than reading them one at a time.

The shadowing here is exact rather than partial. Rule 3's destination is 10.0.5.0/24 and rule 2's destination is 10.0.5.0/24, so the two destination sets are not merely overlapping, they are identical; rule 2 is broader only in that its source and port are wildcards. A candidate can see this without enumerating addresses, and the verification does enumerate them, all 256 of them, to confirm that no host in the server subnet escapes rule 2's pattern.

The item is written so that the wrong answer is the one that looks most like diligence. A candidate who reads the table and looks for the rule about SSH finds rule 3, and rule 3 says exactly what the administrator intended. The mistake is not misreading the rule; it is treating a list as a set. The two flows in the figure are chosen so that the list and the set give different answers: flow 2 is precisely the flow rule 3 was written for, and the list denies it.

The final part makes the repair carry a cost, which is what turns the item from a puzzle into an evaluation. Restoring the intention is one line of reordering, and it simultaneously widens the reach of the allowance from one host to a subnet of 254, because the rule was always written over a subnet and the shadowing was hiding that. So the correct answer has to hold two things at once: the rule was dead, and reviving it grants more than the administrator thought it did. That is the sense in which rule-based filtering has limitations as well as strengths, which is the language the guide uses for this node.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Withdrawn consent against a model that was trained before the withdrawal, where deleting the records changes the corpus but not the model
questions.question:
A clinic uses a machine-learning model to prioritise referrals. The model has been through two runs. The first trained a model from scratch on the whole corpus as it stood at that date. The second produced the model that is currently deployed by continuing to train the first model on records that had arrived since.

Patients consent to their records being used for research, and consent may be withdrawn at any time. A group of patients has now withdrawn consent, and their records must no longer be used. The clinic has deleted those records from the corpus and has asked for advice on what else, if anything, is required before the deployed model can be described as compliant.

The figure gives the dates of the two runs, the size of the corpus at each point, the number of records withdrawn, and how those withdrawn records are distributed between the two runs. The clinic intends to describe the deployed model as compliant once the deletions are complete.

(a)

Using the figure, determine the number of records the corpus holds immediately before the deletions and immediately after them, and determine how many of the withdrawn records were used by the run that trained the first model and how many by the run that produced the deployed model.

[3]

(b)

Determine how many of the withdrawn records were never used in any training run at all, and explain what your answer implies for the two models that have already been produced. Your answer should state what deleting the records changes about those models and what it does not change.

[4]

(c)

The team proposes to continue training the deployed model on the remaining records and then to describe it as compliant. Evaluate that proposal. Your answer should state how many records a model retrained from scratch would be trained on, express the reduction in training data as a percentage of the corpus the deployed model was built from, explain why that percentage is small while the compliance question is not, and reach a judgement on which remedy the withdrawals require.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Before the deletions the corpus holds the 48 000 records the first run trained on plus the 12 000 that arrived afterwards, which is 60 000 (A1). After the 900 withdrawn records are deleted it holds $60\,000 - 900 = 59\,100$ (A1).

The withdrawn records are not all in the same run. Of the 900, 620 had already been used by the run that trained the first model, because they were part of the 48 000. The remaining 280 arrived with the 12 000 and were used by the run that produced the deployed model (A1).

(b) The two runs between them used $620 + 280 = 900$ of the withdrawn records, so the number that were never used in any training run is $900 - 900 = 0$ (A1). Every withdrawn record contributed to at least one training run.

The implication is that both models were trained on data that must no longer be used. The first model was trained on a corpus that contained 620 of the withdrawn records, so its parameters were computed in part from them (A1). The deployed model was produced by continuing to train that first model, so it inherits everything the first model learned and adds what it learned from the remaining 280; its parameters are therefore a function of all 900 (A1).

Deleting the records changes the corpus and does not change either model. What it changes is what the clinic holds and what any future training run would be able to use. What it does not change is what the models already contain: a trained model is a set of parameter values, and those values were fixed at the moment the run finished. They do not refer back to the corpus, and they are not recomputed when the corpus changes. Removing a row from the corpus is therefore not the same operation as removing that row's influence from the model, and only the first of the two has happened (A1).

(c) A model retrained from scratch would be trained on the 59 100 records that remain, because a run that starts from an untrained model and uses only the current corpus would have no access to the 900 (A1).

The reduction in training data is $900/60\,000 = 0.015$, which is 1.5 per cent (A1). That is a small number, and the reason it does not settle the question is that it measures the wrong thing. It compares the size of the remaining corpus with the size of the old one, and it would only be relevant if the obligation were to avoid training on a large fraction of the data. The obligation is to avoid using the withdrawn records at all, and by that measure the withdrawn records are not 1.5 per cent of anything: all 900 of them were used, so 100 per cent of the withdrawn records are represented in the deployed model. A proportion can be made to look small by choosing a large denominator, and the denominator here is irrelevant to whether the obligation has been met (A1).

The proposal to continue training the deployed model on the remaining records does not meet it. Continuing to train starts from the deployed model's existing parameters, and those parameters already encode the withdrawn records. Further training on the remaining 59 100 records moves the parameters towards what those records imply, but it provides no mechanism that removes the influence the earlier records had on the point it started from. In the limit, training for long enough on the remaining records would reduce the dependence on the withdrawn ones, but the proposal does not say how long, and there is no measurement in the figure or in the proposal that would show when the influence had gone (A1).

The judgement is that the withdrawals require the model to be retrained from scratch on the remaining corpus, or rebuilt by a method that can demonstrate the removal of the withdrawn records' influence and is accepted as doing so (A1). Retraining from scratch is the remedy that follows from the evidence in the figure, because it is the only one of the two proposals whose training data can be stated exactly, and the statement is that it contains none of the 900. It is also the more expensive of the two, and the cost is the reason the proposal in the question was made. The clinic should also record what happened rather than only what was done, since the models were trained on the withdrawn data and any account of the deployed system that omits this is incomplete: accountability here means being able to say which corpus produced the model that is making decisions about patients, and that is a question about the past that deleting records now cannot answer (A1).
questions.explanation:
The gap this item is built on is the gap between a dataset and a model trained on it. A dataset is a collection that can be edited: a row can be removed and the collection is then smaller. A trained model is a set of parameter values produced by a process that read the dataset once, and the values do not contain the dataset. They contain whatever the training process made of it. So an obligation that says 'do not use this record' cannot be discharged by editing the collection, because the use has already happened and its result is elsewhere.

The figure is built so that the arithmetic makes this concrete rather than theoretical. The withdrawal is split across the two runs, 620 and 280, so that neither model can be cleared by looking at one of them. The second run is a continuation of the first, so its dependence on the first run's data is not a matter of degree: the deployed model's parameters are a function of everything the first model saw. And the deletion is 1.5 per cent of the corpus, which is small enough that a team looking at the size of the change would conclude it had done something minor and sufficient.

The percentage is the trap. It is computed correctly and it answers a question nobody asked. The obligation is about a set of records, and the fraction of those records that were used is 100 per cent, which is the figure that matters. The item asks the candidate to hold both numbers at once and to say which one bears on compliance, which is the same discipline the guide asks for when it lists transparency and accountability alongside consent as ethical issues for machine learning.

The judgement is deliberately left with two acceptable routes. Retraining from scratch is the route the evidence in the figure supports directly, because the training set of the new model can be stated exactly and it contains none of the 900. An accepted unlearning method is the other route, and it is admitted only with the condition that removal of the influence has to be demonstrated, which keeps the item honest about a methodology that is still developing. What the item does not admit is the third route, which is to continue training and hope, and the reason is that there is no measurement in the problem that would show when the hope had been realised.

Nothing in the item requires knowledge outside the guide. Consent, accountability, transparency and privacy are all named in A4.4.1, and the machine-learning concepts used here, training and continued training, are the ordinary vocabulary of the topic rather than an additional technique.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.4 Binary search on an array that is ordered except for one transposed pair
questions.question:
The figure shows an array of twelve entries held in positions numbered 0 to 11. Reading from position 0 the values are 2, 5, 8, 21, 13, 34, 55, 89, 144, 233, 377 and 610.

Eleven of the twelve entries are in ascending order. Exactly one pair of adjacent entries has been transposed, and the two entries concerned are shaded in the figure. The array belongs to a frozen data set. Its contents may not be changed, no entry may be moved, and the array may not be re-sorted or copied into a new order.

A binary search is used to look for the target value 13. The implementation takes the middle position as the integer part of (lo + hi) divided by 2, compares the entry at that position with the target, moves lo to that position plus one when the entry is smaller than the target, and moves hi to that position minus one when the entry is larger. The figure traces the comparisons the search makes. An entry that has been compared once is never compared again.

(a) State the position and the value examined at each of the three comparisons, and state the position at which 13 is stored.

(b) Explain why the search reports that 13 is absent although 13 is stored in the array, and state the property of the data that the search relies on.

(c) Determine the number of comparisons a linear search from position 0 makes before it finds 13, and determine how many of the twelve stored values this binary search still locates.

(a)

State the position and the value examined at each of the three comparisons the search makes, and state the position at which the value 13 is stored.

[2]

(b)

Explain why the search reports that 13 is absent although 13 is stored in the array, and state the property of the stored data that the search relies on.

[2]

(c)

Determine the number of comparisons a linear search from position 0 makes before it finds 13, and determine how many of the twelve stored values this binary search still locates.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) The first comparison is at position 5, holding 34. Because 34 is greater than the target, hi becomes 4. The second comparison is at position (0 + 4) / 2 = 2, holding 8. Because 8 is less than the target, lo becomes 3. The third comparison is at position (3 + 4) / 2 = 3, holding 21, and because 21 is greater than the target, hi becomes 2 (A1). The value 13 is stored at position 4, one place to the right of the entry it was compared against (A1).

(b) Discarding a half of the array is legitimate only when the entries are in ascending order. In that case an entry greater than the target proves that every entry to its right is at least as great and therefore also greater than the target, so the whole right-hand block can be abandoned with no risk of abandoning the target. That inference is what the third comparison makes, and here it is false: position 3 holds 21 and position 4 holds 13, so the entry immediately to the right is smaller than the entry that was compared, and the half thrown away contains the value being sought. After the third comparison hi has become 2 while lo is 3, so lo is greater than hi, the interval is empty, the loop terminates and the search reports that 13 is not present (M1). The search is behaving correctly as written; the array is not sorted, and sorted order, or at least non-decreasing order, is the precondition it depends on (A1). One adjacent transposition is enough to break it, and the figure places the transposition so that the third comparison lands on the larger of the two entries and draws the false inference from it.

(c) A linear search from position 0 compares 2 with the target, then 5, then 8, then 21, and only at the fifth comparison reaches position 4, where the entry is 13. It therefore makes five comparisons (A1). The binary search still locates eleven of the twelve stored values. Every value other than 13 is found at the position where it is stored, including 21 at position 3, because the comparison at position 3 succeeds and the search stops before any half is discarded. The single value that is unreachable is 13 itself, the smaller of the two transposed entries: it has moved to a position to the right of a larger value, so a comparison against that larger value consults the ordering, finds the ordering wrong, and discards the half that holds the target. The other transposed entry, 21, has moved one place to the left and remains reachable, which is why exactly one value, and not two, is lost (A1). In general a single swap that puts a larger entry before a smaller one can hide the smaller entry and only the smaller entry, because it is the smaller entry that now lies on the far side of a larger neighbour.
questions.explanation:
The item is short and needs almost no arithmetic. What it needs is for the candidate to notice that the array is not what it appears to be, and that the trace in the figure is not an error but a consequence. Every textbook figure for binary search shows a sorted array, so the sortedness is read off the picture and never checked, and the precondition is learned as a remark attached to the algorithm rather than as a load-bearing assumption.

The trace is chosen so that the failure looks like ordinary progress. The first comparison discards the top half, which is correct and unremarkable. The second discards positions 0 and 1, which is also correct: 2 and 5 really are both less than 13, so those two entries are safely abandoned. The third comparison is the one that matters, and it reports 21, a value that is genuinely greater than the target. Every comparison has produced a true statement about the entry it examined. What the search then does with the last true statement is to generalise from it to a whole block of the array, and that generalisation is the only step that is false.

The count in part (c) is where the lesson becomes quantitative. Binary search does not merely fail here; it fails on one of twelve values while succeeding on the other eleven, and the value it loses is the smaller of the two transposed entries. So the damage from a single transposition is exactly one value, and it is predictable in advance: a swap that places a larger entry before a smaller one can hide the smaller entry, and nothing else. That is worth knowing because it tells you which way the failure will show up. A test suite that checks a handful of values chosen from the array will very likely pass, since only one value in twelve is affected, and the defect will surface in production on the one value nobody sampled.

It is also worth stating plainly why linear search is the right tool here. The array is frozen, it is unordered in one place, and no amount of cleverness in the search can recover an ordering that is not there. Five comparisons against a linear scan is the honest cost, and the same five comparisons do not depend on the array being sorted at all. When the data cannot be re-ordered and cannot be trusted to satisfy a precondition, the algorithm that does not need the precondition is the correct choice, whatever its asymptotic cost.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.2 Two hash tables of different sizes holding the same six keys: the load factor is not what decides the number of collisions
questions.question:
A program stores six records in a hash table. Each record is 16 bytes long and they lie consecutively in a memory image, so the six keys passed to the hash function are the byte offsets 4096, 4112, 4128, 4144, 4160 and 4176.

The hash function is h(k) = k mod m, where m is the size of the table and the result is the slot number. Collisions are resolved by chaining, so every slot holds a list of the keys that hash to it and a lookup walks that list. The figure shows the same six keys in two tables, one of size 16 and one of size 17. The load factor of a table is the number of stored keys divided by the number of slots.

A colleague proposes to enlarge the table from 17 slots to 20 slots in order to reduce the number of collisions.

(a) Calculate the load factor of each of the two tables shown, and state the number of slots occupied in each.

(b) Explain why the table of size 16 stores all six keys in one slot although its load factor is the lower of the two, and state which quantity decides how the keys are distributed.

(c) Determine the number of slots occupied for table sizes 8, 16, 17 and 20, and hence determine the smallest table size of 20 or less that stores all six keys in distinct slots.

(a)

Calculate the load factor of each of the two tables shown, and state the number of slots occupied by the six keys in each table.

[2]

(b)

Explain why the table of size 16 stores all six keys in a single slot although its load factor is the lower of the two, and state which quantity decides how the keys are distributed.

[2]

(c)

Determine the number of slots occupied for table sizes 8, 16, 17 and 20, and hence determine the smallest table size of 20 or less that stores all six keys in distinct slots.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) The table of size 16 holds six keys in sixteen slots, so its load factor is 6 / 16 = 0.375 (A1). The table of size 17 holds the same six keys in seventeen slots, so its load factor is 6 / 17 = 0.353 to three decimal places, which is lower. The table of size 16 occupies one slot, because every key hashes to slot 0: 4096 is a multiple of 16, and every other key is 4096 plus a multiple of 16, so every key leaves the same remainder, zero. The table of size 17 occupies six slots, holding 4096 in slot 16, 4112 in slot 15, 4128 in slot 14, 4144 in slot 13, 4160 in slot 12 and 4176 in slot 11 (A1).

(b) The load factor measures how full a table is, not how the keys are arranged within it, and those are different questions. Here all six keys are congruent modulo 16 because the gap between consecutive keys is 16 and 16 divides 16 exactly, so the remainder is the same for every one of them and the chain has length six whatever the load factor says (M1). In the table of size 17 the same gap of 16 shares no common factor with 17, which is prime, so adding 16 repeatedly cycles through six different remainders before repeating. The quantity that decides the distribution is the relationship between the stride, 16, and the table size: the keys collide when the stride and the size have a common factor, and in the extreme case of the size dividing the stride exactly, every key lands in the same slot (A1). A table of size 8 or 16 divides the stride and collapses completely, while a table of size 17 is coprime to it and separates the keys perfectly.

(c) For a table of size 8 every offset is a multiple of 8, so all six keys hash to slot 0 and one slot is occupied. For size 16 the same collapse gives one slot. For size 17 the six remainders are 16, 15, 14, 13, 12 and 11, all different, so six slots are occupied (A1). For size 20 the key 4096 gives remainder 16 and the key 4176 gives remainder 16 as well, because 4176 = 4096 + 80 and 80 is a multiple of 20; the six remainders are 16, 12, 8, 4, 0 and 16, so five slots are occupied. The smallest size of 20 or less that separates all six keys is 7: the remainders there are 1, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 6, six distinct values, and no size below 7 can separate six keys because it does not have six slots (A1). The proposal to enlarge the table from 17 slots to 20 slots would therefore make matters worse rather than better, reducing the number of occupied slots from six to five and lengthening the chain in slot 16 to two keys.
questions.explanation:
The two panels in the figure are arranged so that the smaller table is the better one and the difference is not small. Six keys in one chain against six keys in six chains is a factor of six in the average lookup cost, and the tables it is choosing between have load factors of 0.375 and 0.353, a difference of about six per cent. Anyone who ranks the two by load factor gets the order exactly wrong, and does so with a number that is an accepted measure and is not being misused: the load factor is genuinely 0.375, and it genuinely is lower than 0.353. The error is not arithmetic, it is choosing a measure that does not answer the question.

What does answer the question is the arithmetic of the stride. The keys are not arbitrary; they are consecutive 16-byte records, which is what a real allocator produces, and every key therefore differs from the first by a multiple of 16. The remainder after division by a table size m is the same for all six keys exactly when m divides every one of the five gaps, that is when m divides 16. Sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 destroy the table; every other size gives some spreading, and a size coprime to 16 gives complete spreading, because then the five additions of 16 generate five distinct non-zero residues. Seventeen is prime and coprime to 16, which is why it is perfect; fourteen is not coprime either, but because 16 has only one factor of 2 above 8 the multiples 16, 32, 48, 64 and 80 reduced modulo 14 give 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, which are still six distinct offsets, so it works as well.

The general lesson is that a hash function built from the identity of a key and a modulus is only as good as the relationship between the data and the modulus, and that a prime table size is the standard defence precisely because it removes the possibility of a common factor.
