It is worth noticing that the colleague in the question makes a mistake that looks like prudence. Enlarging a table is the ordinary response to collisions, it costs memory, and here it reduces the number of occupied slots while increasing the longest chain. Raising a resource is not the same as fixing a distribution.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A2.2 Network architecture: device roles, subnets and broadcast domains
questions.question:
The figure shows the network of a small company. A router is connected to two switches, and three personal computers are connected to each switch. The two subnets are labelled in the figure, and the two addresses shown on the links from the router are the addresses of the router's own interfaces, one in each subnet. The company has been allocated the block 192.168.10.0/24 and has decided to use only the first half of it. Each computer is configured with the address of the router interface on its own subnet as its default gateway. Answer all parts with reference to the figure, and show your working where a calculation is involved.

(a)

Explain the role of the switch and the role of the router in this topology, making clear what each device examines when it forwards traffic and what each device does not do.

[3]

(b)

Determine the number of usable host addresses available in each of the two subnets shown, and state the subnet mask for these subnets in dotted decimal notation.

[3]

(c)

Explain why each computer must be configured with the address of the router interface on its own subnet as its default gateway, and why the gateway address must lie inside the same subnet as the computer.

[4]

(d)

Explain why the company has arranged the network as two subnets rather than as a single 192.168.10.0/24 network, and state the effect of the arrangement on the number of computers that receive a broadcast sent by PC1.

[4]

(e)

A technician suggests removing both switches and connecting all six computers to a single switch, leaving the router in place. Explain the effect of this change on the network, referring to broadcast domains and to the addresses that would have to be assigned.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) A switch operates inside a single subnet and forwards frames using the destination MAC address, which it learns by recording the source address of every frame it receives. (M1) It does not examine IP addresses and it does not change the addresses in the frames it forwards, so it cannot connect two different subnets to one another. (A1) A router operates between subnets: it examines the destination IP address of each packet, consults its routing table, and forwards the packet out of the interface that leads towards the destination network, rewriting the link-layer addresses in the process. (A1) The router is therefore the boundary of each broadcast domain, and it does not forward broadcast frames from one of its interfaces to another.

(b) Each subnet has a /26 prefix, so 32 - 26 = 6 bits remain for host addresses and each subnet contains 2^6 = 64 addresses in total. (M1) The lowest address in each block is the network address and the highest is the broadcast address, and neither can be assigned to a host, so each subnet provides 62 usable host addresses. (A1) A /26 prefix means the first 26 bits of the mask are set, so the mask is 255.255.255.192. (A1)

(c) A computer can deliver a frame directly only to another device on the same link, and to do that it must know the destination's MAC address. (M1) When the destination IP address is not in the computer's own subnet, there is no device on the link that can accept the frame on the destination's behalf, so the computer must hand the packet to a router that is on its link and let the router deal with it. (A1) The default gateway is that router, and it must be inside the computer's own subnet, because otherwise the computer would have no way of reaching it at all: it would need a gateway to reach the gateway. (M1) If the gateway were omitted, each computer could still exchange traffic with the other computers on its own switch, but no packet could cross to the other subnet and nothing could reach the internet. (A1)

(d) Dividing the block into two subnets splits one broadcast domain into two. (M1) A broadcast frame sent by PC1 is forwarded by the switch to every port in its own subnet but is not forwarded by the router into the other subnet, so only the other two computers on switch A receive it, rather than all six. (A1) This reduces the amount of broadcast traffic each computer has to process and the amount of processing it triggers. (A1) It also allows the two subnets to be given different access rules, so a fault or a compromised machine on one subnet does not automatically affect the other. (A1)

(e) A single switch would place all six computers in one broadcast domain, because a switch does not partition broadcast traffic. (M1) The two /26 subnets could not simply be kept as they are, because all six computers would then be on the same link and a broadcast from any of them would reach the other five, which defeats the purpose of the split. (A1) Either the computers would all have to be re-addressed into one subnet, or the single switch would have to be configured with virtual local area networks so that the two logical subnets are kept apart, in which case the router would need an interface, or a sub-interface, in each. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The figure looks unremarkable, and that is the point: there is no trick in the topology, so every mark depends on knowing what each device actually does. A switch is a link-layer device. It learns which MAC address is reachable through which port and forwards frames accordingly, and it neither reads nor rewrites IP addresses. A router is an internet-layer device. It reads the destination IP address of every packet, chooses an outgoing interface from its routing table, and forwards the packet on. Because of that difference, a switch cannot separate two subnets and a router is the boundary of a broadcast domain.

Part (b) is arithmetic, but the arithmetic is where candidates lose marks. A /26 leaves six host bits, so each subnet holds 64 addresses, but the first is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, and neither may be given to a host. The answer is 62, not 64. The mask is 255.255.255.192, which is the first three octets set plus the top two bits of the fourth, since 26 = 8 + 8 + 8 + 2.

Part (c) is about a constraint that is easy to state and easy to get wrong. A computer with an address in 192.168.10.0/26 can send a frame directly to any device in 192.168.10.1 to 192.168.10.62, because they share a link. A computer in the other subnet is not on that link, so the frame has to be addressed to a router that is, and the router then forwards the packet onwards. That is why the gateway must lie inside the computer's own subnet: a computer reaches its gateway by the same direct mechanism it uses for any local device. A gateway outside the subnet would be unreachable, because reaching it would itself require a gateway.

Part (d) connects the addressing decision to the traffic. Splitting the block in two halves the size of each broadcast domain, so a broadcast from PC1 reaches the other two computers on switch A and stops at the router. In a network of six computers that saves very little, but the principle scales: in a single flat network of several hundred hosts, every broadcast interrupts every host.

Part (e) is the part that separates understanding from vocabulary. Removing the switches looks like a simplification, but a single switch carrying all six computers creates one broadcast domain, not two. The two subnets could only be preserved by configuring the switch with VLANs, which is exactly the work the second switch was doing for free. A candidate who says the network would simply be faster has not understood what a switch does.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B4 Abstract data types
questions.question:
The central system must (i) buffer sightings at the gantry, (ii) discard duplicate sightings of the same plate within a 24-hour window, and (iii) merge batches that arrive out of order into one chronological list.

(a)

Explain why a queue is a suitable abstract data type for the gantry's local buffer, and explain one advantage of implementing that queue as a circular queue rather than a non-circular one in this context.

[4]

(b)

Two designs are proposed for discarding duplicates. Design 1 keeps accepted plates in an array and uses linear search. Design 2 keeps accepted plates in a binary search tree keyed on the plate.

For $n$ accepted plates, state the worst-case time complexity of a single membership test for each design, and evaluate which design is preferable for a system handling 40 000 plates per day.

[4]

(c)

Describe, using pseudocode or structured English, an algorithm that merges two batches, each already sorted by timestamp, into a single chronological list. State the time complexity of your algorithm in terms of the batch sizes $p$ and $q$.

[5]

(d)

Number plates are issued in blocks, so plates arriving at a gantry are often already in near-alphabetical order. Explain the consequence of this for the shape and performance of the binary search tree in Design 2, and describe one change that would avoid the problem.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) A queue is suitable because sightings must be removed in the same order in which they arrive: FIFO matches exactly the behaviour of a buffer that is filled by the plate reader and drained by the upload process, whereas a stack would upload the most recent sighting first and destroy the chronological order. (A1)(A1)

The buffer is drained completely every 15 minutes and then refilled, so with a non-circular (linear) queue the front and rear pointers march steadily towards the end of the array; the array appears full even when the queue is nearly empty, and the pointers must be reset or the contents shifted. (M1) In a circular queue the vacated positions at the front are reused as the rear wraps around, so no shifting is needed and the fixed memory allocated to the buffer is used repeatedly — important on an embedded gantry controller with limited RAM. (A1)

(b) Design 1: $O(n)$ — in the worst case (a plate that is not present, or the last element) every one of the $n$ entries must be examined. (A1)

Design 2: $O(\log n)$ for a balanced tree — each comparison halves the remaining search space, so the number of comparisons grows as $\log_{2}n$. (A1)

At 40 000 plates, $\log_{2}(40\,000)\approx15.3$, so Design 2 needs about 15 comparisons per test against up to 40 000 for Design 1 — roughly a factor of 2 600. (M1) Across 40 000 tests per day this is the difference between about $1.6\times10^{9}$ and about $6\times10^{5}$ comparisons per day, so Design 1 is not viable at this volume; Design 2 is clearly preferable. (A1)

(c) Two pointers walk the two batches together, always taking the smaller of the two current timestamps:

MERGE(A, B)                       // A has p items, B has q items, each sorted by timestamp
    i = 0
    j = 0
    C = empty list
    while i < p and j < q         // both batches still have items
        if A[i].timestamp <= B[j].timestamp
            append A[i] to C
            i = i + 1
        else
            append B[j] to C
            j = j + 1
        end if
    end while
    while i < p                   // copy any remainder of A
        append A[i] to C
        i = i + 1
    end while
    while j < q                   // copy any remainder of B
        append B[j] to C
        j = j + 1
    end while
    return C
end MERGE

Award up to (M1) for the two-pointer idea, (A1) for comparing the two current timestamps and appending the smaller, (M1) for terminating when one batch is exhausted, (A1) for correctly copying the remainder of the other batch, and (A1) for stable handling of equal timestamps (using <= rather than <).

Each item is examined and appended exactly once, so the time complexity is $O(p+q)$; the space complexity is also $O(p+q)$ for the merged list. No sorting is required, because both inputs are already sorted.

(d) Inserting keys that are already in order makes every new key the rightmost (or leftmost) node, so the tree never branches: it degenerates into a structure with one node per level — effectively a linked list of height $n$. (A1) The search cost then becomes $O(n)$ rather than $O(\log n)$, so Design 2 loses the entire advantage identified in (b) precisely when the data are easiest to predict. (A1)

One fix: build the tree from the sorted keys by choosing the median as the root and recursing on each half, which produces a balanced tree of height $\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil$. Alternative acceptable fixes: use a self-balancing tree (AVL or red-black) that rebalances on insertion, or shuffle the insertion order. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question looks like an ADT-recall question and is not one. The marking points that separate candidates are all quantitative or conditional:

  • In (b) the phrase 'a binary search tree is faster' is worth nothing on its own; the marks are for turning $\log_{2}(40\,000)\approx15$ into a comparison count and then into a per-day total. Students habitually state complexity classes without evaluating them against a real data volume, which is exactly what the command term asks for here.
  • In (c) the trap is to sort. Both inputs are already sorted, so the merge is linear; a candidate who concatenates and sorts gets the right answer for the wrong reason and at much greater cost. The stability detail (<= rather than <) matters in practice because two gantries can legitimately record the same plate within the same second.
  • In (d) the intended insight is that an ADT's advertised complexity is conditional on an assumption about the data. Keys arriving in sorted order is the canonical case where a binary search tree silently degrades to $O(n)$ — the structure students are taught as 'the efficient one' becomes the worst possible shape. Recognising that complexity claims carry assumptions is the transferable idea.

Classic wrong turns: describing a stack rather than a queue in (a); claiming a circular queue 'has no limit'; and answering (d) with 'use a hash table' without explaining why that helps.

Two further wrong turns recur. In (b) candidates quote the *average* case — 'linear search finds the plate about halfway, so $O(n/2)$' — when the question asks for the worst case; halving $n$ does not change the complexity class, and the two designs stay separated by orders of magnitude. In (c) candidates reach for a sort because 'merging' sounds like 'ordering', when the whole point is that each batch is already ordered: a solution that concatenates and re-sorts has thrown away the only structure the question supplied.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1 Computer fundamentals
questions.question:
The drone's on-board computer has a general-purpose CPU and a separate GPU.

(a)

Describe how the control unit, the ALU and the registers interact during one fetch–decode–execute cycle.

[4]

(b)

The obstacle-detection workload runs on the GPU rather than the CPU. Explain two architectural differences between a CPU and a GPU and, for each, why it matters for this task. (HL only)

[4]

(c)

The camera produces $1280\times720$ pixel frames at 24 bits per pixel and 30 frames per second.

(i) Calculate the uncompressed data rate in MB per second.

(ii) A codec compresses the video by a factor of 40. Calculate the storage required for a 90-second flight.

[4]

(d)

The flight-control software is written in a high-level language. Evaluate whether it should be compiled or interpreted for the deployed drone. (HL only)

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Award up to four points from:

  • The program counter / control unit holds the address of the next instruction and copies it into the memory address register; the instruction is fetched from memory into the memory data register and then into the instruction register. (A1)
  • The control unit decodes the instruction — determining the opcode and the operands — and sends control signals along the control bus to coordinate the other components. (A1)
  • The ALU performs the actual operation (arithmetic such as adding a sensor offset, or a logical comparison such as testing whether a distance is below a threshold) on data held in registers, setting status/flag bits as a result. (A1)
  • Registers hold the instruction, the operands and the intermediate results, giving much faster access than main memory; the result is written back to a register or to memory and the cycle repeats. (A1)

(b) Award two differences, each with a reason:

| | CPU | GPU | Why it matters here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core design | Few cores, each large, complex and optimised for sequential tasks with heavy branching | Many hundreds or thousands of small, simple cores optimised for throughput | Obstacle detection applies the *same* operation to every pixel; thousands of cores work on different pixels simultaneously |
| Control vs compute | Much of the silicon is devoted to control logic, branch prediction and large caches | Far more of the silicon is devoted to arithmetic units | Image processing is data-parallel with almost no branching, so spending silicon on control logic is wasteful |

Other acceptable differences: SIMD/single-instruction-multiple-data execution; the GPU's higher memory bandwidth; the CPU's higher clock speed and lower latency per task. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)

(c) (i) Bits per frame $=1280\times720\times24=22\,118\,400$ bits (A1)

$$=\frac{22\,118\,400}{8}=2\,764\,800\ \text{bytes}\approx2.76\ \text{MB per frame}$$ (A1)

Data rate $=2.7648\times30=82.9\ \mathrm{MB\,s^{-1}}$ (A1)

(ii) Compressed rate $=\dfrac{82.9}{40}=2.07\ \mathrm{MB\,s^{-1}}$; for 90 s: $2.07\times90=187\ \mathrm{MB}$ (A1)

(Allow 186–188 MB. If 1 MB is taken as $2^{20}$ bytes throughout, the answers are 79.1 MB/s and 178 MB — credit both conventions if used consistently.)

(d) Indicative content:

  • Compiled: translated once into machine code before deployment; execution is fast and predictable because there is no translation at run time; the executable can be optimised for the specific target processor; the source code is not distributed, which protects intellectual property. (A1)(A1)
  • Interpreted: translated line by line at run time; slower (typically by an order of magnitude) and with less predictable timing; but easier to test and modify, and the same source runs on any hardware with a suitable interpreter. (A1)
  • Evaluation: the drone has fixed, known hardware and a hard real-time constraint of 20 ms, and the code will not be modified in flight. Compilation is therefore clearly preferable: the worst-case response time is shorter and, critically, more *predictable* — an interpreter introduces run-time translation delays that could cause a missed deadline and a collision. (A1)

Accept a contrary conclusion only if justified by a specific constraint (for example, if the software had to be updated in flight).

A third option students sometimes offer is just-in-time (JIT) compilation. It should not earn the evaluation mark on its own: a JIT compiler still translates each method at run time the first time it is executed, so the worst-case timing inside a 20 ms control window is not bounded by the source alone, and a routine that runs once per flight never benefits from the cached native code. It earns the same (A1) as any other answer only if the candidate states that the deadline is set by the worst case, and that compilation removes translation from the flight path altogether.
questions.explanation:
Theme A questions are usually pure recall dressed up in a context, and this one is built to resist that. Three things make it harder than it looks:

  • In (a), 'describe the interaction' is not 'list the components'. The fetch–decode–execute cycle is a *sequence* with data moving between named registers, and answers that simply define the control unit, the ALU and the registers separately cannot access the top marks.
  • In (b) the mark scheme is explicitly looking for a difference and a consequence for this workload. 'A GPU has more cores' is a fact; 'obstacle detection applies one operation to every pixel, so thousands of cores each handle a different pixel at the same time' is an explanation.
  • Part (c) is the pivot. Without the number, part (d) is an opinion. With it, students can see that 82.9 MB/s of raw video cannot be stored or processed casually — the compression ratio is doing real work, and any architecture that has to move uncompressed frames around is in trouble.

The evaluation in (d) then has something to bite on. The 20 ms deadline is the decisive constraint: it is not that compilation is 'faster' in some abstract sense, it is that interpretation makes the *worst-case* timing unpredictable, and a hard real-time control loop is governed by its worst case, not its average case.

Classic wrong turns: describing the GPU as 'a faster CPU'; confusing compression ratio with compression *factor* (dividing by 40 when they should, or multiplying); and in (d), describing both options competently and then never choosing.

One further trap is worth naming, because part (c) carries a mark for it. The arithmetic there mixes bits and bytes: the colour depth is given in bits per pixel, so the frame rate produces a rate in bits per second, while the question asks for megabytes per second. Dividing by 8 is not a tidiness step that can be skipped, and a candidate who omits it obtains a rate eight times too large. That error is easy to miss, because the same factor of eight is then carried silently into the 90-second storage figure, where the answer still looks like a plausible number rather than a wrong one.

questions.subtopic: A2 Networks
questions.question:
The network is also used for staff email, VoIP telephony and building-management sensors.

(a)

Calculate the time to transfer one 1.2 GB study over the existing 100 Mbps link. Hence evaluate whether upgrading the link to 1 Gbps would allow the 15-second clinical standard to be met.

[6]

(b)

Explain how packet switching allows the link to be shared with the other traffic listed, and describe one consequence of this sharing for the image transfer.

[4]

(c)

The network is segmented into a clinical VLAN, a guest Wi-Fi VLAN and an IoT VLAN for building sensors. Explain the purpose of this segmentation and how a firewall enforces it.

[3]

(d)

Patient data are encrypted in transit. Distinguish between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, and explain the role of a digital certificate.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Data: $1.2\ \mathrm{GB}=1.2\times10^{9}\ \text{bytes}=9.6\times10^{9}$ bits. (A1)

Usable bandwidth $=100\times10^{6}\times0.92=92\times10^{6}$ bits per second. (A1)

$$\text{time}=\frac{9.6\times10^{9}}{92\times10^{6}}=104\ \mathrm{s}$$ (A1)

At 1 Gbps: usable $=1000\times10^{6}\times0.92=920\times10^{6}$ bps, so

$$\text{time}=\frac{9.6\times10^{9}}{920\times10^{6}}=10.4\ \mathrm{s}$$ (A1)

Evaluation: the existing link takes about 104 s, roughly seven times the 15 s standard — the requirement is not met and cannot be met by any reasonable tuning. (A1) Upgrading to 1 Gbps gives 10.4 s, which meets the standard but with only about 4.6 s of margin. Since the link is shared with email, VoIP and sensor traffic (see part b), that margin could be eroded at busy times, so a 1 Gbps upgrade is justified but may not on its own be sufficient; the hospital should also consider prioritising (QoS) or transferring studies outside peak hours. (A1)

(b) In a packet-switched network the data is broken into packets, each carrying a destination address and a sequence number. (A1) Packets from different applications are interleaved on the same link, so the link is never idle waiting for one transfer to finish; routers forward each packet independently, possibly by different routes, and the receiving device reassembles them using the sequence numbers. (A1)(A1)

Consequence: the transfer time becomes variable rather than fixed — competing traffic reduces the share of bandwidth available to the image transfer, and because packets may take different routes they can arrive out of order or with varying delay (jitter), so the effective throughput fluctuates and the 104 s figure in (a) is a best case, not a guarantee. (A1)

(c) Segmentation divides one physical network into separate logical networks so that traffic in one segment cannot reach another. (A1) Its purpose here is to contain risk: a compromised guest device or an insecure building sensor cannot reach the clinical network holding patient records, and broadcast traffic is confined. (A1)

A firewall sits between segments and enforces the separation by applying rules — it inspects each packet's source, destination, port and protocol, permits traffic that matches an allowed rule (for example, a clinical workstation on VLAN 10 reaching the image server on TCP port 443) and drops or logs everything else by default. (A1)

(d) Symmetric encryption uses the *same* key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and suitable for bulk data, but the key must be shared securely in advance — if it is intercepted, all communication is compromised. (A1)

Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically related *key pair*: a public key for encrypting and a private key (kept secret) for decrypting. No shared secret needs to be exchanged, but it is far slower, so in practice it is used to exchange a symmetric *session* key, which then encrypts the data. (A1)

A digital certificate solves the remaining problem — how the client knows the public key really belongs to the hospital server and not to an impostor. A trusted certificate authority signs a document binding the server's identity to its public key; the client verifies the signature against the CA's own certificate, and only then uses the public key. (A1)

A self-signed certificate does not solve the problem it appears to. It binds the server's identity to its own key, but the signature is made by the very key being vouched for, so a client that accepts it has no independent evidence of who is at the other end and is open to a man-in-the-middle presenting its own self-signed certificate. Certificates also expire and can be revoked: a client that checks the signature but never checks the validity dates or the revocation information will keep trusting a certificate whose private key has already been compromised.
questions.explanation:
The arithmetic in (a) is easy to get wrong in three specific ways, and each gives an answer that looks plausible: forgetting the 8% overhead (giving 96 s), forgetting that bandwidth is in bits while file size is in bytes (giving 13 s), or applying the overhead by adding rather than multiplying. Only the correct treatment yields 104 s, and without it the evaluation is guesswork.

But the evaluation mark is the real target. '1 Gbps is faster, so upgrade' is not an argument. The student has to notice that 10.4 s leaves under 5 s of headroom on a link that is explicitly shared, and therefore that the upgrade is necessary but possibly not sufficient. That is the difference between describing a network and designing one.

Part (b) is where the two halves of the question connect. The 104 s in (a) is the *unshared* best case. Once packet switching is understood as interleaving rather than queueing, it follows that the real figure will be worse and less predictable — which is exactly why part (a)'s margin matters.

Parts (c) and (d) are deliberately sequenced: segmentation limits *who* can reach the data, and encryption protects it *in transit*. Students commonly conflate the two, or assume that because data are encrypted, network segmentation is unnecessary — it is not, since encryption does nothing to stop an attacker on the clinical VLAN from reaching a server they should not be able to see.

Classic wrong turns: treating 1.2 GB as 1.2 × 2^30 bytes while the question states 10^9; describing circuit switching instead of packet switching; and claiming that a firewall 'encrypts' traffic.

questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A3 Databases
questions.question:
The festival is expanding and the table is causing problems.

(a)

Explain two specific problems with this design, using the data above to illustrate each. For each, name the type of anomaly it represents.

[5]

(b)

Construct a set of tables in third normal form (3NF) to replace PERFORMANCE_BOOKING. State the primary key of each table and show the foreign-key links between them.

[5]

(c)

Using your 3NF design, write an SQL query that lists the customer name, the performance name and the total cost of each booking (quantity × price), for bookings of more than two tickets, ordered by total cost from highest to lowest.

[4]

(d)

Box-office staff need to see booking details but must not see customer email addresses or prices. Explain how a database view solves this. (HL only)

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) Award two from:

  • Update (modification) anomaly. 'Midnight Chorus' and its venue 'East Stage' are repeated in rows 1001, 1002 and 1004. If the performance is moved to another venue, every one of those rows must be changed; if even one is missed, the database holds contradictory answers and a report cannot say where the performance is. (A1)(A1)
  • Insertion anomaly. A newly announced performance cannot be added to the database until someone books it, because the only place a performance name can exist is inside a booking row — and BookingID is the key, so there is no way to store a performance with no bookings. (A1)(A1)
  • Deletion anomaly. If customer L. Oyeka cancels booking 1003, that row is the only record of 'Brass Quartet' at the West Barn; deleting the booking destroys the performance record as well. (A1)(A1)
  • Redundancy / wasted storage. Customer name and email are repeated across every booking that customer makes, so A. Ferrer's details are stored twice and R. Duval's twice, and the repetition grows with the festival. (A1)(A1)

(Maximum 5 marks; at least one answer must name the anomaly type for the higher band.)

(b) A correct 3NF decomposition:

CUSTOMER(CustomerID PK, CustomerName, CustomerEmail)

PERFORMANCE(PerformanceID PK, PerformanceName, VenueName)

SEAT_PRICE(PerformanceID FK, SeatCategory PK *(composite with PerformanceID)*, PricePerTicket)

BOOKING(BookingID PK, CustomerID FK, PerformanceID FK, SeatCategory FK, Quantity)

Award (A1) for separating CUSTOMER, (A1) for separating PERFORMANCE, (A1) for recognising that PricePerTicket depends on the *performance and seat category* pair rather than on the booking (so it needs its own table), (A1) for correct primary keys, (A1) for correct foreign keys linking BOOKING to CUSTOMER and PERFORMANCE.

Why this is 3NF: in every table, each non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. In particular, PricePerTicket is no longer stored against BookingID (a transitive/partial dependency), and VenueName is no longer repeated per booking.

Note: the original table has no CustomerID or PerformanceID, so surrogate keys must be introduced — credit this explicitly if done.

(c) One correct solution:

SELECT c.CustomerName,
       p.PerformanceName,
       b.Quantity * s.PricePerTicket AS TotalCost
FROM BOOKING b
JOIN CUSTOMER    c ON b.CustomerID    = c.CustomerID
JOIN PERFORMANCE p ON b.PerformanceID = p.PerformanceID
JOIN SEAT_PRICE  s ON b.PerformanceID = s.PerformanceID
                  AND b.SeatCategory  = s.SeatCategory
WHERE b.Quantity > 2
ORDER BY TotalCost DESC;

Award (A1) for joining the three or four tables correctly, (A1) for the composite join to SEAT_PRICE (both PerformanceID *and* SeatCategory — joining on SeatCategory alone is the common error and returns wrong prices), (A1) for the computed total and the WHERE b.Quantity > 2 filter, (A1) for ORDER BY TotalCost DESC.

(d) A view is a stored, named query that behaves like a virtual table. (A1) The administrator creates a view exposing only BookingID, CustomerName, PerformanceName, SeatCategory and Quantity, grants box-office staff SELECT on that view, and grants them no privileges at all on the underlying tables. Staff then query the view and cannot reach the excluded columns or the base tables, so security is enforced by the database itself rather than by trusting an application or a member of staff. (A1)

Note for the top band: a view is not a complete security boundary on its own. If the view is updatable, a user granted INSERT or UPDATE on it can change the base tables through the view, so the administrator must grant only SELECT. A user who can see every booking in the view can also infer a customer's identity from a rare performance and a distinctive quantity, so a view controls which columns are visible but not what can be deduced from them. Where the sensitivity lies in the rows rather than the columns, the view must be restricted to a subset of rows as well.
questions.explanation:
Normalisation is one of the topics students can define flawlessly and apply badly. This question is built so that definitions are not enough.

In (a) the anomalies have to be *demonstrated* on the five rows given. 'Repetition causes problems' is not an answer; 'Midnight Chorus is stored three times, so moving it to a different venue means editing three rows, and missing one leaves the database contradicting itself' is. Naming it as an update anomaly is what lifts the answer into the top band.

Part (b) is where the design decisions live, and there are two of them:

1. Customer and performance must be split out — that part is routine.
2. Price is the interesting one. PricePerTicket looks like it belongs to the booking, but it is a property of the (performance, seat category) *pair*: Premium seats for Midnight Chorus cost 85.00 in rows 1001 and 1004, identical because they are the same pair, not because they are the same booking. Leaving price in BOOKING leaves a transitive dependency and the table is not in 3NF. Most candidates miss this.

Part (c) then punishes the mistake automatically: if SEAT_PRICE was not separated out, the query cannot be written correctly, and if it was, the join must be on both PerformanceID and SeatCategory. Joining on SeatCategory alone silently returns several prices per row and a wrong total — the kind of error that produces a plausible-looking report and no error message.

Classic wrong turns: introducing CustomerID but then never using it as a foreign key; writing SELECT with no JOIN conditions (a Cartesian product); and describing a view as a copy of the data (it is not — it is a stored query, and it reflects changes to the base tables immediately).

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A4 Machine learning
questions.question:
The bank intends to deploy the model to make automated decisions.

(a)

Distinguish between supervised and unsupervised learning. Identify which type this system uses and justify your answer.

[4]

(b)

For each of the three data issues identified above, describe one appropriate preprocessing step and justify why it is needed. (HL only)

[5]

(c)

The model is trained on 80% of the data and tested on the remaining 20%. Training accuracy is 98% while test accuracy is 71%. Explain what these two figures tell you and what should be done about it. (HL only)

[4]

(d)

After deployment, the model rejects applications from one postcode district at four times the average rate. Discuss two ethical issues this raises and one action the bank should take.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) In supervised learning the training data are *labelled* — each example is paired with the correct output — and the model learns to map inputs to that known target. In unsupervised learning the data are unlabelled and the model must find structure (clusters, associations) on its own. (A1)(A1)

This system is supervised: each of the 40 000 historical applications carries the recorded outcome (repaid or defaulted), which acts as the label, and the task is to predict that outcome for a new applicant. (A1)(A1) (Specifically it is classification, since the output is one of two categories.)

(b)

| Issue | Preprocessing step | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| 12% of income values missing | Impute the missing values — replace them with the median income (or with the median within a relevant subgroup), or drop the rows if 88% is still a large enough sample | Deleting 12% of 40 000 records throws away 4 800 examples and may bias the sample if the missingness is not random; imputing with the *median* rather than the mean avoids distortion by the extreme incomes noted below |
| Income ranges from 0 to 4 000 000 while age ranges 18–75 | Scale / normalise the features — for example min–max scaling to [0, 1] or standardisation (z-scores) | Many algorithms (distance-based methods, gradient descent, regularised models) are dominated by the feature with the largest numeric range; unscaled, income would swamp age and years-in-employment and the model would effectively ignore them |
| Postcode district: 2 800 distinct values | Reduce cardinality — group districts into broader regions, or replace the district with derived features (e.g. average local income from a lookup) rather than using the raw category | 2 800 categories with few examples each makes the model memorise individual districts (overfitting) and makes one-hot encoding produce thousands of sparse columns; it is also the field through which proxy discrimination enters (see part d) |

Award (A1)(A1) for two well-justified steps and (A1) for a third; up to (A1)(A1) overall for the quality of justification. Accept other valid answers: dropping the field entirely, target/mean encoding, or binning income.

(c) The training set is used to fit the model; the test set is data the model has never seen, and it estimates how the model will perform on future applications. (A1)

A training accuracy of 98% with a test accuracy of 71% is a large generalisation gap: the model has fitted the training data extremely closely — including its noise and quirks — but has not learned patterns that transfer. This is overfitting. (A1)(A1)

What to do: reduce model complexity (fewer features or a shallower model), apply regularisation to penalise overly complex fits, gather more training data, use cross-validation to get a more reliable estimate, and — importantly — treat the 71% test figure as the honest estimate of performance rather than the 98%. (A1)

(d) Ethical issues — award two:

  • Indirect (proxy) discrimination. Even if the protected characteristic is not in the dataset, postcode district correlates with ethnic composition, so the model can reproduce discriminatory outcomes while appearing to be neutral. This may be unlawful and is certainly unfair to individual applicants who are judged by their neighbours rather than by their own circumstances. (A1)
  • Lack of transparency / accountability. If the model cannot explain *why* it rejected an application, the bank cannot give a rejected applicant a reason, cannot check whether the decision was lawful, and cannot be held accountable. Automated decisions with significant effects on people require explainability. (A1)
  • Feedback loop. If the model's rejections are fed back into future training data as 'true' outcomes, the bias is reinforced and amplified over time. (A1)
  • Scale of harm. Because decisions are automated, a biased model harms many people consistently and invisibly, rather than as occasional individual lapses. (A1)

Action — award one:
- Audit for disparate impact, test the model's rejection rates across groups, and if the disparity cannot be justified, remove or transform the postcode field and retrain. (A1)
- Keep a human in the loop for borderline or rejected applications, and publish a meaningful reason for each adverse decision. (A1)
- Use fairness-aware techniques: re-weight or re-sample the training data, or constrain the model so that outcomes are independent of the proxy variable. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Machine learning is new enough in the syllabus that most questions about it are definitional. This one is built so that definitions earn the first four marks and the remaining twelve require judgement.

The three data issues in (b) are not arbitrary — each is the classic symptom that has a specific remedy, and the remedy only makes sense once you know what goes wrong without it. Imputation is not about tidiness; it is about not discarding 4 800 examples and not distorting a distribution that has extreme outliers. Scaling is not cosmetic; with income in the millions and age in double digits, an unscaled distance-based or gradient-based model is effectively a model of income alone. Cardinality reduction is not an efficiency trick; 2 800 categories with a handful of examples each guarantees memorisation.

Part (c) is the standard overfitting diagnosis, but the question is phrased so that the student has to say what the *gap* means rather than compute it. The 98%/71% pair is the signature.

The point of the whole question, though, is (d), and it is deliberately connected back to (b). The postcode field is exactly the one whose 'technical' problem — high cardinality — pushes students towards grouping or encoding it, and it is simultaneously the field through which proxy discrimination enters. A student who handles postcode purely as a technical nuisance has missed that the preprocessing decision *is* an ethical decision. That is the transfer this question is trying to test, and it is why the bank's context matters: an unfair loan model does not produce a wrong answer, it produces a life-changing one, automatically, at scale.

Classic wrong turns: calling the system unsupervised because 'the outcome is just recorded'; imputing missing income with 0 (which the model reads as a real value); suggesting more training data as the only cure for overfitting; and proposing 'remove bias from the data' without explaining how bias would be detected.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.4 Choosing between interpretation and compilation when a script runs N times
questions.question:
A greenhouse controller runs a short rule script once every sampling cycle. The script can be executed in either of two ways.

  • Interpreted. Each statement is translated every time it is met, so nothing is produced in advance. This costs $0.050$ ms per execution of the loop body and has no start-up cost.
  • Compiled. The whole script is translated once into bytecode, at a one-off cost of $6.0$ ms. The bytecode is then executed directly at $0.010$ ms per execution of the loop body.

The figure shows the total time taken by each strategy against $N$, the number of times the loop body executes.

The controller samples every $2$ minutes, and in a typical cycle the loop body executes $400$ times.

(a)

State, for each strategy, when the translation of the source code takes place and what, if anything, is produced by that translation.

[3]

(b)

Show that the two strategies take the same total time when $N = 150$, and determine which strategy is faster, and by how much, for a cycle in which the loop body executes $400$ times.

[4]

(c)

Calculate the total time saved over one day of continuous operation by using the compiled strategy, and express that saving as a percentage of the time the interpreted strategy would have taken.

[4]

(d)

A developer argues that the script should always be compiled, because compiled code runs faster. Justify why this is wrong for a script that is executed only once, and determine the least value of $N$ for which compiling becomes worthwhile if a slower translator raises the one-off cost to $12.0$ ms while both per-execution times are unchanged.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Interpreted. Translation happens at run time, every time the statement is met, and no separate translated version of the program is produced; the source is read, analysed and executed statement by statement. One mark for each of 'at run time' and 'nothing is produced', and one mark for making clear that the translation is repeated on each pass. Note also that the compiled route produces bytecode rather than native machine code, so the output is still executed by a virtual machine; what has changed is that the analysis of the source happens once rather than on every pass. This is why the translated output can be reused without the source being present, and why the advantage of compiling grows with the number of executions instead of being a fixed speed-up applied once.

Compiled. Translation happens once, before execution, and produces a separate translated version — here bytecode — which is then executed without reference to the original source. One mark for 'before execution / once' and one mark for naming bytecode as the output. Up to three marks in total across the two strategies, awarded for the pair of contrasts: when the translation happens, and what it leaves behind.

(b) Interpreted: $T_I = 0.050N$. Compiled: $T_C = 6.0 + 0.010N$. Setting them equal: $0.050N = 6.0 + 0.010N$, so $0.040N = 6.0$ and $N = 150$. At $N = 150$ both take $0.050(150) = 7.5$ ms, which confirms the crossing. For $N = 400$: $T_I = 0.050(400) = 20.0$ ms, while $T_C = 6.0 + 0.010(400) = 6.0 + 4.0 = 10.0$ ms. The compiled strategy is faster by $20.0 - 10.0 = 10.0$ ms per cycle. A sign check confirms the direction: $T_I - T_C = 0.040N - 6.0$, which is negative for $N < 150$ and positive for $N > 150$. Because $400 > 150$ the compiled route must win, and the size of the win, $0.040(400) - 6.0 = 10.0$ ms, agrees with the direct subtraction.

(c) One day is $24(60) = 1440$ minutes, and the controller samples every $2$ minutes, so there are $1440/2 = 720$ cycles per day. The saving is $10.0$ ms per cycle, so the total saved is $720 \times 10.0 = 7200$ ms $= 7.2$ s per day. As a percentage of the interpreted time: $\dfrac{20.0 - 10.0}{20.0} \times 100 = 50\%$. Note that the percentage is a property of the two strategies at $N = 400$ and does not depend on how often the controller samples. The absolute figures behind it are $720 \times 20.0 = 14\,400$ ms $= 14.4$ s per day for the interpreted route against $720 \times 10.0 = 7.2$ s for the compiled route, so the time the controller spends on this script halves. Whether that reduction matters in practice depends on what else the controller has to do inside its two-minute window, which is exactly why the percentage, rather than the absolute saving, is the figure worth quoting.

(d) The developer's argument compares only the per-execution figures, $0.010$ ms against $0.050$ ms, and ignores the one-off translation cost, which is incurred in full however few times the script runs. At $N = 1$ the interpreted route takes $0.050$ ms while the compiled route takes $6.0 + 0.010 = 6.01$ ms — about $120$ times longer. For a script executed once, compiling is therefore plainly wrong; it would also be wrong for any script whose total number of executions is below the break-even. The saving per execution is not $0.010$ ms but the difference, $0.050 - 0.010 = 0.040$ ms, and that is the figure which has to repay the translation. With a one-off cost of $12.0$ ms the condition becomes $0.040N \ge 12.0$, so $N \ge 300$: the least value is $N = 300$. This is exactly double the original break-even, as expected, because the break-even is proportional to the one-off cost. Writing the condition generally, with one-off cost $C$ and per-execution saving $s$, the requirement is $sN \ge C$, that is $N \ge C/s$; the given figures are $C = 6.0$ ms and $s = 0.040$ ms, giving $N \ge 150$. Only the ratio matters, so a change in $C$ rescales the answer directly while a change in $s$ rescales it inversely.
questions.explanation:
The item is not really about compilers; it is about which quantity is the right one to compare. The two per-execution figures, $0.010$ ms and $0.050$ ms, are the numbers on the page and the numbers every candidate reaches for, but the saving per execution is their difference, $0.040$ ms. That single slip moves the break-even from $N = 120$ (if you compare $0.050$ against $6.0$) or from 'immediately' (if you compare $0.010$ against $0.050$) to the correct $N = 150$.

Once the right difference is identified, everything else is a consequence. The break-even is the one-off cost divided by the per-execution saving, so it scales linearly with the translation cost and the item can ask for it again with a different cost. The time saved per cycle is the difference of the two totals, and the daily saving is that times the number of cycles — two separate multiplications that candidates routinely conflate.

The conceptual point behind part (d) is that a fixed cost and a running cost behave differently, and that 'faster per execution' is not the same claim as 'faster overall'. A script that runs once is the limiting case that exposes this immediately. It is also worth noting what the item deliberately leaves out: a just-in-time compiler would sit between the two strategies, translating only the hot parts of the script after observing how often they run, and would avoid paying the full translation cost on code that never executes. That is the reason the break-even exists at all rather than one strategy dominating.

Part (a) is not decoration. The contrast that the rest of the item turns on — a cost paid once against a cost paid every time — is the same contrast that defines the two translation strategies, so a candidate who cannot locate the difference in (a) has no model to bring to (b). Marking it first also gives a route into the arithmetic for candidates who freeze at the algebra.

The lever here is the design decision rather than the computation. Nothing in the item is hard to calculate; what is hard is noticing that the obvious comparison, $0.010$ against $0.050$, is the wrong one, and that the relevant figure is the difference between them. That is a mistake about which quantity governs the decision, not a mistake about arithmetic, and it is the sort of error a competent candidate makes confidently.

The item is adapted from a UK A-level treatment of translation strategies, which typically asks for the contrast qualitatively. The quantitative break-even model, the sampling-rate scaling in (c), and the single-execution counter-example in (d) are all new here, so the mathematical structure rather than the source material is what carries the difficulty.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.4 An algorithm that is correct except for one class of input: the final run is never recorded
questions.question:
A programmer writes the following method to find the length of the longest run of identical adjacent values in a one-dimensional array $A$ of $N$ integers, where $N \geq 1$. The array is indexed from $0$ to $N - 1$.

LONGEST = 0
CURRENT = 1
loop I from 1 to N - 1
    if A[I] = A[I - 1] then
        CURRENT = CURRENT + 1
    else
        if CURRENT > LONGEST then
            LONGEST = CURRENT
        end if
        CURRENT = 1
    end if
end loop
return LONGEST

The programmer tests the method on the array $[3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2]$ and obtains $3$, which is correct.

(a)

Determine the value returned by the method for each of the following arrays.

(i) $[4, 4, 4]$

(ii) $[5]$

(iii) $[2, 7, 7]$

(iv) $[9, 9, 6, 6, 6]$.

For each array, state also the value the method should return.

[4]

(b)

Identify the two classes of input for which the method returns a value that is too small, and explain, by reference to the pseudocode, why each occurs.

[4]

(c)

Rewrite the method so that it returns the correct value for every array of length $N \geq 1$. Your answer must be given in the same pseudocode style, and you must state what you changed.

[4]

(d)

A second programmer suggests correcting the method by changing the first line to LONGEST = 1 and making no other change.

Evaluate this suggestion: state whether it produces the correct answer for every array, and support your answer either by explaining why it works or by giving a specific counter-example and tracing it.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a)(i) The loop runs for $I = 1$ and $I = 2$. At $I = 1$, $A[1] = A[0]$ so $CURRENT = 2$; at $I = 2$, $A[2] = A[1]$ so $CURRENT = 3$. The loop ends with $LONGEST = 0$, so the method returns 0; the correct value is 3 (A1).

(a)(ii) The loop runs from $1$ to $0$, which is empty, so it never executes and the method returns 0; the correct value is 1, since a single element is a run of length one (A1).

(a)(iii) At $I = 1$, $A[1] = 7 \neq A[0] = 2$, so $CURRENT = 1 > LONGEST = 0$ gives $LONGEST = 1$ and $CURRENT$ resets to $1$; at $I = 2$, $A[2] = A[1]$ so $CURRENT = 2$. The loop ends and the method returns 1; the correct value is 2 (A1).

(a)(iv) At $I = 1$, $A[1] = A[0]$ so $CURRENT = 2$; at $I = 2$, $A[2] \neq A[1]$, so $LONGEST = 2$ and $CURRENT = 1$; at $I = 3$ and $I = 4$, $CURRENT$ becomes $2$ then $3$. The loop ends and the method returns 2; the correct value is 3 (A1).

(b) The two classes are:

Arrays of length 1. With $N = 1$ the loop from 1 to N - 1 runs from $1$ to $0$, which is empty, so $LONGEST$ keeps its initial value of $0$ and the method returns $0$ instead of $1$ (A1).

Arrays whose longest run ends at the final element. The variable $CURRENT$ is only ever compared with $LONGEST$ inside the else branch, that is, at the moment a run is discovered to have ended (A1). The run that is still in progress when the loop finishes is never compared with anything (A1). So whenever the longest run is the last one -- as in (i), (iii) and (iv) -- the method reports the longest run it happened to close off, or $0$ if it closed off none (A1).

The programmer's test array $[3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2]$ is misleading: its longest run of three $1$s ends at index $4$ and is closed off by the $2$ at index $5$, so the defect is invisible.

(c) One correct version compares $CURRENT$ with $LONGEST$ once more after the loop has finished:

if N = 0 then
    return 0
end if
LONGEST = 1
CURRENT = 1
loop I from 1 to N - 1
    if A[I] = A[I - 1] then
        CURRENT = CURRENT + 1
    else
        CURRENT = 1
    end if
    if CURRENT > LONGEST then
        LONGEST = CURRENT
    end if
end loop
return LONGEST

The essential change is that the comparison with $LONGEST$ is moved outside the else branch so that it happens on every iteration, including the last (A1). With that change $CURRENT$ is compared after every element is processed, so the run in progress at the end of the loop is included (A1). Initialising $LONGEST = 1$ rather than $0$ handles $N = 1$ (A1), and the guard for $N = 0$ keeps the method defined if the problem statement is ever relaxed (A1).

Alternative correct answers are acceptable, for example initialising $LONGEST = 1$ and appending a single if CURRENT > LONGEST then LONGEST = CURRENT after end loop. Credit the version a candidate gives if it is correct for $N = 1$ and for a final-run array.

(d) The suggestion does not work in general (A1). It does fix the $N = 1$ case: the loop is empty and the method returns $1$, which is correct (A1). It does nothing for the final-run case. Take $A = [4, 4, 4]$ (A1). With $LONGEST = 1$: at $I = 1$, $A[1] = A[0]$ so $CURRENT = 2$ and the else branch is not taken; at $I = 2$, $A[2] = A[1]$ so $CURRENT = 3$, again without the else branch. The loop ends and the method returns $LONGEST = 1$, but the longest run is $3$ (A1).

The lesson is that the two defects have different causes and need different fixes. The $N = 1$ case is an initialisation defect; the final-run case is a structural one, and no choice of initial value can repair an algorithm that never performs the comparison it needs.
questions.explanation:
This is a defect that survives casual testing, which is the only kind of testing most candidates do. The programmer in the stem tests one array and gets the right answer -- not by luck, but because that array's longest run happens to be followed by a different value. Almost any hand-picked test array will behave that way, because a run that ends at the very last element feels like a special case when it is in fact one of the two things that can go wrong.

The structural point is about where the update lives. The variable $CURRENT$ is only compared with $LONGEST$ at the moment a run is *discovered to have ended*, and a run that ends because the array ends is never discovered to have ended at all. There is no event for it. That is why the fix is not a tweak to the initial conditions but a change to where the comparison sits: it has to happen on every iteration, or once more after the loop, and either choice works.

Part (d) is where the two defects get separated, and it is the part that most candidates get wrong in an instructive way. Changing the initial value genuinely does fix the length-1 case, so the suggestion is not obviously bad -- it is half right. Recognising that it is half right, and that the other half cannot be fixed by any initial value, is a stronger claim than simply calling the suggestion wrong. The counter-example does the rest: $[4, 4, 4]$ returns $1$ when the answer is $3$, and there is nothing about the initialisation that could change that.

This is adapted from the US AP Computer Science A free-response tradition of showing a method with a single defect and asking candidates to trace it, identify the failing input, and write a corrected version. The AP item typically supplies the buggy method and asks for the fix. Here the two distinct defect classes are separated into their own part, and a further part asks candidates to evaluate a plausible but incomplete repair -- which the source does not ask, and which is where the discrimination actually lives.

questions.subtopic: A1.2 Overflow in a two's-complement subtraction used as a comparison
questions.question:
An environmental control system stores each temperature reading as an eight-bit signed
integer in two's complement form, so the representable range is $-128$ to $127$. The system
compares two readings, $a$ and $b$, using the single line

if a - b < 0 then output "a is the lower reading"

and the subtraction is performed in eight bits, with no overflow detection.

(a) Explain what happens when the line is executed with $a = 100$ and $b = -50$, and state the
value the system compares with zero. \tag{3}

(b) Determine the range of values of the true difference $d = a - b$ for which the comparison
gives the correct result. \tag{4}

(c) Determine the number of ordered pairs $(a, b)$, with $a$ and $b$ each in the range
$-128$ to $127$, for which the comparison gives the wrong result, and hence the proportion of
all pairs that fail. \tag{5}

(d) State a comparison that is correct for every pair in the range, and justify it. \tag{4}

(a)

Explain what happens when the line is executed with $a = 100$ and $b = -50$, and state the value compared with zero.

[3]

(b)

Determine the range of values of the true difference $d = a - b$ for which the comparison gives the correct result.

[4]

(c)

Determine the number of ordered pairs $(a, b)$ in the range $-128$ to $127$ for which the comparison gives the wrong result, and hence the proportion that fail.

[5]

(d)

State a comparison that is correct for every pair in the range, and justify it.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The true difference is $100 - (-50) = 150$ (A1). Eight-bit two's complement can only
represent $-128$ to $127$, so $150$ cannot be stored; the value wraps by subtracting $256$ and
the system obtains $150 - 256 = -106$ (M1). Since $-106 < 0$ the system reports that
$a$ is the lower reading, which is wrong: $100 > -50$ (A1).

The general rule is that a result outside the representable range has $256$ added to or
subtracted from it until it falls inside, which is exactly what modular arithmetic does. No
flag is raised and no exception is thrown, so the error is invisible at run time.

(b) The comparison is correct exactly when the subtraction does not overflow, that is when the
true difference is itself representable (M1):

$$-128 \le a - b \le 127 \tag{A1}$$

Equivalently $-128 \le d \le 127$ (A1). Outside that interval the stored value differs from the
true difference by a multiple of $256$ and, because the magnitude of the correction is larger
than the magnitude of the value being represented, the sign is reversed (A1). For example
$d = 150$ is stored as $-106$, and $d = -150$ is stored as $+106$; in both cases the sign is
wrong and so is the comparison.

(c) For a given difference $d$, the number of ordered pairs with $a - b = d$ and both values
in $[-128, 127]$ is $256 - |d|$, valid for $-255 \le d \le 255$ (M1). Summing over the correct
range from part (b),

$$N_{\text{correct}} = \sum_{d=-128}^{127} (256 - |d|) = 24512 + 256 + 24384 = 49152 \tag{A1}$$

The total number of ordered pairs is (A1)

$$N_{\text{total}} = 256 + \sum_{d=-255}^{255} (256 - |d|) - 256 = \sum_{d=-255}^{255}(256-|d|) = 65536$$

so the number that fail is (A1)

$$N_{\text{wrong}} = 65536 - 49152 = 16384 \tag{A1}$$

and the proportion is $\dfrac{16384}{65536} = 0.25$: exactly one quarter of all comparisons
give the wrong answer.

(d) Compare the signs first, and subtract only when the signs match (M1):

if (a < 0) and (b >= 0) then output "a is the lower reading"
else if (a >= 0) and (b < 0) then output "a is the higher reading"
else if a - b < 0 then output "a is the lower reading"
else output "a is the higher reading"

Justification (A1): if the signs differ, the comparison is settled by the signs alone and no
subtraction is needed, which is precisely the case in which the true difference is largest and
the subtraction most likely to overflow. If both values are non-negative then
$a - b$ lies between $-127$ and $127$; if both are negative then $a - b$ also lies between
$-127$ and $127$ (A1). In either case the result is representable, so the subtraction cannot
overflow and the test is safe (A1).

An alternative correct answer is to widen the stored type before subtracting — for example by
promoting both operands to sixteen bits — since the difference of two eight-bit values always
fits in nine bits. This is simpler but costs memory in a system that stores thousands of
readings, which is why the sign test is preferred here.
questions.explanation:
The bug is a classic and it survives code review, because the line reads like arithmetic
and the arithmetic is correct. The problem is that it is not arithmetic — it is a range
question wearing arithmetic's clothes. The subtraction has to produce a result in eight bits,
and the result of a subtraction of two eight-bit values needs nine.

The reason the failure rate is exactly a quarter is worth seeing rather than taking on trust.
For any particular difference $d$, the number of ordered pairs that produce it is
$256 - |d|$, because the larger the difference the fewer starting values leave room for it.
Summing that over the representable differences gives $49152$ of the $65536$ possible pairs,
and the complement is $16384$, which is exactly one quarter. The figure is not an artefact of
the numbers chosen: it is $\frac{1}{4}$ for any even word length, and getting close to it for
any word length at all.

What makes this dangerous in a control system is the absence of any signal. There is no
exception, no overflow flag that the high-level code checks, and no value that looks wrong. The
program compares $-106$ with zero, correctly concludes that $-106 < 0$, and proceeds. The only
way to find the bug is to reason about the range of the operands, which is exactly what the
question asks for.

The fix in part (d) is worth dwelling on because it is not the obvious one. The obvious fix is
to widen the integer, and that works — nine bits are always enough for the difference of two
eight-bit numbers. But it costs memory in exactly the applications where eight-bit
representation was chosen for compactness, and it is not needed. The sign test costs two
comparisons and removes the problem entirely, because the dangerous case is precisely the case
where the signs differ, and in that case the answer is known without subtracting anything.

More generally, this is the reason comparisons in serious code are written as comparisons
rather than as subtractions. A compiler may or may not be able to prove that a subtraction is
safe; a sign test is safe by construction, and "safe by construction" is worth more than "safe
because the inputs happen to be small".

questions.subtopic: B2.4 A nested loop whose inner trip count depends on the outer index
questions.question:
A programmer writes the following routine to count the divisors of every integer up to
$N$.

COUNT = 0
for I = 1 to N
    for J = I to N step I
        COUNT = COUNT + 1
    next J
next I
output COUNT

(a) Trace the routine for $N = 6$ and state the value output. \tag{4}

(b) Show that the number of times the inner loop body executes is

$$\sum_{I=1}^{N} \left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor . \tag{4}$$

(c) Determine the value output when $N = 1000$, and hence determine the ratio of the number of
iterations to $N^{2}$. \tag{5}

(d) Explain why the time complexity of the routine is $\mathrm{O}(N \log N)$ rather than
$\mathrm{O}(N^{2})$. \tag{3}

(a)

Trace the routine for $N = 6$ and state the value output.

[4]

(b)

Show that the number of inner-loop executions is the sum from I = 1 to N of the floor of N divided by I.

[4]

(c)

Determine the value output when $N = 1000$, and hence determine the ratio of the number of iterations to $N$ squared.

[5]

(d)

Explain why the time complexity is O(N log N) rather than O(N squared).

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Tracing the outer loop (M1):

| $I$ | values taken by $J$ | inner iterations |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 | 6 |
| 2 | 2, 4, 6 | 3 |
| 3 | 3, 6 | 2 |
| 4 | 4 | 1 |
| 5 | 5 | 1 |
| 6 | 6 | 1 |

The inner counts are $6, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1$ (A1) and the total is $6 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 14$
(A1). So the routine outputs $14$ (A1). Note that only the first of the six passes runs the
full $N$ times; by the fourth pass the inner loop executes once.

(b) On the pass with outer index $I$, the inner variable $J$ takes the values
$I, 2I, 3I, \ldots$ up to $N$ (M1). The largest multiple of $I$ not exceeding $N$ is
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor \cdot I$ (A1), so the number of values taken is exactly
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor$ (A1). Summing over the $N$ passes of the outer loop
gives the stated expression (AG).

(c) Evaluating the sum for $N = 1000$ (M1):

$$\sum_{I=1}^{1000} \left\lfloor \frac{1000}{I} \right\rfloor = 7069 \tag{A1}$$

The ratio to $N^{2}$ is (M1)

$$\frac{7069}{1000^{2}} = \frac{7069}{1000000} = 0.00707 \tag{A1}$$

so the routine performs about $0.7\%$ of the iterations a quadratic algorithm would. Equally
tellings is the comparison with $N\ln N$:

$$N\ln N = 1000 \times 6.908 = 6908 \qquad \frac{7069}{6908} = 1.02 \tag{A1}$$

so the actual count is within about $2\%$ of $N\ln N$. A candidate who assumed $\mathrm{O}(N^{2})$
would predict roughly half a million iterations and would be wrong by a factor of about
seventy.

(d) From (b), the iteration count is $\sum_{I=1}^{N} \left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor
\le \sum_{I=1}^{N} \frac{N}{I} = N \sum_{I=1}^{N} \frac{1}{I}$ (M1). The sum on the right is
the $N$th harmonic number, $H_{N}$, which satisfies $\ln(N+1) \le H_{N} \le 1 + \ln N$ and is
therefore $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ (A1). It follows that the whole expression is
$\mathrm{O}(N\log N)$ (AG). The bound is tight rather than merely an upper limit, as the
numerical comparison in (c) shows: at $N = 1000$ the actual count of $7069$ sits about $2\%$
above $N\ln N = 6908$, and the gap between the two is the linear term that the floors and the
Euler–Mascheroni constant contribute.

It is worth being explicit about what the bound does and does not say. Replacing the floor by
$\frac{N}{I}$ can only increase the total, so the argument gives a genuine upper bound on the
running time and never an underestimate; and since the harmonic sum is also $\Omega(\log N)$,
the estimate is of the right order and not merely safe. What the argument does not do is give
a constant: $\mathrm{O}(N\log N)$ says nothing about whether the constant is $1$ or $100$, and
for small $N$ the constant can matter more than the growth rate. The numerical work in (c) is
what supplies the constant, which is why both parts are needed.

One further observation, for a candidate who wants to check the result independently: the sum
$\sum \lfloor N/I \rfloor$ counts the pairs $(I, J)$ with $I \mid J$ and $J \le N$, so it is
the total number of divisors possessed by all the integers from $1$ to $N$. It is therefore
also the number of times a naive divisor-counting routine would increment its counter, which
is exactly what the code in the stem is doing. Recognising that gives the answer a second
meaning and a second way to verify it.
questions.explanation:
Nested loops are taught with a rule of thumb — multiply the trip counts — and the rule
of thumb is right often enough to become a reflex. It fails here because it assumes the inner
count is independent of the outer index, and here it is the outer index itself that sets it.

Once the count is written as $\sum \lfloor N/I \rfloor$, the growth rate is a known quantity.
The floors can only reduce the total, so bounding above by $N\sum \frac{1}{I}$ is legitimate,
and the harmonic sum is $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$. That gives $N \log N$ rather than $N^{2}$, and
the numerical check in part (c) confirms the bound is not merely an upper limit: $N \ln N$ at
$N = 1000$ is $6908$ against an actual count of $7069$, about $2\%$ apart.

The factor-of-seventy gap between $7069$ and the half-million a quadratic estimate predicts is
the practical reason this matters. A programmer who believes the routine is quadratic will
refuse to run it at $N = 1000$ and will rewrite it unnecessarily; one who recognises
$N \log N$ will not. The difference between the two growth rates only widens with $N$: at
$N = 10^{6}$ the true count is about $1.4 \times 10^{7}$ against $10^{12}$ for a genuinely
quadratic routine.

There is also a substantive point hiding in the trace. The routine looks like it might be
counting something more exotic than it is, but $\sum \lfloor N/I \rfloor$ counts the number of
pairs $(I, J)$ with $I \mid J$ and $J \le N$ — that is, the total number of divisors possessed
by all the integers up to $N$. Recognising that gives the result a second, independent meaning,
and it is why the count grows the way it does: most integers have few divisors, and only the
small values of $I$ contribute many terms.

Finally, note that the floors matter for the exact value but not for the order of growth.
Dropping them changes the answer by at most $N$ out of roughly $N \ln N$, which is a lower-order
term — and knowing which simplifications change the answer and which do not is most of what
algorithm analysis consists of.
