questions.subtopic: A2.3 Bandwidth-delay product: when increasing the link rate changes nothing
questions.question:
A remote backup service transfers files between two sites. The connection has a round-trip
time of $40\ \mathrm{ms}$. The sending software uses a sliding window of $64\ \mathrm{kB}$
($65536$ bytes): it may send that much data before it must stop and wait for an
acknowledgement. The situation is shown in the diagram.

(a) Calculate the time taken to transmit one window at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$, and hence the
maximum throughput achievable with this window. \tag{3}

(b) The link is upgraded to $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$. Calculate the new transmission time for one
window and the new maximum throughput. \tag{4}

(c) Determine the window size, in bytes, that would be needed to make full use of the
$1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link. \tag{5}

(d) Explain why the upgrade produced no improvement, and state what should be changed. \tag{4}

(a)

Calculate the time to transmit one window at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ and hence the maximum throughput achievable with this window.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the new transmission time for one window at $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ and the new maximum throughput.

[4]

(c)

Determine the window size, in bytes, needed to make full use of the $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link.

[5]

(d)

Explain why the upgrade produced no improvement, and state what should be changed.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) One window is $65536 \times 8 = 524288$ bits (A1). At $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ the
transmission time is

$$t = \frac{524288}{1.00 \times 10^{8}} = 5.24\ \mathrm{ms} \tag{A1}$$

The sender must then wait for the acknowledgement, so one window is delivered per round-trip
time and the maximum throughput is

$$\frac{524288\ \mathrm{bits}}{0.040\ \mathrm{s}} = 1.31 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bps}
= 13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps} \tag{A1}$$

Note that this is $13.1\%$ of the link rate, even though the sender is idle for
$40 - 5.24 = 34.8\ \mathrm{ms}$ of every $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ cycle.

(b) At $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ the transmission time falls by a factor of ten (A1):

$$t = \frac{524288}{1.00 \times 10^{9}} = 0.524\ \mathrm{ms} \tag{A1}$$

The throughput is unchanged, because the amount sent per round trip has not changed (A1):

$$\frac{524288}{0.040} = 13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps} \tag{A1}$$

The sender is now idle for $39.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ of every $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ — it finishes sooner
and then waits longer, and the two effects cancel exactly.

(c) To keep the link busy the window must be at least the bandwidth-delay product (M1):

$$W = B \times \mathrm{RTT} = 1.00 \times 10^{9} \times 0.040 = 4.0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bits}
\tag{A1}$$

$$W = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{7}}{8} = 5.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{bytes} = 5.0\ \mathrm{MB}
\tag{A1}$$

Compared with the existing window this is (A1)

$$\frac{5.0 \times 10^{6}}{65536} = 76.3$$

times larger (A1). Equivalently, the existing window keeps the link busy for
$\frac{5.24}{40} = 13.1\%$ of the cycle at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ and for
$\frac{0.524}{40} = 1.31\%$ at $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$, so the utilisation falls by a factor of ten
exactly as the rate rises by a factor of ten, and the two effects cancel precisely.

Two checks are worth applying to the answer. First, the required window scales with the
round-trip time as well as with the rate, so halving the latency would halve the window
needed — a reminder that latency and bandwidth are separate constraints and can be traded
against each other. Second, $5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$ of unacknowledged data is a large amount to have
in flight, and in practice the window would be limited by the receiving system's buffer and by
congestion control rather than by the arithmetic here; the bandwidth-delay product gives the
minimum window that makes the link usable, not a window that any real system would necessarily
grant.

(d) The upgrade improved the rate at which data is placed on the link but not the amount that
may be in flight (A1). With a windowed protocol the throughput is
$\frac{\text{window}}{\mathrm{RTT}}$ whenever the window is smaller than the bandwidth-delay
product, and the link rate does not appear in that expression at all (R1). The window here,
$64\ \mathrm{kB}$, is well below the $5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$ bandwidth-delay product of the upgraded
link, so the link is idle for $98.7\%$ of each cycle and the tenfold increase in rate is
invisible (A1).

What should be changed is the window, not the link (A1): the sending software needs a window of
about $5\ \mathrm{MB}$ to use the $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link, and with the existing $64\ \mathrm{kB}$
window there was no point buying the upgrade at all. The general diagnostic is to compute the
bandwidth-delay product before paying for bandwidth; if the window is smaller, the money is
being spent on the wrong thing.
questions.explanation:
The result is counter-intuitive enough that it is worth stating in one sentence: with a
windowed protocol, throughput is the amount you may have in flight divided by the time a
round trip takes, and the speed of the link does not appear in that expression at all until the
window exceeds the bandwidth-delay product.

The arithmetic makes it concrete. At $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ the $64\ \mathrm{kB}$ window takes
$5.24\ \mathrm{ms}$ to put on the wire, and then the sender sits idle for the remaining
$34.8\ \mathrm{ms}$ of the round trip. It is using the link $13.1\%$ of the time. Upgrade to
$1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ and the same window takes $0.524\ \mathrm{ms}$ — the sender finishes sooner
and waits longer, and since the amount delivered per round trip has not changed, neither has the
throughput. Utilisation drops to $1.31\%$. The tenfold improvement in rate is exactly cancelled
by a tenfold drop in utilisation.

This is why the bandwidth-delay product is the first thing to compute. It is the amount of data
that must be in flight to keep the pipe full: rate times round-trip time. For the upgraded link
that is $1\ \mathrm{Gbps} \times 40\ \mathrm{ms} = 5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$, which is $76$ times the
window the software actually uses. Until the window is increased — in the protocol
configuration, not in the hardware — the upgrade buys nothing.

The practical lesson generalises well past this question. Latency and bandwidth are different
constraints and they bind at different times: if the window is small, latency binds and
bandwidth is irrelevant; if the window is large enough, bandwidth binds and latency stops
mattering. Buying more of the one that is not binding is the commonest way to spend money on a
network and get nothing for it, and the way to tell which one is binding is to compare the
window with the bandwidth-delay product.

The figure is there to make the idle time visible. Both rows show the same $64\ \mathrm{kB}$, and
what changes between them is only how much of the $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ is coloured in.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A3.3 One row that changes every aggregate: COUNT(*), COUNT(column), AVG, and NULL propagating through a computed column
questions.question:
A manager is asked three things about this table: what the average unit price is, which customers have placed more than one order, and how much each of those customers has spent. The manager writes a set of queries without reading the note on how the engine treats NULL.

(a)

Explain the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(unit_price) in a query over this table, and state the value that each of the two returns.

[4]

(b)

The manager writes SELECT SUM(unit_price) / COUNT(*) AS average_price FROM orders; and reports the result as 18.00. Determine the value that the engine's own AVG(unit_price) returns, and explain why the two expressions give different answers.

[5]

(c)

Determine which customers the query
``
SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS spend
FROM orders
WHERE order_id > 2
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
``
returns, and the value it reports for each. State the result the manager intended, and identify the single clause responsible for the difference.

[4]

(d)

Explain why SUM(quantity * unit_price) for customer 104 returns NULL rather than 0, and state one change to the query that would make the reported total well defined for every customer.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) COUNT(*) counts rows and COUNT(unit_price) counts values, so the first returns 7 and the second returns 6. The difference is exactly one row -- order 7 -- and the gap between the two numbers is the number of NULLs in the column being counted (A1)(A1).

The two functions are not two spellings of the same count. COUNT(*) answers "how many orders are there", which is a property of the table; COUNT(unit_price) answers "for how many orders do we know the unit price", which is a property of one column. On a table with no missing prices the two agree, which is why the distinction is invisible until the first NULL arrives (M1)(A1).

(b) AVG(unit_price) returns 21.00. The engine sums the six non-NULL prices (M1):

$$10.00 + 4.00 + 99.00 + 7.50 + 2.50 + 3.00 = 126.00 \tag{M1}$$

and divides by the number of values it actually summed, which is six (A1):

$$\frac{126.00}{6} = 21.00 \tag{A1}$$

The manager's expression uses the same numerator, because SUM also ignores NULL, but divides by COUNT(*) instead (M1):

$$\frac{126.00}{7} = 18.00 \tag{A1}$$

So SUM(x) / COUNT(*) is not a way of computing the average of $x$. It is the average of $x$ diluted by every row in which $x$ is unknown. The error is systematic rather than random: whenever some values are missing and the remaining values are positive, the reported figure is too low, and the size of the error grows with the *proportion* of missing values rather than with the size of the table. The gap here is $126.00/6 - 126.00/7 = 3.00$, which is the price of one row spread across the whole report.

(c) WHERE is evaluated before grouping, so the rows it removes are gone by the time HAVING counts anything (M1). WHERE order_id > 2 keeps orders 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, which is one row for customer 101, two rows for customer 102, one row for customer 103 and one for customer 104 (M1). HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 then keeps only customer 102, whose two surviving rows contribute (A1)

$$1 \times 99.00 + 6 \times 3.00 = 117.00$$

The query therefore returns a single row, $(102,\ 117.00)$ (A1).

The manager intended the two customers who have placed more than one order, which are 101 and 102. Customer 101 has orders 1, 2 and 5, worth

$$3 \times 10.00 + 5 \times 4.00 + 4 \times 2.50 = 60.00$$

and customer 102 is worth 117.00, so the intended answer is a total of 177.00 across the two customers (M1). The clause responsible is the WHERE: a row filter and a group filter are not interchangeable when the group filter is a count, because the count is taken over whatever the row filter happened to leave behind. Deleting the WHERE clause and keeping the HAVING clause gives the intended result.

(d) For order 7 the expression quantity * unit_price is 10 * NULL, and any arithmetic expression containing NULL evaluates to NULL, so that row yields no value at all rather than the value $10 \times 0 = 0$ (M1). SUM ignores NULLs, but customer 104 has only one row, and ignoring the only value in a group leaves nothing to sum, so the aggregate over that group returns NULL rather than 0 (A1).

A change that makes the total well defined is to wrap the aggregate: COALESCE(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 0). Wrapping the product instead, SUM(COALESCE(quantity * unit_price, 0)), also returns 0 here (A1).

The two placements are not equivalent and neither is a correction. The outer form reports 0 only for a group in which *no* line has a price, and it leaves every other group untouched; the inner form treats each unpriced line as zero revenue, which quietly understates any customer who has a mix of priced and unpriced orders. Neither recovers the missing price, so the choice is a decision about what an unknown is worth in the report, and a business that needs the real figure has to obtain the price rather than choose a default for it.
questions.explanation:
Every one of the three failures in this item comes from the same place: the query says what the engine should compute but not which rows it should compute it over, and those two things come apart as soon as a value is missing. That is why the item is not really about SQL syntax. Writing SELECT AVG(unit_price) FROM orders is a two-line exercise that any student can produce, and it is also the version that gets the right answer, so the difficulty cannot live in the syntax.

What makes the item hard is that the naive path is *self-consistent*. Treating NULL as zero gives an average of 18.00, a spend of 0.00 for customer 104, and a report in which no row is ever missing. Nothing in the output looks broken, and nothing in the code raises an error. The student has to know, in advance, that NULL is a marker for "unknown" rather than a synonym for zero, and that the standard's choice to exclude NULLs from aggregates is a deliberate rule rather than an implementation detail. A student who does not know that will not be able to tell the two answers apart by inspection, because both are plausible numbers.

Part (c) adds a second layer that is independent of NULL and is the one most often missed in practice. WHERE and HAVING look like two ways of writing the same filter, and they are not: one selects rows and the other selects groups, and a filter on a count is only meaningful after the rows have been collected. Combining them wrongly produces a query that runs, returns a plausible row, and answers a different question -- the same failure mode as part (b), arriving by a different route.

Part (d) is the conceptual close, because it asks what the fix means rather than how to write it. Both placements of COALESCE make the output well defined and only one of them is safe for a report, and the reason is that a business total is a claim about money while a NULL is a claim about ignorance. Deciding that an unknown price is worth zero is a business decision, not a database operation, and an item that pushes the student to say so is testing judgement rather than recall.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B4.1 Choosing an implementation for a priority queue when the number of extractions, not the complexity class, decides the winner
questions.question:
A student claims that the binary heap is the right implementation because its operations are $O(\log n)$ while the unsorted array's are $O(n)$, and that this settles the choice. The claim is to be tested against the counting model above, first with the full workload and then with the number of extractions reduced.

(a)

Determine the total number of steps taken by the unsorted array and by the binary heap when 1024 items are inserted and then all 1024 are extracted, and hence show that the heap performs about 25.6 times fewer steps.

[4]

(b)

Show that the sorted array performs exactly the same total number of steps as the unsorted array on this workload, and explain why two structures with opposite cost profiles can produce the same total.

[4]

(c)

The number of extractions is now reduced from 1024 to $k$, with the 1024 insertions unchanged. Determine the largest value of $k$ for which the unsorted array is still the cheaper choice, and state the smallest value of $k$ at which the heap is cheaper.

[5]

(d)

Explain why the student's complexity-class argument is not by itself a sufficient reason to choose the heap for this workload.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) For the unsorted array, an insertion appends to the end and costs 1 step, and an extraction scans the array and costs $n/2 = 512$ steps (M1):

$$1024 \times 1 + 1024 \times 512 = 1024 + 524\,288 = 525\,312 \tag{M1}$$

For the heap, every operation costs $\log_2 1024 = 10$ steps, so the insertions and the extractions are charged alike (M1):

$$1024 \times 10 + 1024 \times 10 = 10\,240 + 10\,240 = 20\,480 \tag{A1}$$

The ratio is (A1)

$$\frac{525\,312}{20\,480} = 25.65$$

so the heap performs about 25.6 times fewer steps on this workload.

(b) For the sorted array, an insertion has to find the insertion point and shift the items above it, which costs $m/2 = 512$ steps, while an extraction takes the item at the front and costs 1 step (M1):

$$1024 \times 512 + 1024 \times 1 = 524\,288 + 1024 = 525\,312 \tag{M1}$$

which is the same total as the unsorted array (A1).

The two totals agree because the two structures pay the same linear cost the same number of times, in opposite phases (A1). The unsorted array does nothing to maintain order on insertion and pays for the disorder on every extraction; the sorted array pays for the order on every insertion and collects it back for free on every extraction. With $n$ insertions and $n$ extractions the two phases have equal length, so the cost simply changes place. The equality is a property of this workload and not of the structures: if the workload were 1024 insertions and 10 extractions, the sorted array would be far more expensive, and if it were 1024 insertions and 1024 extractions of a *known* minimum the unsorted array's scan could be avoided altogether.

(c) With $k$ extractions the unsorted array costs (M1)

$$1024 + 512k$$

and the heap costs (M1)

$$10\,240 + 10k$$

Setting them equal (M1):

$$1024 + 512k = 10\,240 + 10k \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 502k = 9216 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k = \frac{9216}{502} = 18.36 \text{ (to 2 d.p.)}$$

Since $k$ counts extractions it must be a whole number, so the crossover lies between 18 and 19 (A1). Substituting both:

| $k$ | unsorted array | binary heap | cheaper |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | $1024 + 9216 = 10\,240$ | $10\,240 + 180 = 10\,420$ | unsorted array |
| 19 | $1024 + 9728 = 10\,752$ | $10\,240 + 190 = 10\,430$ | binary heap |

So the largest $k$ for which the unsorted array is still cheaper is 18, and the smallest $k$ at which the heap is cheaper is 19 (A1). The threshold is about 1.8% of $n$: unless the structure is drained of more than roughly one item in fifty, the array wins.

(d) The statement "$O(\log n)$ beats $O(n)$" compares how the cost of each structure *grows* as $n$ increases without bound, and it is true. It says nothing about which is cheaper at a particular $n$, and it says nothing at all when the mixture of operations is allowed to vary (M1). Here $n$ is fixed at 1024 and the number of extractions is the free variable, so the comparison has to be made at a point rather than in the limit (M1).

The reason the limit is misleading in this case is that the heap's advantage is paid for in advance. It commits 10 steps to each of the 1024 insertions, which is 10 240 steps before a single extraction has happened, whereas the unsorted array has spent only 1024. The array's expensive operation is the one that may never occur in large numbers, and the heap's expensive operation is the one that always occurs (A1). An argument from complexity classes cannot see either of those facts, because both of them are about the workload rather than about the growth rate.
questions.explanation:
This item is about a mistake that survives because the statement behind it is true. "A binary heap is $O(\log n)$ per operation and an unsorted array is $O(n)$" is not an approximation or a simplification; it is correct, and it is the reason heaps exist. The student's error is not in the mathematics but in the belief that a correct asymptotic statement answers a question about a finite workload with a particular mixture of operations. Complexity classes describe the shape of a curve as its argument grows; they do not compare two points on it.

The item is built so that the student has to do the comparison twice, once where the heap wins by a wide margin and once where it loses, and the two answers have to come from the same arithmetic. Part (a) makes the heap look obviously right, part (b) shows that the two arrays tie, and part (c) asks for the threshold. By the time the threshold appears -- eighteen extractions against nineteen -- the claim in the stem has already been dismantled, because a structure that loses to the naive one until it is drained of nearly two percent of its contents is not the structure the complexity class recommends.

The conceptual content is the idea that the operation *mixture* is part of the specification of a data structure choice, and that it is usually the part that is left unwritten. A priority queue is described by its operations, and any real use of one weights those operations very unevenly. A scheduler that inserts thousands of jobs and extracts a handful of the most urgent ones is a different problem from one that drains the queue as fast as it fills, and the same abstract type is the right answer to both -- while the same implementation is not.

The item also rewards the student who notices that the tie in part (b) is not a coincidence. Two structures with opposite cost profiles produce the same total exactly when the workload is symmetric between the cheap and the expensive operation, and recognising that symmetry is what makes part (c) tractable: once the total is understood as "a fixed cost plus a per-extraction cost", the crossover is one linear equation. The final part then asks the student to say out loud why the asymptotic argument could not have found it, which is the step that turns a calculation into a principle.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic
questions.question:
The 12-bit register stores values in units of 0.0625 degrees Celsius per least significant bit, with the most significant bit carrying the sign.

(a)

Determine the 12-bit two's complement representation of a reading of -37.5 degrees Celsius, giving your answer in binary and in hexadecimal.

[3]

(b)

Explain why the summation register can overflow even when every individual reading is representable, and determine the minimum register width needed to sum any 16 consecutive readings without overflow.

[5]

(c)

Explain why converting a stored reading to degrees Celsius by multiplying by 0.0625 introduces no error, whereas converting it to degrees Fahrenheit does, in both cases assuming the arithmetic itself is performed exactly.

[4]

(d)

Show that F simplifies to P + T.O, and state the number of two-input gates needed for the reduced expression.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) One least significant bit represents $0.0625$ degrees Celsius, so the stored integer is the temperature divided by $0.0625$: $-37.5/0.0625=-600$. (M1)

To store $-600$ in 12-bit two's complement, represent $+600$ first. $600=512+64+16+8$, which is $001001011000$ in 12 bits. (A1)

Inverting every bit gives $110110100111$ and adding 1 gives $110110101000$, so $-600$ is stored as $1101\,1010\,1000$. Grouping into fours from the right: $1101$ is D, $1010$ is A, $1000$ is 8, so the answer is $\mathrm{0xDA8}$. (A1)

*Check: $1101\,1010\,1000$ is $3496$ unsigned, and $3496-4096=-600$. Correct.*

*Representable: $-600$ lies inside the 12-bit signed range $-2048$ to $+2047$, so no clamping is needed.*

(b) A 12-bit two's complement register holds values from $-2048$ to $+2047$. Each individual reading is comfortably inside this range because the largest magnitude the sensor can report is about $128$ degrees Celsius. (M1)

Overflow is a property of the accumulator, not of the sensor. Two readings of $+2047$ already sum to $4094$, which is more than the largest 12-bit signed value, so the sum wraps and a positive result can appear negative. In practice the readings are far smaller than the maximum, but the accumulator has no way of knowing that: it is only 12 bits wide, so any pair of readings above about $1023$ will overflow it. (M1)(A1)

Sixteen readings can each be as large as $2047$, so the largest possible sum is $16\times 2047=32\,752$. (M1) A 15-bit two's complement register reaches only $+16\,383$, which is not enough; a 16-bit register reaches $+32\,767$, which is. The minimum width is therefore 16 bits. (A1)

In general an accumulator summing $k$ readings of width $w$ must satisfy $2^{W-1}-1\ge k(2^{w-1}-1)$; for $w=12$ and $k=16$ the smallest satisfying width is $W=16$, which is why the answer is 16 and not 15.

(c) $0.0625=2^{-4}$. Multiplication by a power of two does not change the digits of a binary number, it only moves the binary point, so the multiplication can be performed by a shift and the result is exact. Every value the sensor can produce is mapped to an exact value in degrees Celsius. (M1)(A1)

The conversion to Fahrenheit is $F=1.8C+32$, so it requires multiplication by $1.8$, which is $9/5$. In binary, $9/5$ is the recurring fraction $1.1100110011\ldots$, which cannot be stored in a fixed number of bits. (M1) Rounding that factor introduces an error that grows with the magnitude of the reading, and because $1/5$ has a factor of 5 in the denominator it can never be represented exactly in binary. (A1)

The Celsius conversion is therefore exact by construction, while the Fahrenheit error is one of representation rather than arithmetic: using more bits shrinks the rounding error but never removes it, because the expansion of $9/5$ does not terminate.

(d) $P.T+P.T'=P.(T+T')=P.1=P$ by the distributive and complement laws. (M1)

Substituting: $F=P+P'.T.O$. (M1)

By the rule $A+A'.B=A+B$ (absorption, or the consensus theorem), with $A=P$ and $B=T.O$, this becomes $F=P+T.O$. (A1)

The reduced expression needs one AND gate for $T.O$ and one OR gate to combine it with $P$, so two two-input gates. (A1) The two inverters required by the original expression are no longer needed, so the gate count falls from five to two and the propagation delay falls as well.

A truth-table cross-check over all eight combinations of $P$, $T$ and $O$ gives identical outputs for the original expression and for $P+T.O$, confirming the simplification.
questions.explanation:
Three separate ideas about fixed-width arithmetic are packed into one device, and they are usually taught separately.

The first is that the representable range depends on the declared width, not on the physical sensor. A 12-bit signed register spans $-2048$ to $+2047$, which comfortably covers a temperature sensor, so a student may reasonably conclude that overflow is impossible. It is not: the accumulator is the same width, and summing is exactly the operation that pushes values out of range. This is why real systems widen the accumulator or use saturating arithmetic, and it is worth knowing that the failure mode of wrapping is silent — a plausible-looking wrong number rather than an error.

The second idea is that exactness in conversion depends on the base representation, not on the size of the number. Multiplying by 0.0625 is exact because it is a power of two. Multiplying by 1.8 is not, and no amount of extra precision fixes it, because 1/5 has no finite binary expansion. This is the same reason that 0.1 cannot be stored exactly as a binary floating-point number, and it is the root cause of a large class of reported bugs in software that handles money.

The third is that a Boolean expression can look as though it needs every term it contains. The term $P.T'$ appears to add information about temperature, but it is redundant: whenever $P$ is true the whole expression is already true, and whenever $P$ is false the term contributes nothing. Recognising this is what the absorption rule formalises. The practical consequence is two gates instead of five, which matters because the alarm output is clocked and every extra gate adds propagation delay.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems
questions.question:
The four tasks A, B, C and D all become ready simultaneously when the controller wakes. Their processor requirements are 5 ms, 3 ms, 8 ms and 2 ms.

(a)

Describe how a closed-loop control system would maintain soil moisture at a target level, identifying the input, the process, the output and the feedback in your answer.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the average waiting time for the four tasks under first-come-first-served scheduling and under round-robin scheduling with a time quantum of 3 ms, then recalculate each total if every context switch costs 0.5 ms and the tasks are executed in the order A, B, C, D.

[6]

(c)

Explain why the average waiting time alone is a misleading basis for choosing between the two policies, using your figures, and state which policy you would deploy.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate the use of polling for the soil-moisture probe against the use of interrupts for the rain sensor, and explain one additional operating system function that the network connection makes necessary.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) In a closed-loop system the controller measures the actual soil moisture, compares it with the target value, and uses the difference to decide how much water to release; the measurement is then repeated so that the effect of the action is observed and corrected. (M1)

Input: the reading from the soil-moisture probe, converted to a digital value. Process: the controller compares this reading with the target and computes the valve opening and the duration of watering. Output: the signal that opens the irrigation valve, and the water delivered to the plot. Feedback: the next reading from the same probe, which shows whether the moisture has reached the target and allows the next decision to be adjusted. (M1)(A1)(A1)

The feedback path is what makes the system closed-loop and is what distinguishes it from an open-loop system, which would water for a fixed time regardless of the resulting moisture level.

(b) First-come-first-served, executing in the order A, B, C, D:

| Task | Starts | Runs | Completes | Waiting time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 5 | 5 | 0 |
| B | 5 | 3 | 8 | 5 |
| C | 8 | 8 | 16 | 8 |
| D | 16 | 2 | 18 | 16 |

Average waiting time $=(0+5+8+16)/4=7.25$ ms. (M1)(A1)

Round robin with a quantum of 3 ms, queue order A, B, C, D:

| Slice | Task | Runs | Remaining |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A | 3 | 2 |
| 2 | B | 3 | 0 completes at 6 ms |
| 3 | C | 3 | 5 |
| 4 | D | 2 | 0 completes at 11 ms |
| 5 | A | 2 | 0 completes at 13 ms |
| 6 | C | 3 | 2 |
| 7 | C | 2 | 0 completes at 18 ms |

Waiting times are A 8 ms, B 3 ms, C 10 ms and D 9 ms, so the average is $(8+3+10+9)/4=7.50$ ms. (M1)(A1)

Both schedules take 18 ms of processing. First-come-first-served needs 3 context switches, adding 1.5 ms, for a total of 19.5 ms. Round robin needs 7 switches, adding 3.5 ms, for a total of 21.5 ms. (M1)(A1)

(c) Under round robin the average waiting time is 0.25 ms worse and the total time is 2 ms worse, so on the average the two policies are almost indistinguishable and the familiar claim that round robin is fairer is not visible. (M1)

What the average hides is the distribution. Under first-come-first-served the shortest task waits 16 ms, eight times its own running time, and a task that became ready just after a long one would wait longer still. Round robin bounds the wait for any task that is ready: with four tasks and a 3 ms quantum, no task is ever bypassed for more than three slices, so the worst case is 9 ms of other work. (A1)

For a controller whose main job is to keep the valves responding, the bounded worst case is worth more than a marginally better average, so round robin is the defensible choice, with the caveat that the context-switch cost should be reduced before the quantum is made smaller. (A1)

(d) Polling the moisture probe every 30 seconds is cheap and predictable. The probe changes slowly, the event rate is two checks per minute, and the processor overhead of reading a value on a timer is negligible; an interrupt-driven design would add hardware complexity for no benefit. (M1)(A1)

Polling the rain sensor is not acceptable. Drops arrive unpredictably and the required response is within 5 ms, so a polling loop would need a period shorter than 5 ms, consuming processor time continuously and still risking a missed event between samples. An interrupt lets the processor sleep until a drop arrives, which also suits a battery-backed device, and it guarantees the latency requirement rather than merely making it likely. (A1)

The network connection makes authentication and access control necessary: the gateway must be able to accept uploads and possibly commands from the farm network, so the operating system must identify who is allowed to talk to it and protect its memory from a malicious or faulty remote message.
questions.explanation:
The scheduling part of this question is arranged so that the standard intuition fails. Round robin is usually described as fairer, and it is, in the sense that no task is starved. But on this specific workload the average waiting time is very slightly worse and the total time is worse once the context-switch cost is included, because the longest task is interrupted and restarted and the switching overhead is not free. A student who answers 'round robin is fairer' without computing anything has not answered the question, and a student who computes only the averages is forced to choose round robin for a reason the numbers do not support.

The way out is to look at the distribution rather than the mean. Under first-come-first-served the two-millisecond task waits sixteen milliseconds; under round robin nothing waits more than about nine milliseconds. For a device whose purpose is to keep responding to field conditions, the bound matters more than the mean, and that is a genuine engineering judgement rather than a textbook answer.

The second half of the question is about matching a mechanism to an event's statistics. Polling and interrupts are not better or worse in themselves: polling is simpler, has no hardware setup, and is entirely adequate when the event rate is low and the latency requirement is loose, which is exactly the situation of a moisture probe read twice a minute. Interrupts become necessary when the event is rare but must be handled quickly, because a polling loop fast enough to guarantee five-millisecond latency would run continuously and defeat the low-power design. The fact that the two sensors sit on the same device and require opposite answers is the point of the question, and it is the reason a blanket rule such as 'interrupts are more efficient' is unhelpful.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only)
questions.question:
The operations director wants the monthly report produced without the dispatch system losing responsiveness. The data described above is available, and management accepts that the reporting and dispatch workloads must be separated.

(a)

Explain why the monthly report is slow and why running it affects the dispatch system, referring to the difference between the workloads the two stores must support.

[4]

(b)

Design a star schema for the monthly report. State the grain of the fact table, name the fact table and three dimension tables, and give two measures that the fact table must hold.

[5]

(c)

Calculate the volume of raw report data generated in one year, and the volume if every record is stored with a replication factor of three. State one consequence of your answer for the choice of database.

[4]

(d)

Justify the use of a key-value or wide-column store for the incoming position reports rather than the relational database, and state one capability that is given up by doing so.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The dispatch system performs online transaction processing: many small reads and writes, each touching a few rows, each required to complete almost immediately. The monthly report performs online analytical processing: it reads almost every row that exists and aggregates it, and it does not care whether the answer arrives in a millisecond. (M1)(A1)

The relational store is organised to make the first workload fast. Its indexes are built on the columns the dispatch system filters on, and those indexes are of no use to a query that must scan the whole of a large table. The monthly report therefore degenerates into a full scan of the position reports, and because the tables are also being written to continuously, the scan has to take locks or work against a moving target. (M1)

Running both workloads on one server means they compete for the same resources: the report's long scan occupies processor time, memory for buffers and disk bandwidth, so the transactional queries queue behind it and the dispatch screen stops responding. This is the standard argument for separating the operational store from a reporting store. (A1)

(b) The grain must be stated before anything else can be decided, because a fact table is only meaningful at one level of detail. Grain: one row per van per completed delivery. (M1)

Fact table: fact_delivery, with one row per delivery and foreign keys to each dimension. (M1)

Dimension tables: dim_date (day, month, year, weekday), dim_depot (depot identifier, depot name, region), and dim_van (van identifier, model, refrigeration capability). A fourth, dim_route, would be defensible if routes are named rather than being defined by origin and destination, and should be accepted. (M1)

Measures: at least two numeric, additive quantities such as delivery_duration_minutes and distance_km, together with temperature_excursions, which is stored as a count of qualifying events rather than as a duration so that it can be summed. (M1)(A1)

Storing the delivery duration as a measure rather than deriving it from timestamps is what makes the average delivery time per depot obtainable without touching the raw reports at all.

(c) 340 vans write one report every 0.4 seconds for 14 hours a day: each van produces $14\times 3600/0.4=126\,000$ reports per day, so the fleet produces $340\times 126\,000=42\,840\,000$ reports per day. (M1)

At 80 bytes each, that is $42\,840\,000\times 80=3.43\times 10^{9}$ bytes, which is 3.43 GB per day. (A1)

Over 365 days the raw volume is $3.43\times 365=1\,251$ GB, approximately 1.25 TB per year. (A1) With a replication factor of three the stored volume is about 3.75 TB. (A1)

One consequence follows directly: a single relational server cannot be the store for this data, because the write rate alone is over a million rows per minute across the fleet at peak and the table grows by terabytes annually. A distributed store that partitions the data across nodes is required, and retention policy becomes a design decision rather than an afterthought.

(d) The incoming reports have a very simple shape and an extremely high write rate, and the query pattern is almost always 'give me the reports for this van between these two times'. (M1) A key-value or wide-column store matches this exactly: the key is the van identifier combined with the timestamp, writes are append-only and can be spread across nodes, and a time-range read is a contiguous scan within one partition. No joins are required, so the relational model's main advantage is not being used.

The capability given up is transactional consistency across records: ACID guarantees are weakened in exchange for availability and partition tolerance, so a system reading the store may see data that is not yet complete or not yet consistent everywhere. (A1)(A1) For position reports this is acceptable; for the financial records of the same company it would not be, which is why the two stores coexist rather than one replacing the other.
questions.explanation:
The question turns on a distinction that is easy to state and hard to apply: the same data can require two different storage systems because the two workloads have opposite shapes. The dispatch system does many small operations that must each finish quickly; the monthly report does one enormous aggregation that nobody minds waiting for. A schema optimised for the first is actively hostile to the second, because the indexes that make row lookups fast are irrelevant to a full scan, and because the scan competes for resources with the transactions.

Part (b) is the part most likely to be attempted without the necessary discipline. A star schema is defined by its grain, and the grain must be the finest thing the measures are meaningful at. Writing 'per depot per month' produces a table that already contains the answer and cannot be re-aggregated differently, which defeats the purpose of a warehouse. Stating the grain as one row per van per completed delivery keeps the table re-aggregatable by any dimension, and that is precisely the flexibility a warehouse is bought for. The dimension tables exist so that the query can group by month, depot or van without a join to the operational database.

Part (c) is arithmetic with a design consequence. Roughly 43 million reports a day at 80 bytes gives about 3.4 GB daily and about 1.25 TB a year before replication; the moment a replication factor is added, the figure is well beyond what a single server should hold. The useful observation is not the number itself but what it rules out: the storage decision is forced by the write rate, not by a preference for novel technology.

Part (d) closes the argument. A time-series access pattern with no joins is exactly what a key-value or wide-column store is good at, and choosing it costs the transactional guarantees that the financial system still needs. Both stores therefore exist, and the fact that they hold overlapping data is a deliberate redundancy rather than a design failure.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B3.1 Fundamentals of OOP for a single class
questions.question:
The window size is a property of the device, not of any individual object, and several SensorReadings objects may exist at once for different sensors.

(a)

Explain why CAPACITY should be a class-level constant rather than an instance variable set by __init__, and state one invariant that the class must maintain.

[3]

(b)

Construct the completed class, including __init__, add, mean and __len__, so that it maintains the invariant you stated and never holds more than CAPACITY readings.

[6]

(c)

Explain the error in the draft mean method and the effect it has after three readings have been added to a buffer whose capacity is five, and state the corrected line.

[4]

(d)

Explain why a method that returns self.values directly breaks encapsulation, and describe one way of giving the caller the data without doing so.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The window size is a property of the device, is the same for every object created, and must not vary between objects; making it a class-level constant expresses that and prevents one instance from being given a different capacity from another. (M1) It also removes the risk that the value is reassigned after construction, which would make the buffer's behaviour depend on when a method was called. (A1)

An invariant the class must maintain: the number of readings held is never greater than CAPACITY, and the values held are always the most recent ones added, in order. (A1)

(b)

class SensorReadings:
    CAPACITY = 5

def __init__(self):
self._values = []

def add(self, reading):
if len(self._values) == self.CAPACITY:
self._values.pop(0)
self._values.append(reading)

def mean(self):
if not self._values:
return None
return sum(self._values) / len(self._values)

def __len__(self):
return len(self._values)
```

The critical construction is the eviction in add: the oldest reading is removed before the new one is appended, which is what keeps the length bounded. (M1)(A1) The guard inside mean handles the empty buffer, which would otherwise raise a division by zero; the guard must be present because the class is usable before any reading arrives. (M1)(A1)

Using len(self._values) rather than a stored count means the count cannot fall out of step with the list. (M1) The attributes are prefixed with a single underscore to signal that they are internal, and __len__ gives callers the size without exposing the list. (A1)

(c) The error is that mean divides the total by self.capacity, the maximum number of readings the buffer can hold, instead of by the number of readings it actually holds. (M1)

With a capacity of five and three readings added, say 10, 20 and 30, the total is 60 and the correct mean is $60/3=20$. The draft returns $60/5=12$. (M1)(A1) The error is therefore not a failure but an understatement: the displayed average is too low by a factor of 3/5, and because the divisor is fixed, the error shrinks as the buffer fills and disappears entirely once five readings have been added. That is why testing with a single reading and then a few more gives values that look plausible. (A1)

The corrected line is:

        return total / len(self.values)

The same correction is what makes the earlier version of mean safe against an empty buffer, since a division of zero by zero would otherwise raise an exception.

(d) Returning self.values hands the caller a reference to the internal list, not a copy. (M1) The caller can then append to it, sort it in place or clear it, and every one of those operations changes the state of the object without going through add, which is the only method that enforces the capacity limit. The invariant established in part (b) is then broken from outside the class, and the object can end up holding more readings than CAPACITY or in an order that no longer reflects when they arrived. (A1)

One way to avoid this is to return a copy of the list, for example return list(self._values), so that the caller's changes affect only their own copy. (A1) A generator that yields each reading in turn achieves the same protection while avoiding the cost of copying a large buffer.

Note that list(self._values) is a shallow copy: it protects the list itself, but if the readings were mutable objects rather than numbers the caller would still share the same objects and could mutate them in place. For numeric readings the distinction does not bite, which is why the question uses temperatures; a class holding mutable records would need a deep copy, or better, to hand back immutable values.
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a bug that a cursory test will not find. When only one reading has been added, the draft's mean divides by the capacity and returns a number that is wrong but not obviously so; as more readings arrive the divisor becomes closer to the truth, and once the buffer is full the bug disappears entirely. A student who tests with a full buffer will conclude that the class works. That is exactly the failure mode of real code that maintains a rolling statistic, and it is why the question asks for the effect after three readings out of five rather than at the end.

The design issue underneath is the difference between the capacity and the count. They are equal only when the buffer is full, and code that uses them interchangeably is correct in the case people test and wrong in the case that matters. Writing the class so that the count is always derived from the data, rather than stored separately, removes the possibility of the two drifting apart — a small decision with a large effect on how many bugs the class can have.

The encapsulation part is not a formality. Returning the internal list gives the caller a reference, and the caller can then violate the invariant that add was written to protect. This is the most common way that a class with a carefully written interface is broken from the outside, and the fix is not to document the danger but to remove it by returning a copy or yielding values. The same reasoning explains why the attributes are private: the capacity rule lives in add, and nothing should be able to bypass it.

Finally, making the capacity a class-level constant expresses something true about the problem — the window size belongs to the device, not to an individual window object — and it makes the invariant checkable, since a value that cannot be reassigned per object cannot be violated per object.

questions.subtopic: A2.3 Why lowering a DNS time-to-live barely changes the latency a busy site's users see, while the same value governs the latency of a quiet one completely
questions.question:
A web page references resources from $D = 6$ distinct host names. Each name must be resolved before the resource can be fetched. The organisation runs its own resolving name server, which serves a cached record in $t_{\rm hit} = 2\ {\rm ms}$ and, on a miss, performs a full recursive resolution taking $t_{\rm rec} = 180\ {\rm ms}$. Every record carries the same time-to-live $T$, measured in seconds, and a cached record expires $T$ seconds after it was obtained; the first request arriving after an expiry is the one that pays for the recursive resolution. Requests for the page arrive uniformly at a constant rate $R$ pages per second.
Two services use the same infrastructure. The public service receives $R = 2.0$ requests per second; an internal reporting service, using the same six host names, receives $R = 1.0$ request per minute. In both cases the current value is $T = 300\ {\rm s}$.

(a)

For the public service, calculate the number of recursive resolutions the resolver performs per second, and hence the fraction of page loads that trigger at least one of them.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the average time per page load spent on name resolution for the public service, and repeat the calculation for $T = 60\ {\rm s}$. State how much DNS traffic increases and how much the average resolution time increases.

[3]

(c)

Determine the request rate below which the cache is effectively cold, in the sense that essentially every lookup misses, and hence determine the average resolution time per page load for the internal reporting service at $T = 300\ {\rm s}$.

[3]

(d)

Explain why the time-to-live is not the quantity that governs the resolution time a user experiences, identify the dimensionless ratio that does, and state what value of that ratio separates the two regimes. Explain also why the two services experience the same $T = 300\ {\rm s}$ so differently.

[4]

(e)

A colleague proposes lowering the time-to-live to $10\ {\rm s}$ 'so that records are always fresh'. Comment on this proposal with numbers, treating the public service and the internal service separately, and referring to a stated latency budget of $200\ {\rm ms}$ for resolution.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Each of the $D = 6$ records expires once every $T = 300$ s, so the resolver performs

$$\frac{D}{T} = \frac{6}{300} = 0.020 \ \text{resolutions per second }\;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

in total. Pages arrive at $R = 2.0$ per second, so the fraction of page loads that trigger a recursive resolution is

$$\frac{D/T}{R} = \frac{0.020}{2.0} = 0.010 \;\text{(A1)}$$

about one page load in a hundred. (This assumes the fraction is below one; part (c) examines what happens when it is not.)

(b) Each page load performs $D = 6$ lookups. In the steady state, $0.010$ of them are misses at $180$ ms and effectively all the rest are hits at $2$ ms, so

$$t_{ m DNS} = 6 \times 2 + 0.010 \times (180 - 2) = 12 + 1.78 = 13.8\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

With $T = 60$ s the expiry rate is $6/60 = 0.10$ per second and the miss fraction is $0.10/2.0 = 0.050$, giving

$$t_{ m DNS} = 12 + 0.050 \times 178 = 12 + 8.9 = 20.9\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(A1)}.$$

So the resolver's query traffic rises fivefold, from $0.020$ to $0.10$ recursive resolutions per second, while the average resolution time the user sees rises from $13.8$ ms to $20.9$ ms — about $7$ ms, which is well inside any plausible latency budget and barely measurable against the hundreds of milliseconds a page takes to load.

(c) The cache is effectively cold when the expiry rate reaches the arrival rate, that is when

$$\frac{D}{T} \ge R \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R \le \frac{6}{300} = 0.020\ \text{requests per second} = 1.2\ \text{per minute} \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

Below that rate, essentially every lookup misses, because the record has expired again before the next request arrives. The internal service receives $1.0$ request per minute $= 0.0167$ per second, which is below $0.020$, so all six of its lookups are misses and

$$t_{ m DNS} = 6 \times 180 = 1080\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(A1)}$$

more than a second of pure name resolution on every page load.

(d) The resolution time a user experiences is set by how often a lookup misses in the moment it is made, and that is governed by the ratio

$$\frac{D/T}{R} = \frac{D}{RT} \;\text{(M1)}$$

the number of records expiring per second divided by the number of requests arriving per second — equivalently, the number of requests that arrive during one lifetime of a record, inverted (A1). The value $1$ separates the regimes: below it the cache is warm and only that fraction of lookups miss; at or above it the cache is cold and every lookup misses, at which point $T$ has no further effect at all because there is nothing left to degrade (A1). The time-to-live alone cannot say which regime a service is in, because it carries no information about $R$: the same $T = 300$ s puts the public service at a ratio of $0.010$, comfortably warm, and the internal service at a ratio of $1.2$, fully cold — a hundredfold difference in resolution time produced by identical configuration (A1).

(e) For the public service, $T = 10$ s gives an expiry rate of $6/10 = 0.60$ per second, a miss fraction of $0.60/2.0 = 0.30$, and

$$t_{ m DNS} = 12 + 0.30 \times 178 = 12 + 53.4 = 65.4\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(A1)}$$

which is thirty times the recursive resolution traffic of the current setting ($0.60$ against $0.020$ per second) and is still within the $200$ ms budget, though it now consumes a third of it on a component that previously used under seven per cent. For the internal service the proposal changes nothing measurable: its ratio is already above $1$ at $T = 300$ s, so it is already paying $1080$ ms on every load, and lowering $T$ further cannot raise a fraction that is already saturated at unity — it only adds resolver load for no benefit (A1). The proposal is therefore poor value at both sites: it buys no freshness that anyone can perceive, since records change rarely, and it spends a large multiple of the query budget to do so. The change that would actually help the internal service is one that raises the ratio above unity by a different route: a longer time-to-live, a scheduled prefetch that refreshes records before expiry, or a local resolver on the reporting host itself (A1).
questions.explanation:
The reason this trips people up is that a time-to-live is a duration and a latency is a duration, so it feels natural to expect one to set the other. It does not. What determines whether a given user's lookup hits the cache is whether anybody else arrived recently enough to have warmed it, and that is a statement about arrivals per unit time — a rate — compared against the expiry rate. Two rates, one ratio.

Writing the ratio explicitly is the whole move. Expiries per second is $D/T$; requests per second is $R$; the fraction of lookups that miss is their ratio, capped at one. Everything else in the item follows from that one expression, including the two facts that make it interesting: the cap at one, which is why there is a threshold at all, and the fact that $R$ appears in it, which is why the same configuration behaves differently for two services.

The numbers were chosen so the two services sit on opposite sides of the threshold with nothing in between. At $R = 2.0$ per second the ratio is $0.010$ and the resolution cost is $13.8$ ms, essentially all of it the six cheap hits. At $R = 1/60$ per second the ratio is $1.2$, the cache is cold, and the cost is $1080$ ms. Same $T$, same $D$, same resolver, seventy-eight times worse. Nothing about the configuration changed; only the traffic did.

The cap at unity is the part worth carrying away, because it is the source of the asymmetry in part (e). Above the threshold, changing $T$ does nothing at all — the service is already paying the maximum and there is no headroom to lose. Below it, changing $T$ scales the miss fraction linearly but only shifts a small component of a mostly-hit workload. So lowering a time-to-live is either useless or mildly expensive, and raising it is either transformative or mildly beneficial, and which you get is decided entirely by the traffic. That is a genuinely useful thing to know before touching a DNS setting.

One more lesson hides in part (b), which is about the difference between cost and cost-per-user. The resolver's query traffic went up fivefold, which sounds alarming, while the user-visible latency went up by seven milliseconds, which is not. Both are true. A change can be expensive for infrastructure and invisible to users, and deciding which of those matters is a judgement the numbers cannot make for you.

questions.subtopic: A3.1 Database fundamentals
questions.question:
The scheme is expanding to five more cities and the spreadsheet is becoming unworkable. The operator has asked you to review the design before the data is migrated to a relational database management system.

(a)

Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key, and identify the primary key of the table above. Explain why MemberID cannot serve as the primary key of this table.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the volume of duplicated member-contact data held in one year of rows, and the number of rows that must be edited when 10% of members change their phone number, given that a member makes an average of ten journeys a year. Explain one way in which storing ChargeCents as text prevents a report from working correctly.

[5]

(c)

Explain how replacing the single table with MEMBER, BIKE and TRIP tables removes the two problems you calculated in part (b). Name the primary key and the foreign keys of each table, and state one referential-integrity rule the DBMS should enforce.

[4]

(d)

The developer proposes that deleting a bike from BIKE should automatically delete that bike's rows from TRIP. Evaluate this proposal using the figures above, and recommend what the referential rule should be instead.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) A primary key is the column, or the smallest set of columns, whose value uniquely identifies one row of a table; it must be unique and it cannot be null. (M1) A foreign key is a column in one table whose values must match the primary key of another table, and it is how a relationship between two tables is recorded. (A1) In TRIPS the primary key is TripID, because one row is one completed journey. MemberID cannot be the primary key because one member makes many journeys: 12,000,000 journeys are made by 1,200,000 members, an average of ten rows per member, so MemberID is repeated and does not identify a single row. (A1)

(b) Each row repeats the member's name, phone number and email address, which occupy about 50 bytes, and there are 12,000,000 rows in a year. (M1) The duplicated volume is

$$12{,}000{,}000 \times 50 = 600{,}000{,}000\ \text{bytes} = 600\ \text{MB per year}$$

and because the redundancy is stored once per journey it grows by 600 MB every year, reaching about 3 GB after five years. (A1) In a relational design the same 50 bytes are stored once per member, so the redundancy disappears.

Ten per cent of 1,200,000 members is 120,000 members. (M1) Because each of them makes about ten journeys a year, those members appear in $120{,}000 \times 10 = 1{,}200{,}000$ rows, so a change of phone number needs 1,200,000 edits in the spreadsheet against 120,000 — one per member — in the relational design. (A1)

ChargeCents is declared as text, so the DBMS treats "1,050" as four characters rather than as a number. (A1) It cannot be summed to give total revenue, it cannot be compared numerically, and it sorts by character order, so "1,050" is placed before "525"; any report must parse every one of the 12,000,000 values before it can add them.

(c) A relational design stores each fact once and links the tables by key:

  • MEMBER(MemberID PK, MemberName, MemberPhone, MemberEmail)
  • BIKE(BikeID PK, BikeModel, CommissionedDate)
  • TRIP(TripID PK, MemberID FK, BikeID FK, StartDock, EndDock, DurationMinutes, ChargeCents)

(A1) for splitting MEMBER and BIKE out of TRIPS; (A1) for placing the two foreign keys in TRIP and pointing them at the correct primary keys. Changing a phone number is now one row in MEMBER, not 1,200,000 rows, and the 50 bytes of contact data are held 1,200,000 times rather than 12,000,000 times, which removes both problems from part (b). (A1) The DBMS should enforce referential integrity: every value of TRIP.MemberID must exist in MEMBER, and every value of TRIP.BikeID must exist in BIKE, so a journey cannot be recorded against a member or a bike that does not exist. (A1)

(d) The proposal is technically correct and wrong for this requirement. If deleting a row from BIKE cascades to TRIP, then retiring a bike destroys its journeys:

  • 2% of the 15,000 bikes is 300 bikes retired each year. (M1)
  • Each bike averages $12{,}000{,}000 / 15{,}000 = 800$ journeys a year. (A1)
  • So $300 \times 800 = 240{,}000$ journey records would be silently deleted every year. (A1)

Nothing would raise an error. Ridership totals, revenue history and the city-to-city comparisons the operator is about to need would simply lose 240,000 true facts a year, and no later query could recover them, because the facts would no longer exist. The proposal confuses two different things. Cascading deletes are appropriate for rows that have no meaning without their parent — a saved payment method, for example, is meaningless once the member is gone. A journey is not like that: it happened, it was paid for, and it is the data the scheme reports on. The referential rule should therefore refuse to delete a bike while journeys still reference it (RESTRICT or NO ACTION), or, better, the bike should never be deleted at all: a Status column set to retired keeps the row, keeps the foreign key valid and keeps the history intact. A nullable foreign key with SET NULL is a weaker third option: it preserves the journey but loses the link to the bike, so the record can no longer say which bike was used. (A1) for a recommendation that is justified by the requirement to preserve history rather than by tidiness.
questions.explanation:
The question is built so that the cost of a design decision can be counted, and so that the decision that looks tidiest is the destructive one.

The flat file's real problem is not that it is a spreadsheet. It is that facts about members and bikes are stored *inside* journey rows, so their multiplicity becomes the journey count. Every number in part (b) follows from that single structural fact: 50 bytes multiplied by 12,000,000, and 1,200,000 edits instead of 120,000 for the same administrative event. A student who thinks the problem is "the file is big" has not found the mechanism, and their answer to part (c) will be a list of table names rather than an explanation of why the multiplicity changed.

Part (d) is where the trap is. Cascading deletes are widely taught as good practice because they prevent orphan rows, and a student who has learned that rule will recommend the cascade without hesitating. But preventing an orphan has two implementations with opposite consequences: RESTRICT refuses the delete and keeps the child; CASCADE allows the delete and destroys the child. Cascade is right only when the child row has no independent meaning. A journey has independent meaning — it is the thing the scheme measures — so the "clean" option is the one that quietly deletes 240,000 records a year. That is the sense in which the obvious answer is wrong.

Two further wrong turns are common. The first is treating 600 MB as too small to matter; the argument is not the bytes but the unbounded growth and the 1,200,000-row update multiplicity. The second is treating ChargeCents as text as a cosmetic issue, because in a spreadsheet the value is right-aligned and looks like a number. It only fails when a query tries to aggregate it — which is exactly when the report is due. Data types are not decoration; they determine which questions the database can answer at all.

questions.subtopic: B2.1 Programming fundamentals
questions.question:
The rewritten system must be available in both Python and Java, and the two versions must behave identically.

(a)

Explain the difference between a floating-point number and an integer as a way of storing an amount of money, and state why the balance in this system should be held in pence rather than pounds.

[3]

(b)

Construct a Python function settle(balance_pence, minutes, points) that returns the balance remaining after the stay, or None if the balance is insufficient. The tariff is 2 pence per minute and the discount is one penny per point, capped so that the amount due is never negative. Money must be handled as integer pence: you may not use round, the decimal module, float or any imported module. A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm, so write the algorithm rather than a demonstration of syntax.

[5]

(c)

Explain why the loop above prints 15.999999999999945 rather than 16.00, and why can_buy_pass therefore returns False. Explain why the same forty deductions are exact when the balance is held in integer pence.

[4]

(d)

Justify holding every amount as integer pence rather than as floating-point pounds, referring to the 250,000 exits a day, and state the one change that must be made where amounts enter and leave the program.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) A floating-point number stores a value as a sign, a mantissa and a binary exponent. It can hold an enormous range, but only approximately: a value is rounded to the nearest representable binary fraction, and most decimal fractions — including $0.10$ — have no exact binary representation. (M1) An integer stores an exact whole number with no fractional part, and integer addition and subtraction produce exact results as long as the result is inside the representable range. (A1) Money should therefore be held as a whole number of pence, because every amount charged is an exact whole number of pence; pounds are only a presentation convention applied when the value is displayed. (A1)

(b)

def settle(balance_pence, minutes, points):
    charge = minutes * 2          # 2 pence per minute, exact
    discount = points             # 1 penny per point
    if discount > charge:
        discount = charge         # the amount due is never negative
    due = charge - discount
    if balance_pence < due:
        return None               # insufficient: the barrier stays down
    return balance_pence - due    # exact remaining balance, 0 when equal

(M1) for computing the charge as an integer product rather than a floating-point rate. (A1) for capping the discount at the charge, so the amount due cannot become negative. (A1) for the balance test. (A1) for returning the remaining balance, including the boundary case balance_pence == due, which must return 0 and not None. (A1) for using only integer arithmetic throughout.

A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm. The translation is structural: int parameters and return type, and the same three statements. Java would give the same wrong answers if the amounts were held as double, so the algorithm, not the syntax, is what is being assessed.

(c) The literal 0.10 is not exactly one tenth. The nearest 64-bit floating-point value is slightly larger than $0.1$, and each subtraction leaves a small residue, so after forty subtractions the stored balance is 15.999999999999945 rather than 16.00. (M1)(A1) The comparison balance >= 16.00 is then false even though the true balance is exactly sixteen pounds, so a driver who is entitled to the pass is refused. (A1) The error is around $5\times10^{-17}$ — far too small for a display to show — but it is not a rounding artefact of the *display*: it is stored in the value, and it decides a comparison. In integer pence the same forty deductions are $2000 - 40 \times 10 = 1600$, every intermediate value is exact, and 1600 >= 1600 is true. (A1)

Note how well the bug hides. The arithmetic expression 20.00 - 40 * 0.10 evaluates to exactly 16.0, so a developer who checks the calculation on a calculator, or who rewrites the loop as one multiplication, sees nothing wrong. Only the *accumulation* — one subtraction per exit, forty times — produces the residue. That is why the fault survives the obvious test.

(d) Holding amounts in integer pence is justified by exactness, and the exactness has a measurable cost when it is absent. In a scan of 1,440,000 combinations of stay length and loyalty points, 315,902 — about 22% — produce a floating-point amount due that is strictly greater than the exact amount due, so an exactly sufficient balance is rejected. (M1)(A1) The car park handles 250,000 exits a day. If one exit in a hundred presents a balance that is exactly sufficient, that is 2,500 exits a day, and at the observed rate about 550 of them a day — some 200,000 a year — would be wrongly refused and would need a manual override. (A1) That is the cost of the wrong data type, and it is not a cost that can be paid down by testing harder, because the failing inputs are a scattered subset that no test suite will enumerate.

One change is needed where the value crosses the boundary of the program. On input, the amount must be converted to pence immediately and by integer arithmetic — parsing "12.30" as 1230, never as float("12.30") * 100, which reintroduces the error. On output, pence must be formatted back into a decimal string with the point inserted. Inside the program, every amount is an integer. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The lever here is a correctness bug that survives the obvious test, and the reason it survives is worth stating precisely: the error is far too small to see, but it is compared, not displayed.

A developer testing this system would try a single stay. 20.00 - 0.10 gives 19.9, which prints as 19.9, and the balance check works. They might also check the total with a calculator, or rewrite the loop as 20.00 - 40 * 0.10 — and that expression is exactly 16.0, so it passes too. The fault appears only when the balance is *accumulated*, one subtraction at a time, which is what a real system does. The discrepancy between 20.00 - 40 * 0.10 and forty separate subtractions is the whole question: floating-point arithmetic is not associative, so the order of operations changes the answer, and the order is fixed by the program's control flow rather than by the mathematics.

The deeper point is that >= on computed floating-point values is not a reliable test, and no amount of care in choosing the comparison operator fixes it. A tolerance comparison (abs(balance - due) < 0.005) looks like the standard remedy and is the most tempting wrong turn: it hides this bug by accepting a balance that is a fraction of a penny short, which is a different defect — the system now lets a driver through who has not paid. The requirement is exactness, so the representation has to be exact, and the only exact representation of a whole number of pence is an integer.

Two further wrong turns are common. The first is using round(x, 2) on the balance after each subtraction; rounding a float does not remove the residue, and Python's round uses banker's rounding, so round(2.5) is 2 and round(0.5) is 0, which introduces a new and equally silent error. The second is believing that Python's 64-bit floats are "precise enough"; they are precise enough to *display* money, which is why the bug is invisible, and not precise enough to *compare* it, which is why it matters. The same reasoning applies to Java's double, and that is why the fix is a change of data type rather than a change of language.
```
