```
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.5 File processing
questions.question:
The ingestion runs once a night on a single machine, must not exhaust memory, and must finish before the next upload arrives.

(a)

Explain why stream.read() cannot be used here, referring to the size of the file and the memory available, and state what a streaming implementation does instead.

[3]

(b)

Explain why data.split("\n") followed by line.split(",") produces errors that the developer would not see when testing on a small file. Describe how a record containing a comma inside a quoted field must be parsed.

[4]

(c)

Construct a Python function ingest(stream, max_errors) that consumes the stream exactly once and returns a summary, an error report and an error count. stream is a file-like object that supports iteration and cannot be rewound. The summary must give, for each station, the count, minimum, maximum and sum of temperatures. The error report must hold the line number and a reason for at most max_errors malformed records, and the count must be the exact total of malformed records. You may not import any module, and you may not call stream.read() or stream.seek(). A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm.

[5]

(d)

Evaluate the decision to keep only the first max_errors malformed records while still counting all of them, against the provider's requirement to receive the line number of every malformed record. State what is given up and recommend a design.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The file is 40 GB and the machine has 8 GB of RAM, so stream.read() tries to build a string five times larger than the memory available; the process would be killed before any summary was produced, and the failure would happen after the whole file had been transferred. (M1) The stream also cannot be rewound: it arrives compressed over a socket and the raw file is never written to disk, so the program cannot read part of it, release the memory and then return to the beginning. (A1) A streaming implementation reads one record at a time and keeps only the running state it needs — for each station a count, a minimum, a maximum and a running total — so its memory use is proportional to the number of stations, not to the size of the file, and 500 stations need only a few tens of kilobytes. (A1)

(b) There are two faults, and neither is visible on a small test file.

The first is data.split("\n"). It splits the entire 40 GB string and, because a text file normally ends with a newline character, it produces a final empty element. That empty element is counted as a malformed record, so the reported error count is wrong by one before any real error is found. (M1)(A1) Iterating the file object directly avoids this, because a text stream yields one line per record and never yields a phantom line at the end.

The second is line.split(","), which splits on every comma, including a comma that is inside a quoted field. A record such as ST04,"North, West",4.0,60 contains four fields, but split(",") returns five pieces, so a perfectly valid record is rejected and the field boundaries of the following fields are wrong. (M1)(A1) A correct parser scans the line character by character, keeps a flag for whether it is inside a quoted field, treats a doubled quote as a literal quote character, and splits only on commas seen outside quotes.

(c)

def ingest(stream, max_errors):
    summary = {}
    errors = []
    total_errors = 0

for lineno, raw in enumerate(stream, start=1):
line = raw.rstrip("\r\n")
if line == "":
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "empty line"))
continue

fields = split_csv(line)
if len(fields) != 4:
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "field count %d" % len(fields)))
continue

station, timestamp, temp, humidity = fields
try:
t = float(temp)
except ValueError:
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "non-numeric temperature"))
continue

if station in summary:
count, low, high, total = summary[station]
summary[station] = (count + 1, min(low, t), max(high, t), total + t)
else:
summary[station] = (1, t, t, t)

return summary, errors, total_errors

def split_csv(line):
fields, current, in_quotes = [], [], False
i = 0
while i < len(line):
ch = line[i]
if ch == '"':
if in_quotes and i + 1 < len(line) and line[i + 1] == '"':
current.append('"')
i += 2
continue
in_quotes = not in_quotes
elif ch == "," and not in_quotes:
fields.append("".join(current))
current = []
else:
current.append(ch)
i += 1
fields.append("".join(current))
return fields
```

(M1) for consuming the stream exactly once, with enumerate supplying the line number, and never calling read() or seek(). (A1) for holding only bounded state per station — a count, a minimum, a maximum and a running total — so memory is proportional to the number of stations. (A1) for capping errors at max_errors while total_errors still counts every malformed record, so the exact scale of the corruption is preserved. (A1) for the quoted-field parser, which is what makes the field count correct for records such as ST04,"North, West",4.0,60. (A1) for validating the numeric field and continuing rather than crashing, so that one bad record does not abandon the remaining 400,000,000.

The time is $O(n)$ in the number of records and the memory is $O(S)$ for $S$ stations plus at most max_errors small tuples. A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm: a BufferedReader read line by line, a HashMap of running statistics, and the identical two-state parser.

(d) The requirement and the cap are in direct conflict. The provider must receive the line number of *every* malformed record, and a corrupt upload can contain millions of them, so an in-memory list capped at max_errors will be full almost immediately and the line numbers beyond the cap are lost. (M1) The cap does bound memory — max_errors tuples of an integer and a short string is a few tens of kilobytes, which is safe on an 8 GB machine — so the design trades completeness for a memory guarantee. (A1)

That trade is unnecessary, because the error report does not have to live in memory. Each malformed record can be written to a second output stream as it is found: memory stays bounded at one record, and the provider receives every line number. (A1) The costs are a second output to manage and the throughput the writes consume, but the error file is normally tiny — it is only large when the upload is genuinely corrupt, which is exactly when the provider needs it in full. The running total_errors count should be kept regardless, so that the summary can state the scale of the corruption even if the provider's tooling truncates the error file.

The recommendation is therefore to stream the errors out, and to fall back to a capped in-memory list only when no second output is available. In that fallback the report must say so: it must state that line numbers beyond the cap are missing while the total count remains exact, so that the provider knows how much of the report is absent rather than believing the report is complete. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Three requirements appear to conflict: process the file in one pass, keep memory bounded, and report every malformed record. The obvious way to satisfy any two of them is to break the third, and most students will break the third — they will cap the error list and accept that some line numbers are lost. The insight the question is testing is that the conflict is not real: it exists only because the error report was assumed to be an in-memory object. Move it to a different sink and all three requirements hold at once. That is a design move, not a coding trick, and it is the reason the final part carries the marks.

The memory arithmetic is the part that must be done rather than estimated. Forty gigabytes against eight gigabytes is a factor of five, and that is *before* the overhead of a Python string object; a list of 400,000,000 line objects would need several times the raw file size. A student who says "the file is large" has not established that the naive approach is impossible, and the difference between "slow" and "impossible" matters, because a slow program can be left to run and an impossible one cannot.

The two parsing faults are the classic reasons that file-processing code passes its tests and fails in production. A small test file written by hand often has no trailing newline and no quoted commas; a real 40 GB export has both. split("\n") on a file that ends with a newline produces a phantom empty record, which inflates the error count by one and, worse, trains the developer to ignore the error report. And splitting on commas is only correct for files whose fields never contain commas — which is a property of the data, not a guarantee, and CSV quoting exists precisely because that property fails. Both faults are invisible on the obvious test and both are trivially avoided by the right primitive: iterate the file object, and parse fields with a state machine that knows about quotes.

The final wrong turn is worth naming because it is the most reasonable-looking. A student who caps the error list has correctly identified that memory must be bounded and has made a defensible engineering trade. What they have missed is that the requirement they sacrificed was the one the *user* cared about, and that it could be satisfied at almost no cost. Recognising which constraint is genuinely binding — and which one is an artefact of an implementation choice — is the transferable skill.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B4.1 Binary search trees: traversal, insertion, deletion and search cost
questions.question:
A public library is building a catalogue system. Each book is identified by a numerical accession number, and the catalogue must support three operations: finding the record for a given accession number, adding a new accession number, and printing the whole catalogue in ascending order of accession number. The system designer decides to hold the accession numbers in a binary search tree. The figure shows two binary search trees, A and B, that were built from the same five accession numbers, with the insertion order used for each tree given above it. The height of a tree is taken to be the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf. Answer all parts with reference to the figure, and justify each answer.

(a)

State the in-order traversal of tree A, and explain why an in-order traversal of any binary search tree returns its keys in ascending order.

[2]

(b)

Determine where the accession number 40 would be inserted in tree A, and state the height of the tree after that insertion.

[3]

(c)

Describe the steps needed to delete a node that has two children from a binary search tree, and apply your description to the deletion of the node holding 45 from tree A.

[4]

(d)

The library's catalogue will eventually hold 200 000 accession numbers. Compare the greatest number of comparisons a search might need in a tree shaped like tree A with the greatest number it might need in a tree shaped like tree B, and comment on the practical significance of the difference.

[4]

(e)

A colleague suggests replacing the tree with a hash table, which would give constant-time lookup. Explain whether a hash table could satisfy all three of the operations the catalogue must support.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) An in-order traversal visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and applied to tree A it yields 20, 30, 35, 45, 50. (A1) The traversal is ascending because of the ordering property of a binary search tree: every key in the left subtree of a node is smaller than the node's key, and every key in the right subtree is larger. (M1) Visiting left, then node, then right therefore emits each key only after every smaller key in its subtree, and before every larger one, so the output is sorted whatever the shape of the tree.

(b) Insertion compares the new key with each node from the root downwards and moves left when the key is smaller and right when it is larger. Starting at 30, the key 40 is larger, so it goes right; at 45 it is smaller, so it goes left; at 35 it is larger, so it goes right, and the position is empty. (M1)(A1) The key 40 therefore becomes the right child of 35. (A1) That path visits four nodes, 30, 45, 35 and 40, so the height of the tree rises from 3 to 4.

(c) A node with two children cannot simply be removed, because the two subtrees would have to be reattached. The standard method is to replace the key being deleted with its in-order successor, which is the smallest key in its right subtree, and then delete that successor from the right subtree, where it is guaranteed to have at most one child. (M1)(A1) For tree A, the in-order successor of 45 is 50, since 50 is the only key in 45's right subtree and is therefore its smallest. (A1) The key at the node is overwritten with 50, and the original node holding 50, which is a leaf, is then removed. The resulting tree has root 30, left child 20, and right child 50 with left child 35, so its height is 3. (A1)

(d) In a tree shaped like A the height grows with the logarithm of the number of keys, because each comparison halves the range still to be searched. (M1) For 200 000 keys the height is about log2(200000), which is 17.6, so a search visits at most 18 nodes and needs at most 18 comparisons. (A1) In a tree shaped like B, each node has only one child, so the tree is a chain and a search may have to visit every node. (M1) For 200 000 keys that is 200 000 comparisons, which is roughly 11 000 times as many as the balanced shape needs. The practical significance is that the degenerate shape offers no improvement over scanning a list, so the choice of a tree delivers nothing unless the shape is controlled. (A1)

(e) A hash table computes the position of a key from the key itself, so lookup, insertion and deletion are all constant-time on average, and the three operations would be fast. (M1) However, the keys in a hash table are stored in an order determined by the hash function, not by the keys, so the third operation, printing the catalogue in ascending order of accession number, cannot be done without retrieving every key and sorting it, which costs O(n log n) each time. (A1) The hash table is therefore the better structure only if the ordered listing is not required, or if it is produced once and cached; as specified, it does not satisfy the third requirement. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The figure makes one point very clearly: two trees can hold the same data and behave completely differently. Tree A and tree B contain the same five accession numbers, and an in-order traversal of either returns 20, 30, 35, 45, 50. Nothing about the contents of the trees distinguishes them. What differs is their shape, and shape is what determines the cost of every operation performed on them.

The traversal part of the question is the part that shape cannot affect, and that is worth seeing. The ordering property guarantees that the left subtree of any node holds only smaller keys and the right subtree only larger ones, so visiting left, node, right emits the keys in ascending order regardless of how the tree is arranged. This is the property that makes a binary search tree useful for the library's third requirement, printing the catalogue in order, which is the requirement a hash table cannot meet.

Insertion follows one path from the root, turning left or right at each node, and the new key always becomes a leaf. In tree A the key 40 travels 30, then 45, then 35, and lands to the right of 35. The tree's height becomes 4, which is worth noting because insertion can change the height without changing the number of nodes on the old longest path.

Deletion is the operation that cannot be inferred from insertion. Removing a leaf is trivial, and removing a node with one child is easy, but a node with two children has two subtrees to preserve and only one slot to put them in. The standard solution is to overwrite the node's key with its in-order successor, the smallest key in its right subtree, and then delete that successor, which by construction has at most one child. Here the successor of 45 is 50, and after the operation the tree has 50 where 45 was, with 35 still as its left child.

The comparison in part (d) is the reason any of this matters. A balanced tree of 200 000 keys has height about 18, so a search visits at most 18 nodes. A tree shaped like a chain visits up to 200 000. Both are valid binary search trees, so the structure guarantees nothing on its own; the guarantee comes from controlling the shape. Part (e) closes the argument by asking whether a different structure would avoid the problem, and the answer is that a hash table solves the lookup problem while creating a new one, because it has no notion of order.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A3.2 Database design
questions.question:
Using the case study, answer all four parts. Assume a month is 30 nights of batch processing.

(a)

Explain why a big-bang cutover is a poor choice for this system, referring to specific figures in the case study rather than to general principles.

[4]

(b)

Construct an incremental migration plan. State the mechanism that routes each request, the order in which you would move functions and why that order, and how the two systems are kept consistent while both are live.

[5]

(c)

Calculate the total cost of nine months of dual running, including the analyst time spent on reconciliation. Show your working.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate the two proposals. If a failed big-bang cutover causes an 8-hour outage in which 3 200 payments per hour are missed and each missed payment costs EUR 120 in penalties and remediation, compare that with your answer to (c) and state which proposal you recommend.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The decisive figure is the fallback: restoring from the previous night's backup takes 14 hours, during which roughly $14 \times 3200 \approx 45\,000$ payment instructions are not processed. (A1) A single failed cutover therefore risks a full working day of missed payments on a book of 18 million policies. (A1)

The staff position removes the option of a leisurely recovery. Only four people can maintain the old system, so if the new system fails and the old one must be restored and then kept running, there is almost no capacity to diagnose and fix the new one. (A1)

There is also no way to validate the new system at full scale before committing: 240 000 transactions per night cannot be simulated faithfully enough to be confident, and the first genuine run would also be the production run. (A1)

(b) *Mechanism:* place a facade in front of both systems. Every request arrives at the facade, which inspects the function being invoked and routes it either to the mainframe or to the new service. Callers never know which is serving them, so functions can be moved one at a time and moved back if necessary. (M1)(A1)

*Order:* move the read-mostly reference functions first, then simple queries, then writes, and leave the nightly batch and the payment instruction generation until last. (A1) The reason is that a read that goes wrong is visible immediately and is cheap to reverse, whereas a write that goes wrong corrupts data that may not be discovered for weeks; and the batch window is the most complex and least reversible part of the system, so it should be migrated only when everything feeding it is already new. (A1)

*Consistency while both are live:* run both systems for each migrated function and compare their outputs automatically every night, logging any disagreement as an exception for an analyst. The mainframe remains the system of record until a function has run clean for a sustained period, at which point the new system becomes the record for that function and the old one stops being authoritative for it. (A1)

(c) Infrastructure: $9 \times 14\,000 = \text{EUR }126\,000$. (A1)

Exceptions per night: $0.02\% \times 240\,000 = 48$. (M1)
Time per night: $48 \times 6 = 288$ minutes $= 4.8$ hours. (A1)
Over nine months, $9 \times 30 = 270$ nights: $270 \times 4.8 = 1296$ hours, at EUR 65 per hour:
$$1296 \times 65 = \text{EUR }84\,240$$
Total: $126\,000 + 84\,240 = \text{EUR }210\,240$. (A1)

(d) A failed cutover misses $8 \times 3200 = 25\,600$ payments, costing (M1)
$$25\,600 \times 120 = \text{EUR }3\,072\,000.$$
Comparing with the EUR 210 240 for nine months of dual running, a single failure costs about (A1)
$$\frac{3\,072\,000}{210\,240} \approx 15$$
times as much as the entire incremental programme. (A1)

Recommendation: Proposal B. Even if one assumed a failure probability for the big-bang cutover as low as one in ten, its expected cost would be about EUR 307 000, still above the full cost of dual running, and the incremental route has the further advantages of keeping the old system available as a live fallback for every function not yet moved, of building operational confidence gradually, and of allowing the four remaining experts to be consulted steadily rather than in a crisis. The one real drawback is the nine-month cost of running both, which the calculation shows to be small relative to the risk avoided.
questions.explanation:
Migration questions are usually answered with principles: do it incrementally, keep a fallback, test thoroughly. Those are all true and none of them is an argument. This question is built so that the argument is arithmetic. The cost of nine months of dual running, including every exception being investigated by a human being, is a little over two hundred thousand euro. The cost of one failed cutover, priced at the contractual penalty per missed payment, is over three million. That is a factor of about fifteen, and it means the incremental route is not merely more cautious but cheaper even if you assume the big-bang would usually succeed.

The design part is where the real difficulty sits, and it is not the routing mechanism, which is straightforward. It is deciding the order. The principle is that the cost of being wrong should rise as slowly as possible, which means moving functions whose failure is immediately visible and cheaply reversed before functions whose failure is silent and expensive. Read-only reference data is the obvious first candidate: if the new system returns the wrong address, someone notices the same day and nothing is corrupted. Writes are the opposite. And the nightly batch, which is the most intricate part and the one whose failure is discovered last, must go last, when everything that feeds it has already been proven.

Keeping the two systems consistent is the part students underestimate. It is not enough to say the databases are synced; the schemas differ, the semantics of a forty-year-old flat-file system rarely map cleanly onto a relational model, and the only practical approach is to run both and compare the outputs, treating every disagreement as an exception to be investigated. That is why the reconciliation cost is built into the calculation rather than treated as an afterthought: the 0.02 percent mismatch rate is not a rounding error, it is forty-eight investigations a night for nine months, and any plan that ignores it is not a plan.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking
questions.question:
You are asked to choose the order in which the four cars enter the booth. Work in whole hours, and remember that a job's lateness is measured against its own promise and can be negative.

(a)

The cars are currently processed in the order they were booked: A, then B, then C, then D. Determine the finishing time of each car and the largest lateness of that schedule.

[3]

(b)

Apply the shortest-job-first rule, that is, process the cars in increasing order of painting time, breaking any tie by the earlier promise. Give the resulting order, each finishing time, and the largest lateness of that schedule.

[4]

(c)

Explain why the schedule that puts the car with the earliest promise first can never produce a larger worst-case lateness than the schedule you found in part (b), however the remaining cars are then arranged. Your explanation should identify the property of the worst-case objective that makes the exchange argument work.

[5]

(d)

A fifth car, E, is added. E takes 3 hours and is promised at hour 9. Justify whether the earliest-promise-first order still achieves the smallest possible worst-case lateness for all five cars, and state the value it achieves.

[4]
questions.answer:
Part (a). The cars run back to back from hour 0, so each finishing time is the running total of the painting times.

A finishes at 0 + 5 = 5. B finishes at 5 + 2 = 7. C finishes at 7 + 4 = 11. D finishes at 11 + 7 = 18. (M1) for the running total, (A1) for all four finishing times.

The lateness of each car is its finishing time minus its own promise. A: 5 - 8 = -3. B: 7 - 6 = +1. C: 11 - 20 = -9. D: 18 - 16 = +2. (A1) The largest lateness is therefore +2, set by car D.

Part (b). The painting times are A 5, B 2, C 4, D 7, so increasing order is B (2), C (4), A (5), D (7). No ties arise, so the tie-break is not needed. (M1)

Finishing times: B at 2, C at 2 + 4 = 6, A at 6 + 5 = 11, D at 11 + 7 = 18. (A1)

Lateness: B is 2 - 6 = -4; C is 6 - 20 = -14; A is 11 - 8 = +3; D is 18 - 16 = +2. (A1) The largest lateness is +3, set by car A. (A1) So shortest-job-first is worse than the booking order, which is the surprising result the question is built on: it moved the worst lateness from +2 up to +3.

Part (c). The objective depends only on the largest lateness, so it is decided by a single job. Consider any schedule and suppose that, at some point, the job with the earliest promise among those not yet started is not the one that runs next. (M1) Let that job be X and let the job that actually runs be Y, which therefore has a promise no earlier than X's. Swap X and Y so that X runs in Y's slot and Y runs immediately after. (M1)

The jobs before the swap are untouched, and the jobs after the two swapped ones still finish at the same times, because the pair still occupies the same total length of time. So only X and Y can have their lateness changed. (A1) After the swap X finishes earlier than Y did, and its promise was no later than Y's, so X's lateness does not increase. Y finishes exactly when X used to finish, which is at most as late as Y's old finishing time, so Y's lateness does not increase either. (M1)

Every swap of this kind therefore leaves the largest lateness no larger than it was, and repeated swapping sorts the schedule into earliest-promise-first order without ever making the worst case worse. Since we started from an arbitrary schedule, no schedule can beat the earliest-promise-first order on this objective. (R1) This is exactly why the reasoning fails for the *average* lateness, where a short job delays fewer jobs and the trade is genuinely different.

Part (d). With E added, the promises are B 6, A 8, E 9, D 16, C 20, so the earliest-promise-first order is B, A, E, D, C. (M1)

Finishing times: B 2, A 7, E 10, D 17, C 21. Lateness: B -4, A -1, E 10 - 9 = +1, D 17 - 16 = +1, C 21 - 20 = +1. The largest lateness is +1. (A1)

The exchange argument of part (c) never used the number of jobs, only the fact that swapping an earlier-promise job forward cannot worsen either swapped job, so it applies unchanged to five jobs. (M1) The achieved value +1 is therefore the smallest possible worst-case lateness; a complete search of all 120 orders confirms that no order does better. (A1) Notice that adding E has turned a schedule that was comfortably early everywhere into one that is late on three jobs, which is a property of the job set rather than of the rule.
questions.explanation:
The item is a trap built out of two heuristics that are both taught, in different contexts, without the objective they belong to.

Shortest-job-first is the correct answer to a different question. It minimises the *average* time a job spends in the system, and it is genuinely optimal for that. Students meet it as the scheduling rule and reach for it here. But the workshop is not judged on the average; it is judged on the single worst customer, and those two objectives order the jobs differently. On this job set shortest-job-first produces a worst lateness of +3 while the booking order produces +2 and the earliest-promise order produces -1. The rule that is right for the average is the *worst* of the three candidates for the maximum.

The second trap is the sign. Because lateness is defined as finish minus promise, a good schedule has a *negative* maximum. A student who is looking for the largest number and who discards signs will report -14 from part (b), or +3 when the answer is -1, and will have inverted the objective without noticing. This is why the stimulus states the convention explicitly and why part (a) is deliberately a schedule that is early on three cars and late on one.

The reasoning in part (c) is an exchange argument, and the point worth seeing is that the argument is *tight*: it works because the two swapped jobs are adjacent, so nothing after them moves, and because the job moved forward had the earlier promise. Change either condition and it collapses. Part (d) tests whether the student understood the argument or merely memorised its conclusion, by changing the instance in a way that makes the answer worse without changing the rule.

The classic wrong turn in part (c) is to argue from the first job only, or to claim that the rule is obviously optimal because it is named after the deadline. Neither is a proof: the first job being on time says nothing about the last one, and the whole content of the result is that the swap does not harm the job it displaces.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.2 Data structures
questions.question:
The department expects two different workloads and has not yet decided which one it will have. Workload X builds the list once and then performs 4096 lookups for the fifth most urgent patient. Workload Y performs 4096 rounds, where each round is one lookup for the fifth most urgent patient followed immediately by one insertion. You should count operations for both structures under both workloads.

(a)

Calculate the cost of one lookup for the fifth most urgent patient under each structure, and explain briefly why the two costs differ.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the total number of operations each structure needs for workload X, taking account of the cost of building the structure as well as the cost of the lookups. State which structure is cheaper and by what factor, to one decimal place.

[5]

(c)

Carry out the same comparison for workload Y, and state which structure is cheaper for that workload.

[4]

(d)

A colleague concludes from the two structures' usual descriptions that the heap must be the right choice because insertion is logarithmic rather than linear. Justify whether that reasoning is sufficient, referring to your answers in parts (b) and (c).

[3]
questions.answer:
Part (a). In the max-heap the largest patient is at the root, but the fifth most urgent is not at any fixed position. To reach it you remove the largest patient, restore the heap, and repeat until five patients have come out; then you put the four removed patients back. Each removal costs 12 operations to restore the heap, so the lookup costs 5 x 2 x 12 = 120 operations. (M1) for the 12, (A1) for 120.

In the ordered array the patients are already in descending order, so the fifth most urgent is simply at index 4. Reading it costs 1 operation. (A1)

The costs differ because the heap is arranged by a *partial* order: it guarantees only that a parent is at least as urgent as its children, which is enough to place the single most urgent patient but says nothing about where the fifth belongs. The array is arranged by a *total* order, which places every patient, and that is what makes an arbitrary rank cheap to read. (A1)

Part (b). Workload X: 4096 lookups, each 120 operations, gives 4096 x 120 = 491 520 operations. (M1) Building the heap from 4096 patients costs 4096 operations. (A1) Total for the heap: 4096 + 491 520 = 495 616 operations.

For the ordered array, building means sorting, which costs 4096 x 12 = 49 152 operations. (A1) The 4096 lookups cost 4096 x 1 = 4096 operations. Total: 49 152 + 4096 = 53 248 operations. (M1)

The ordered array is cheaper, by 495 616 / 53 248 = 9.3 times to one decimal place. (A1)

Part (c). Workload Y: each round is a lookup followed by an insertion, and there are 4096 rounds.

For the heap, a round costs 120 + 12 = 132 operations, so the total is 4096 x 132 = 540 672 operations. (M1)(A1)

For the ordered array, a round costs 1 + 2048 = 2049 operations, because inserting into a sorted array of 4096 elements shifts half of it on average. The total is 4096 x 2049 = 8 392 704 operations. (M1) The heap is cheaper for this workload, by 8 392 704 / 540 672 = 15.5 times. (A1)

So the two structures swap places: the array wins workload X by 9.3 times and the heap wins workload Y by 15.5 times.

Part (d). The colleague's reasoning is not sufficient, because it is a statement about *insertion* alone and the two workloads do not weight insertion the same way. (M1) In workload X there are no insertions after the list is built, so the heap's logarithmic insertion is worth nothing and the array's constant-time rank lookup decides the whole comparison, which is why the array wins by 9.3 times. (A1) In workload Y every lookup is followed by an insertion, and there the linear insertion cost of the array dominates everything else, which is why the heap wins by 15.5 times. (A1) The conclusion the colleague should draw is that the heap's advantage is conditional on insertions being frequent relative to rank lookups, and the department must first know which workload it has.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the standard complexity comparison is not wrong, but is incomplete in a way that changes the answer.

The textbook statement is that a heap gives logarithmic insertion and constant-time access to the maximum, while a sorted array gives linear insertion. A student who has learned that sentence has learned something true, and it is enough to answer the question the course usually asks, which is about a priority queue that only ever needs the maximum. This item asks for the *fifth* largest, and that single change moves the heap's lookup from constant to linear in the rank, which is the crack the whole question turns on.

The deeper point is about what each structure orders. A heap enforces a partial order: every parent is at least as large as its own children, and nothing more. That is exactly enough to guarantee the root is the maximum, and it is why the root is cheap and everything else is not. A sorted array enforces a total order, which costs a great deal to maintain under insertion but makes every rank addressable. Students who can say this have understood the structure rather than memorised its cost table.

The two workloads are the mechanism. Under workload X the array wins by 9.3 times; under workload Y the heap wins by 15.5 times. Neither structure is simply better, and the arithmetic is deliberately close enough that neither answer can be reached by intuition. A student who answers only from the asymptotic descriptions will get part (d) wrong in a specific and diagnosable way, which is the point of asking it.

The classic wrong turn is to treat the heap as if it were sorted, and to assume that the k-th largest is somewhere convenient. It is not: the only guarantee is that it is not an ancestor of anything larger than itself. The second wrong turn is to forget the cost of building the structure in part (b) and to compare only the lookups, which happens to preserve the direction of the answer here but not the factor.

questions.subtopic: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs
questions.question:
The cache must support two operations at constant cost: looking up whether a page is present, and moving a page to the front of the recency order after it is used. You are asked to evaluate the two policies and then to design a structure that meets the cost requirement.

(a)

With room for three pages, determine the number of misses for each of the two policies over the twelve requests, and state which policy has fewer misses.

[4]

(b)

The cache is now given room for four pages. Determine the number of misses for each policy at this size, and explain what the results show about how the first policy's miss count behaves as the cache is enlarged.

[5]

(c)

Design a structure, or a combination of structures, that supports both the presence lookup and the move-to-front operation at constant cost, and explain how each of the two operations is carried out.

[4]

(d)

Justify why the second policy can be supported by your structure at constant cost while the first policy cannot, even though both policies evict exactly one page per miss.

[3]
questions.answer:
Part (a). With room for three pages, the first policy evicts in arrival order. Tracing the requests: 1 misses, cache {1}; 2 misses, {1,2}; 3 misses, {1,2,3}; 4 misses and evicts 1, {2,3,4}; 1 misses and evicts 2, {3,4,1}; 2 misses and evicts 3, {4,1,2}; 5 misses and evicts 4, {1,2,5}; 1 hits; 2 hits; 3 misses and evicts 1, {2,5,3}; 4 misses and evicts 2, {5,3,4}; 5 hits. That is 9 misses. (M1)(A1)

The second policy evicts the least recently used page. Tracing: 1 misses, {1}; 2 misses, {1,2}; 3 misses, {1,2,3}; 4 misses and evicts 1, {2,3,4}; 1 misses and evicts 2, {3,4,1}; 2 misses and evicts 3, {4,1,2}; 5 misses and evicts 4, {1,2,5}; 1 hits, order {2,5,1}; 2 hits, order {5,1,2}; 3 misses and evicts 5, {1,2,3}; 4 misses and evicts 1, {2,3,4}; 5 misses and evicts 2, {3,4,5}. That is 10 misses. (M1)(A1)

So at three pages the first policy has fewer misses, by one. (A1)

Part (b). With room for four pages, the first policy evicts 1 at the fourth request, then 2, then 3, then 4, then 5. The misses are at requests 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 12, which is 10 misses. (M1)(A1)

The second policy with four pages: 1, 2, 3, 4 all miss; 1 hits; 2 hits; 5 misses and evicts 3; 1 hits; 2 hits; 3 misses and evicts 4; 4 misses and evicts 5; 5 misses and evicts 1. That is 8 misses. (M1)(A1)

What the results show is that enlarging the cache made the first policy worse: its miss count rose from 9 to 10 when the room available rose from three pages to four. The second policy behaved as expected, falling from 10 to 8. (A1) A policy whose miss count can increase when it is given more memory is not merely inefficient, it is unsafe to size by experiment, because adding capacity cannot be relied upon to help.

Part (c). The structure is a combination of a hash map and a doubly linked list. (M1)

The hash map is keyed by page number and maps to the node in the list that holds that page. The list holds the pages in recency order, with the most recently used at the head. (A1)

For the presence lookup, the page number is hashed and the map is consulted, which is constant cost on average; if the key is absent the page is not cached. (A1)

For the move-to-front operation, the map gives the node directly, and the node is unlinked from its position and relinked at the head. Because the list is doubly linked, both the node's predecessor and its successor are reachable from the node itself, so a fixed number of pointer changes suffices and no search along the list is needed. (A1)

Part (d). The second policy needs to know, for each page, when it was last used, and the move-to-front structure maintains exactly that as the order of the list, so the least recently used page is the tail and can be evicted by unlinking it. (M1)

The first policy needs to know when each page *arrived*, which is a different order from the recency order and cannot be read off it: a page at the head of the recency list may have arrived long before a page at the tail. (A1) Maintaining the arrival order as well would require a second ordering, and the point is that the recency list is the only order the structure carries, so the policy that needs a different order cannot use it. The deeper reason is that the second policy's eviction rule is a *function of the state the structure already maintains*, while the first policy's is not. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The item is built around a result that surprises almost everyone the first time they meet it: giving a cache more room can make it perform worse. The first policy's miss count rises from 9 to 10 when the cache grows from three pages to four, while the second policy's falls from 10 to 8. The two policies are tied on the small cache and separated on the large one, which means the intuitive experiment of "try it with more memory and see" gives a different recommendation at each size.

The mechanism is that the second policy is a *stack algorithm* and the first is not. A policy is a stack algorithm when the set of pages it holds at any moment, with a cache of size k, is always a subset of the set it would hold with a cache of size k + 1. Least-recently-used has this property, because adding a slot never changes which pages are more recent than which. Evict-the-oldest does not, because a page that arrived early can be kept longer in a larger cache and thereby survive to displace a page that a smaller cache would have kept. Once the student sees that the property is about *nesting of the cache contents* rather than about hit rates, the anomaly stops being paradoxical.

Part (c) is where the abstract data type content lives. The requirement is two constant-cost operations, and neither obvious structure delivers both: a hash map gives the lookup but has no order, and a list gives the order but needs a search to find a page. The answer is a composition, and the composition works only because the list is *doubly* linked, so that a node can be unlinked without walking to find its predecessor. That detail is the whole of part (c)'s last mark and is the most commonly missed step.

Part (d) closes the loop by asking why the same structure cannot serve the first policy. The answer is not that the first policy is harder but that it needs a *different order* from the one the structure maintains. Students who answer that the first policy needs a queue have noticed something true and stopped one step short: a queue would work, but the structure is already maintaining an order and it is the wrong one.

questions.subtopic: A4.2 Choosing a scaling method when one outlier dominates the range
questions.question:
A hospital logistics team is building a machine-learning model to predict delivery times.
One of the features is the loading time, in minutes, for the ten most recent deliveries:

$$10,\ 11,\ 12,\ 13,\ 14,\ 15,\ 16,\ 17,\ 18,\ 1400$$

The final value, $1400$ minutes, is a data-entry error: the true value was $14.00$ and the
decimal point was lost. The team has not yet cleaned the data and is comparing two ways of
scaling the feature before clustering.

(a) Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the ten values as recorded. \tag{3}

(b) Determine the min–max scaled values of $10$, $18$ and $1400$, and calculate the scaled gap
between consecutive typical values. \tag{4}

(c) Determine the standardised (z-score) values of $10$, $18$ and $1400$, calculate the
corresponding scaled gap, and compare the two methods. \tag{5}

(d) Hence explain which scaling method the team should prefer for this data set. \tag{3}

(a)

Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the ten values as recorded.

[3]

(b)

Determine the min-max scaled values of 10, 18 and 1400, and calculate the scaled gap between consecutive typical values.

[4]

(c)

Determine the standardised values of 10, 18 and 1400, calculate the corresponding scaled gap, and compare the two methods.

[5]

(d)

Hence explain which scaling method the team should prefer for this data set.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The nine typical values are the integers $10$ to $18$, whose sum is
$\frac{9(10 + 18)}{2} = 126$; adding $1400$ gives $1526$ and the mean is

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1526}{10} = 152.6 \tag{A1}$$

Note that the mean already sits far above every genuine reading: the true centre of the nine
typical values is $14$, and the single error has moved it by $138.6$.

The sum of squared deviations is most safely found from
$\sum x^{2} - n\bar{x}^{2}$ (M1). Here

$$\sum x^{2} = 100 + 121 + \cdots + 324 + 1960000 = 1824 + 1960000 = 1961824$$

and $n\bar{x}^{2} = 10 \times 152.6^{2} = 10 \times 23286.76 = 232867.6$, so

$$\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2} = 1961824 - 232867.6 = 1728956.4 \tag{A1}$$

The outlier contributes $1247.4^{2} = 1556006.8$ of that, which is $90.0\%$ of the whole
total. The population variance is $\frac{1728956.4}{10} = 172895.6$ and

$$\sigma = \sqrt{172895.6} = 415.8 \tag{A1}$$

(b) Min–max scaling maps $x$ to $\frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}$, and here
$x_{\min} = 10$ and $x_{\max} = 1400$, so the divisor is $1390$ (M1):

$$\frac{10 - 10}{1390} = 0.000, \qquad \frac{18 - 10}{1390} = 0.00576, \qquad
\frac{1400 - 10}{1390} = 1.000 \tag{A1}$$

The typical values therefore occupy the interval $[0,\ 0.00576]$ — the bottom $0.58\%$ of the
range — and the outlier sits alone at $1.000$ (A1). The scaled gap between consecutive typical
values, which are one minute apart in the original data, is

$$\frac{1}{1390} = 0.000719 \tag{A1}$$

(c) Standardising maps $x$ to $\frac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma}$ (M1):

$$\frac{10 - 152.6}{415.8} = -0.343, \qquad \frac{18 - 152.6}{415.8} = -0.324, \qquad
\frac{1400 - 152.6}{415.8} = 3.00 \tag{A1}$$

The typical values occupy $[-0.343,\ -0.324]$ and the outlier sits at $3.00$ (A1). The scaled
gap between consecutive typical values is

$$\frac{1}{415.8} = 0.00241 \tag{A1}$$

which is $\frac{0.00241}{0.000719} = 3.34$ times the min–max gap (A1). Standardisation
therefore preserves about three and a third times as much resolution among the typical readings
as min–max does, even though it is far from ideal: the outlier still inflates $\sigma$ from
about $2.4$ to $415.8$ and drags the mean to $152.6$, more than ten times the largest genuine
reading. Note also that $3.00$ is the largest z-score any value in a data set of ten can have,
so the outlier is pressing against the ceiling that the sample size allows.

(d) Neither method should be used on the raw data (A1). The right first step is to correct or
remove the erroneous $1400$, since it is a known data-entry fault rather than a genuine
observation; with it removed the range is $8$, the mean is $14$ and the choice of scaler barely
matters (A1). If the value must be retained, standardisation is preferable to min–max because
the mean and standard deviation are less sensitive to a single extreme value than the minimum
and maximum are — the outlier moves $\sigma$ but does not set it, whereas it sets $x_{\max}$
directly (A1). Better still is a robust scaler based on the median and interquartile range,
which for this data gives a scaled gap of $\frac{1}{5} = 0.2$, about $278$ times the min–max
resolution.
questions.explanation:
Min–max scaling has a single point of failure: it is defined by the two most extreme
values in the data set. If one of those is wrong, the whole scaling is wrong, and it is wrong in
a way that is easy to miss because the output still looks like a properly scaled feature —
values in $[0, 1]$, outlier at the top, everything else near the bottom. Nothing announces the
problem.

Quantifying the damage is what makes the choice a decision rather than an opinion. Consecutive
typical readings are one minute apart, and after min–max scaling they sit $0.000719$ apart. For
a distance-based algorithm such as k-means, that is very close to indistinguishable: the
distances between ordinary points have been compressed by a factor of $1390$ relative to what
they were, while the distance to the outlier has been set to the maximum the scale allows.

Standardisation does better, and the reason is structural. It is defined by the mean and the
standard deviation, which are computed from every value, so a single extreme reading shifts them
without determining them. Here the outlier is worth $3.0\sigma$ — large, but finite, and it
does not set the scale. The resolution improves by a factor of about $3.3$. That is a real
improvement, but it should not be oversold: the outlier has inflated $\sigma$ from roughly
$2.4$ to $415.8$, so standardisation is compromised too, just less catastrophically.

The honest answer to (d) is that both are the wrong question. The value $1400$ is a known
decimal-point error; there is no statistical method that is the right response to a typo. Clean
it, and with the remaining nine values the range is $8$, the standard deviation is about $2.4$,
and the choice between scalers has almost no effect on the model. Where cleaning is not
possible — because the extreme value might be genuine — a robust scaler based on the median and
interquartile range gives a resolution of $0.2$ here, roughly $278$ times what min–max
delivers.

The more general lesson is that preprocessing choices are not neutral. Two defensible scalings
of the same feature can put the ordinary values $0.0007$ apart or $0.2$ apart, and a
distance-based model will behave completely differently in the two cases. Measuring the
resolution, rather than asserting that one method is "better", is what turns that choice into
something a data scientist can defend.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.3 A process whose working set exceeds the available frames, where the cost of traversing a large array depends on the access order by a factor equal to the number of elements that fit in one page
questions.question:
A server has $4\ {\rm GiB}$ of physical memory, of which the operating system and other resident processes occupy $2\ {\rm GiB}$, leaving $2\ {\rm GiB}$ of frames available to a numerical application. Memory is paged with a page size of $4\ {\rm KiB}$ $(4096\ {\rm bytes})$; a memory access that hits takes $t_{m} = 80\ {\rm ns}$, and a page fault costs $t_{d} = 8\ {\rm ms}$ because the page must be fetched from a solid-state device. The effective access time is
$$t_{\rm eff} = (1 - p)\,t_{m} + p\,t_{d},$$
where $p$ is the probability that a given access faults.
The application must traverse a square array of double-precision numbers, each occupying $8$ bytes, stored in row-major order, with $32\,768$ rows and $32\,768$ columns. Its declared working set is therefore the whole array. Two traversals are considered: one that visits the elements in row-major order and one that visits them in column-major order.

(a)

Calculate the number of frames available to the application and the number of frames the array requires, and state whether the working set fits.

[2]

(b)

Calculate the page-fault probability $p$ at which the effective access time is double the fault-free time, and comment on the magnitude of that probability.

[3]

(c)

Determine the number of page faults generated by each traversal, assuming in the row-major case that each page is read once and in the column-major case that every element access faults. Determine the ratio of the two, and explain where that ratio comes from.

[4]

(d)

Calculate the time taken by each traversal at $8\ {\rm ms}$ per fault, giving your answers in hours for the row-major case and in days for the column-major case.

[3]

(e)

A colleague proposes moving to huge pages of $2\ {\rm MiB}$ $(2\,097\,152\ {\rm bytes})$. Explain, with numbers, what this does for each of the two traversals, and explain why the same change has two such different effects.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The available memory is $2\ {\rm GiB} = 2 \times 1024^{3} = 2\,147\,483\,648$ bytes, giving

$$\frac{2\,147\,483\,648}{4096} = 524\,288\ \text{frames} \;\text{(A1)}$$

The array occupies $32\,768 \times 32\,768 \times 8 = 8\,589\,934\,592$ bytes $= 8\ {\rm GiB}$, so it needs

$$\frac{8\,589\,934\,592}{4096} = 2\,097\,152\ \text{frames} \;\text{(A1)}$$

four times what is available, so the working set does not fit and the process must fault under any policy.

(b) Setting $t_{\rm eff} = 2t_{m} = 160\ {\rm ns}$:

$$160 = 80(1-p) + p(8\times10^{6}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 80 = p(8\times10^{6} - 80) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-5} \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

A fault probability of one in a hundred thousand — a tenth of a basis point — is enough to double the time of every memory access, because a fault costs about $10^{5}$ times as much as a hit (A1). This is why paging systems are designed so that the fault rate stays several orders of magnitude below that; once it rises to even one per cent, the effective access time is roughly a thousand times the nominal one.

(c) The array holds $4096/8 = 512$ doubles per page (M1).

*Row-major.* Consecutive elements of a row are consecutive in memory, so a full traversal reads each page once and never revisits it. The number of faults is the number of pages:

$$\frac{8\,589\,934\,592}{4096} = 2\,097\,152 \;\text{(A1)}$$

*Column-major.* Consecutive elements of a column are $32\,768 \times 8 = 262\,144$ bytes apart, which is $64$ pages apart, so each access lands on a different page and the traversal revisits every page $512$ times over the course of a column pass. Since the whole array needs $2\,097\,152$ frames and only $524\,288$ are available, pages are evicted long before they are revisited, so essentially every access faults. The number of faults is therefore approximately the number of elements:

$$32\,768 \times 32\,768 = 1\,073\,741\,824 \;\text{(A1)}$$

The ratio is

$$\frac{1\,073\,741\,824}{2\,097\,152} = 512 \;\text{(A1)}$$

exactly the number of doubles that fit in one page. That is not a coincidence: in row-major order one fault serves $512$ consecutive element accesses, while in column-major order one fault serves one, so the ratio is precisely the number of elements per page.

(d) Row-major:

$$2\,097\,152 \times 8 \times 10^{-3} = 16\,777\ {\rm s} = 4.66\ {\rm hours} \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

Column-major:

$$1\,073\,741\,824 \times 8 \times 10^{-3} = 8.59 \times 10^{6}\ {\rm s} \approx 99\ {\rm days} \;\text{(A1)}$$

The same computation, on the same data, differing by a factor of $512$ purely because of the order in which the elements are visited.

(e) With $2\ {\rm MiB}$ pages the array occupies $8\,589\,934\,592 / 2\,097\,152 = 4096$ huge pages (M1). For the row-major traversal this reduces the fault count from $2\,097\,152$ to $4096$, a factor of $512$, and the time from $4.66$ hours to $4096 \times 0.008 = 32.8$ seconds (A1). For the column-major traversal it changes nothing: the number of distinct pages is still far more than the available frames can hold, and the access pattern still touches a different page on every single element, so the fault count remains of the order of $10^{9}$ and the traversal still takes about three months (A1). The change has two different effects because the two traversals are limited by different things. The row-major case is limited by the *number* of fault events, and larger pages reduce that number proportionally. The column-major case is limited by the *locality* of the access pattern, and no page size can create locality where the program does not have it: with $512$ doubles per page the row-major case amortises one fault over $512$ accesses, and the column-major case amortises it over one, whatever the page is called.
questions.explanation:
The numbers here are large enough to be genuinely alarming, which is the point: a 512-fold difference in running time produced by the order of two nested loops, with no change to the data, the algorithm's output, or the hardware. Four and a half hours against three months.

It is worth being precise about the two conditions, because the item is built on their conjunction and candidates regularly attribute the disaster to only one. If the array fitted in memory, the column-major traversal would still touch memory in a poor order, but it would cost a modest multiple rather than a catastrophe, because nothing would ever be evicted. If the array did not fit but the traversal were row-major, the cost would be one fault per page, which is the minimum possible for streaming through data larger than memory. It takes both — an oversized working set *and* an access pattern with no locality — to reach a fault per element.

That conjunction is exactly why part (e) is interesting. Huge pages reduce the number of pages by a factor of 512, and for a streaming traversal that translates directly into 512 times fewer faults: 4.66 hours becomes 33 seconds. For the strided traversal it is worth nothing at all, because the number of distinct pages was never the binding constraint — the absence of locality was. The same change, applied to the same array, on the same machine, is either a 500-fold win or nothing.

Part (b) deserves a moment on its own, because the number is so small that it looks wrong. A fault probability of one in a hundred thousand doubles the effective access time. The reason is the ratio $t_d/t_m$, which is about $10^{5}$: a fault costs five orders of magnitude more than a hit, so a fault rate of one in ten to the five contributes as much delay as all the hits combined. This is the arithmetic behind the folklore that paging either works or does not — there is no regime in which it degrades gracefully.

The practical lesson generalises past arrays. Any data structure whose traversal order does not match its memory layout pays a fixed penalty per element, and the penalty is the ratio of elements per page. Row-major arrays traversed by column, linked lists where arrays would do, hash tables with poor locality, structures of arrays split into arrays of structures: the underlying arithmetic is the same, and it is the number of useful accesses served per fault.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A2 Networks
questions.question:
There is more than enough address space for all six requirements, but only if the block is divided unevenly. Design the division, then justify it.

(a)

Design a subnetting scheme using variable-length subnet masks. For each of the six requirements give the network address in dotted decimal, the prefix length, and the number of usable host addresses it provides.

[5]

(b)

Determine how many addresses in the /24 block remain unused by your scheme, and compare this with the number that would remain if the block had instead been divided into four equal subnets.

[4]

(c)

Explain how a host uses its own address and subnet mask to decide whether a destination address is on its own subnet, and what it does if it is not.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate one advantage and one disadvantage of the variable-length scheme compared with using four equal subnets, in a network that may grow.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Work downwards in size so that each block starts on a boundary its own prefix length divides. A prefix that leaves $h$ host bits provides $2^{h} - 2$ usable addresses. (M1)

| requirement | network address | prefix | usable hosts |
|---|---|---|---|
| science, needs 60 | $192.168.40.0$ | $/26$ | $62$ |
| humanities, needs 28 | $192.168.40.64$ | $/27$ | $30$ |
| administration, needs 12 | $192.168.40.96$ | $/28$ | $14$ |
| library, needs 6 | $192.168.40.112$ | $/29$ | $6$ |
| WAN link 1, needs 2 | $192.168.40.120$ | $/30$ | $2$ |
| WAN link 2, needs 2 | $192.168.40.124$ | $/30$ | $2$ |

(A1) for each correct prefix, (A1) for the complete set of addresses, (A1) for the usable-host counts. The blocks occupy $0$–$63$, $64$–$95$, $96$–$111$, $112$–$119$, $120$–$123$ and $124$–$127$ with no overlap, because each block begins at an address divisible by its own size.

(b) The six blocks consume $64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 4 = 128$ addresses, so $256 - 128 = 128$ addresses remain free for growth. (M1)(A1) Four equal subnets would each be a $/26$, giving $4 \times 64 = 256$ addresses and leaving none at all; in that scheme $62 + 30 + 14 + 6 = 112$ required hosts are spread across $248$ usable addresses, so $136$ are wasted inside the subnets, and the two WAN links would not fit. (M1)(A1)

(c) The host performs a bitwise AND between its own address and its subnet mask to obtain its network address, then does the same to the destination address using its own mask. (M1) If the two network addresses are equal, the destination is local and the host sends the frame directly, using ARP to find the destination's MAC address. (A1) If they differ, the host sends the frame to its default gateway instead, addressing the frame to the gateway's MAC address while leaving the destination IP address untouched; the gateway then routes the packet onwards. (A1)

(d) The advantage is that the variable-length scheme leaves $128$ addresses free and can absorb growth in any department by allocating from that pool, or by renumbering only the department that has outgrown its block. (A1) The disadvantage is that it is harder to manage and harder to read: the six prefixes have to be recorded in the routing table individually rather than summarised, and a technician who sees a $/29$ and a $/30$ side by side has more to hold in their head than one who sees four identical entries. (A1) If the network is expected to grow unevenly, or to need small links like these, the extra complexity is worth it; if all four departments are likely to grow at the same rate, the simpler scheme is the better choice. (A1)

A useful check on any scheme is to write the blocks out in order and confirm that each one finishes exactly where the next one begins: $0$ to $63$, $64$ to $95$, $96$ to $111$, $112$ to $119$, $120$ to $123$ and $124$ to $127$. A scheme that leaves a gap or overlaps two blocks has placed a block on a boundary its own size does not divide, and the check takes seconds.
questions.explanation:
Subnetting is usually taught as a procedure and examined as an arithmetic exercise, and this item is built to make the procedure itself the thing under examination. The constraint that does the work is that a block of size $2^{k}$ must start at an address divisible by $2^{k}$. Students who have memorised 'work out how many host bits you need' will compute the correct prefix lengths and then place the blocks in the wrong order, putting the $/27$ at $.96$ where it cannot legally start. Allocating in descending size order avoids the problem automatically, which is why part (a) awards a method mark for it.

Part (b) is the part that justifies variable-length masks at all. Four equal $/26$ subnets consume the entire $/24$, give $62$ usable addresses to a library that needs $6$, and leave nothing for the two router links. The variable-length scheme consumes $128$ addresses and leaves $128$ free. The comparison is not subtle, but it is invisible unless someone asks for it, and a student who produces a valid scheme has still not explained why the scheme is worth producing.

Part (c) addresses a different and equally common gap. Many candidates can calculate a subnet mask and cannot say what it is for, and the honest answer is that it is the operand of a single bitwise AND. Once the mask is understood as something the host applies to both addresses to answer one yes-or-no question — is the destination local — the rest of the behaviour, including why the frame goes to the gateway while the packet keeps its original destination address, follows without being memorised. That is also why the follow-up distinction matters: the MAC address changes at every hop and the IP address does not, and students who have not separated the two will say that the router rewrites the destination.

questions.subtopic: Round-robin and first-come-first-served scheduling
questions.question:
A single-core processor runs three processes that are all held in the ready queue. The figure gives the arrival time and the burst time of each process, and the round-robin schedule that the scheduler produced with a time quantum of four units. The scheduler always adds a process that has just arrived to the back of the ready queue before it adds a process that has used its whole quantum, and a process that finishes inside its quantum is removed immediately. The operating system designer is choosing between this scheduler and a first-come-first-served scheduler, and wants to know which of the two gives the better average waiting time and which gives the better response for an interactive workload.

(a)

Determine the completion time of each of the three processes under the round-robin schedule shown in the figure. Show the order in which the processes are dispatched and the length of each dispatch.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the waiting time of each process under this round-robin schedule and hence the average waiting time. Define the waiting time you use.

[4]

(c)

Calculate the average waiting time if the same three processes were scheduled first-come-first-served in order of arrival, and state which scheduler gives the smaller average.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate which of the two schedulers is more suitable for an interactive system, using your results and considering how the two schedulers behave when a long process arrives before a short one.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Under round-robin the ready queue is ordered by arrival, and each process runs for at most four units before returning to the back of the queue.

At time 0 only P1 has arrived, so P1 is dispatched and runs from 0 to 4, using a whole quantum and leaving 3 units of work (A1). P2 arrives at time 2 and P3 at time 4, so both are waiting when the quantum expires; P2 is added before P1 because P2 arrived first. P2 is dispatched from 4 to 8 and finishes inside its quantum, so it is removed at time 8 (A1). P3 is dispatched from 8 to 9, finishes inside its quantum, and is removed at time 9 (A1). P1 is dispatched again from 9 to 12 and finishes at time 12 (A1).

The completion times are therefore P2 at 8, P3 at 9 and P1 at 12.

(b) The waiting time of a process is the total time it spends in the ready queue, which is its completion time minus its arrival time minus its burst time.

For P1: $12 - 0 - 7 = 5$ units (M1). For P2: $8 - 2 - 4 = 2$ units (A1). For P3: $9 - 4 - 1 = 4$ units (A1).

The total waiting time is $5 + 2 + 4 = 11$ units, so the average is $11 \div 3 = 3.67$ units (A1).

Note that P3, the shortest process, has a longer waiting time than P2. It arrives at time 4, exactly when P1's first quantum expires, and P2 is placed ahead of it because P2 arrived earlier. This is a property of the queue order, not an error in the trace.

(c) First-come-first-served runs the processes to completion in order of arrival. P1 runs from 0 to 7 and finishes at 7 (A1). P2 runs from 7 to 11 and finishes at 11, so its waiting time is $11 - 2 - 4 = 5$ units (A1). P3 runs from 11 to 12 and finishes at 12, so its waiting time is $12 - 4 - 1 = 7$ units.

The total is $0 + 5 + 7 = 12$ units, so the average is $12 \div 3 = 4.00$ units (A1). Round-robin therefore gives the smaller average waiting time, 3.67 against 4.00.

(d) Round-robin is the more suitable scheduler for an interactive system, and the reason is the response time rather than the average waiting time. The response time of a process is the delay before it first receives the processor. Under round-robin P1 first runs at 0, P2 at 4 and P3 at 8, so the response times are 0, 2 and 4 units and the average is 2.0 units (A1). Under first-come-first-served P1 first runs at 0, P2 at 7 and P3 at 11, so the response times are 0, 5 and 7 units and the average is 4.0 units (A1). A user interacting with the system perceives the delay before the first response, so halving it is a substantial gain even though the two schedulers differ by only 0.33 units in average waiting time.

The behaviour when a long process arrives first is the decisive case. Under first-come-first-served a process that needs a long burst blocks every process behind it for the whole of that burst, so a short interactive job can be delayed by the full length of an unrelated long job; this is the convoy effect, and P3's waiting time of 7 units is a small example of it (A1). Round-robin bounds the delay before any waiting process is dispatched by one quantum, so a long job can delay a short one by at most the quantum rather than by its whole burst.

The cost of that bound is context switching, since every quantum boundary forces the processor to save one process and restore another, and a smaller quantum means more such switches (A1). Round-robin is therefore the better choice for interactivity, provided the quantum is large enough that the switching overhead stays small relative to the work done in a quantum.
questions.explanation:
Scheduling questions are usually answerable from a definition, because the marks are for naming the algorithm that suits a stated workload. This item makes the two candidate algorithms produce answers that are close enough that a slogan cannot separate them, and then asks a question whose answer is not the one the slogan predicts.

Round-robin gives an average waiting time of 3.67 units and first-come-first-served gives 4.00. The difference is small, and a candidate who reasons that first-come-first-served is unfair to short jobs would expect a larger gap. The reason the gap is small is that the trace itself has a surprise in it: P3, the shortest process, waits longer than P2, because it arrives exactly at the moment P1's first quantum expires and P2 has an earlier arrival time. The queue order, not the algorithm's reputation, determines that waiting time.

The part that separates the two schedulers properly is response time. Round-robin gives first responses at 0, 4 and 8, so the average is 2.0; first-come-first-served gives 0, 7 and 11, so the average is 4.0. Response time is what an interactive user experiences, and it is not the same quantity as waiting time, so a candidate who answers part (d) from the part (b) numbers alone will reach the right conclusion for the wrong reason and will not be able to say what the round-robin quantum is buying.

The convoy effect is the general statement of the difference. Under first-come-first-served a long burst delays everything behind it by its full length, so the worst-case delay is unbounded in the length of the longest job. Under round-robin the worst-case delay before a waiting process is dispatched is one quantum. That bound is what makes the algorithm suitable for interactive use, and it is paid for with context switches, which is the trade-off a complete answer names.

The figure is required for parts (a) to (c). The arrival and burst times appear only in the process table, and the round-robin schedule is drawn as a Gantt chart whose blocks give the dispatch order and the quantum boundaries directly. A candidate cannot trace the schedule without reading the chart, and the chart is generated from the same simulation the markscheme uses, so the drawn blocks and the quoted completion times cannot disagree.
