questions.subtopic: A2.4 A security incident caused by a legitimate account with excessive privilege, where the control that would have prevented it conflicts with the requirement that clinical staff must not be blocked out of records in an emergency
questions.question:
The trust's board has asked for an analysis of the incident against the three components of the CIA triad, a design for a replacement role-based access-control scheme, the working arithmetic of the current audit coverage and the proposed quarterly permission review, and an evaluation of the information-governance officer's objection.

(a)

Analyse the incident against the three components of the CIA triad, identifying for each component whether it was breached and giving the specific evidence from the case that supports your answer.

[3]

(b)

Design a role-based access-control scheme for this trust, stating how many roles the strict scheme described in the case would need and explaining how your design resolves the conflict between the trust's policy on emergency access and the principle of least privilege.

[4]

(c)

The auditor reviews $4.2$ million log entries a year in two days a week. Determine what fraction of the log is currently reviewed, and determine the review workload the proposed scheme implies if each role must be reviewed quarterly at fifteen minutes per role.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate the proposal against the information-governance officer's objection, and state which of the two requirements -- least privilege or unblocked clinical access -- your design sacrifices and why.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) *Confidentiality* was the component actually breached, and the breach was large and deliberate: $1{,}180$ patients' records were copied by someone who had no legitimate reason to see any of them. The evidence is the volume, the four departments outside his own and the eleven days over which he worked (A1).

*Integrity* was not breached on the evidence given. Every operation was a copy out of the system; the case records no modification, deletion or insertion of records, and none of the $1{,}180$ records is stated to have been altered. It is worth saying plainly that the absence of an integrity breach is a fact about this incident and not a property of the design -- the same account carried write access to the full records of every department, so integrity was equally exposed and was simply not attacked (A1).

*Availability* was not breached either. The systems remained available to the clinicians who needed them throughout, and nothing in the case suggests service loss. The relevant observation is that the compromise was found two months late, which is a failure of detection rather than of availability; the log contained the evidence from the first day (A1).

The interesting finding is that two of the three components were untouched and the third was breached completely, by a user whose permissions were only what the trust had given him. In a CIA-triple analysis of this incident the useful output is not the tally but the reason each answer comes out as it does.

(b) The strict scheme described in the case needs a role for every combination of site, department and job function:
$$3 \times 6 \times 5 = 90 \ \text{roles} \;\; (A1).$$
Against the forty roles in use now, that is a little over twice the number of roles and it is what the governance officer means by an administration burden -- part (c) puts a figure on it.

The design should keep least privilege as the default and treat emergency access as an explicitly-granted, self-expiring exception (M1). Concretely:

1. Roles are the union of department and job function, not the cross product with site. A ward nurse is a ward nurse at any of the three sites; the site is an attribute of the *record*, not of the person. That reduces the role count to $6 \times 5 = 30$ and leaves the site as a condition evaluated at request time (A1).
2. Emergency access is a break-glass grant, not a role. A clinician who needs a record outside their role requests it, states a reason code, and is given time-limited access -- an hour is long enough for a clinical decision -- with notification to the responsible manager and an entry in the log that is machine-flagged. The clinical requirement is met in seconds, and the exception is narrow, time-bound and attributable (A1).
3. The audit becomes targeted. What matters for detection is the small set of accesses outside a member's usual pattern, not the $4.2$ million entries. Flagging break-glass grants, out-of-own-department reads and reads at volume per user per day reduces the reviewer's queue to something a human can actually read (A1).

(c) The auditor works two days a week, which is $2 \times 52 = 104$ working days a year, or about $\dfrac{104}{5} = 20.8$ working weeks (M1). Reviewing $4.2$ million entries at, say, one entry per second would take
$$\frac{4{,}200{,}000}{3600 \times 7} = 166.7 \ \text{seven-hour days},$$
against the $104$ days available; so even at one entry per second the log cannot be read in the time the trust gives it, and the true coverage is a small fraction of a per cent (A1). The practical statement is that the log as configured is not a control at all: it is a record that exists so that a breach can be reconstructed afterwards, which is exactly how this incident was found.

The proposed scheme's review workload is a different quantity and it is small by comparison. Ninety roles reviewed quarterly at fifteen minutes each:
$$90 \times 15 = 1{,}350 \ \text{minutes} = 22.5 \ \text{hours per quarter},$$
or $7.5$ hours a month (A1). Under the reduced design of part (b), with thirty roles, the same review costs $30 \times 15 = 450$ minutes $= 7.5$ hours per quarter, a third of the strict scheme's burden. Note the direction of the comparison: the *permission review* is affordable under either scheme and the *log review* is not affordable under either, so the governance officer's objection is about the wrong quantity.

(d) The objection is half right. The administration burden of ninety roles is real but small in absolute terms -- $22.5$ hours a quarter is a fraction of one person's time -- and it is not the reason the strict scheme should be rejected. The patient-safety objection is the serious one, because a system that refuses a clinician access to a record in an emergency has converted a security control into a clinical hazard, and no audit finding justifies that (A1).

My design sacrifices something, and it is least privilege in the strict sense: a break-glass grant means that for a short period a member of staff holds access their role does not include. What is preserved is the part of least privilege that matters -- that the excess access is bounded in time, requires a stated reason, is attributable to a person and is reported rather than discovered (A1). The alternative, refusing the request, protects the principle absolutely and harms patients; the alternative of granting standing access to everyone who might ever need it, which is what the trust actually did, is what produced this incident. Sacrificing a strict reading of the principle in favour of an auditable exception is the trade the case is designed to force, and the mark is for saying which side of it the design comes down on and why.
questions.explanation:
The most useful thing about this case is what it does not contain. There is no attacker, no exploit, no stolen credential and no unpatched system. A member of staff with a valid account read records he was allowed to read. Every control that a checklist would name as present *was* present, which is why the case is worth studying: the failure is in the permission model, and the permission model was somebody's deliberate answer to a real operational problem.

The problem it answered is stated in the case and it is usually stated in real hospitals too: staff must never be blocked from a record they need in order to treat a patient. The cheapest way to guarantee that is to give a support role every permission any of its thirty-four holders might need, because then no request is ever refused. The cost of that answer is invisible until it is not: one analysis of the log would have shown that a service-desk analyst was reading four departments he had never worked in, eleven days running, and the log had the evidence from the first day. Detection failed because there was nothing small enough to look at -- $4.2$ million entries, one auditor, two days a week -- and the arithmetic in part (c) is there to make that failure a number rather than an opinion.

The design question is therefore not "how do we stop insiders" but "how do we keep the guarantee without the blanket permission", and the answer that works is to make the exception explicit and short-lived. Break-glass access is a genuine technique and its properties are exactly the ones the case needs: the clinician gets the record in seconds, the grant expires on its own, the reason is recorded, and the manager is notified. Least privilege in the strict sense -- nobody holds any permission they do not need -- is given up for the duration of the grant, and part (d) asks the candidate to say so out loud rather than pretend the trade does not exist.

The role arithmetic is deliberately unremarkable. Three sites times six departments times five functions is ninety, and a candidate who sees that the site belongs to the record rather than to the person gets it down to thirty. Neither number is frightening on its own -- twenty-two hours a quarter is not a burden -- and the point of computing both is to show that the governance officer has objected to the wrong quantity. The scheme that the trust actually ran had forty roles and still produced this incident, which is the clearest evidence that counting roles is not the control.

questions.subtopic: A3.2 A relation that satisfies third normal form because the attribute on the right of the offending dependency is prime, and therefore fails Boyce-Codd normal form, so that no decomposition of it can be lossless, in Boyce-Codd normal form and dependency preserving at the same time
questions.question:
The relation Enrolment has the attributes Student, Subject and Teacher, and the school has stated two rules. A student is taught a given subject by exactly one teacher, so Student together with Subject determines Teacher. Each teacher teaches exactly one subject, so Teacher determines Subject, although a subject may be taught by more than one teacher. The school has observed two problems in practice. When a teacher changes the subject they teach, many rows have to be changed together, and a change that touches only some of them would leave the relation contradicting its own rule. The school also cannot record that a teacher teaches a subject unless some student is taking that subject from that teacher, so a newly appointed teacher who has not yet been assigned a student cannot be entered at all. The head of computing has proposed splitting the relation into two relations, one over Student and Teacher and one over Teacher and Subject, and has asked whether that proposal solves the problems.

(a)

Determine every candidate key of the relation Enrolment, and justify each one by naming the attributes that it determines.

[3]

(b)

Show that the relation satisfies third normal form but does not satisfy Boyce-Codd normal form, naming the functional dependency that makes the difference and explaining why it is tolerated by one normal form and not by the other.

[4]

(c)

Determine whether the proposed decomposition into the relations (Student, Teacher) and (Teacher, Subject) is lossless and whether it preserves every functional dependency, justifying each answer.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate whether the school should adopt the proposed decomposition or leave the relation in third normal form, given the two problems the school has already observed.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The attribute set is {Student, Subject, Teacher}. The given dependencies are {Student, Subject} -> Teacher and Teacher -> Subject.

The pair {Student, Subject} determines Teacher by the first dependency, so its closure is the whole attribute set {Student, Subject, Teacher} and the pair is a superkey. Neither Student alone nor Subject alone determines anything else, so no proper subset of the pair is a superkey, and {Student, Subject} is a candidate key.

The pair {Student, Teacher} determines Subject by the second dependency, since Teacher alone determines Subject, so its closure is also the whole attribute set and the pair is a superkey. Neither Student alone nor Teacher alone determines the other, so {Student, Teacher} is a candidate key as well.

There are exactly two candidate keys, {Student, Subject} and {Student, Teacher}. The prime attributes, which are the attributes belonging to at least one candidate key, are therefore Student, Subject and Teacher: all three attributes of the relation are prime.

(b) Third normal form requires that for every functional dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. Take the first dependency, {Student, Subject} -> Teacher. The determinant {Student, Subject} is a candidate key and therefore a superkey, so this dependency satisfies the condition. Take the second, Teacher -> Subject. The determinant Teacher is not a superkey, because the closure of Teacher is {Teacher, Subject}, which does not contain Student. The dependent, Subject, is a prime attribute, since Subject belongs to the candidate key {Student, Subject}. The dependency therefore satisfies the condition through its second clause, and the relation is in third normal form.

Boyce-Codd normal form requires that for every functional dependency X -> A, X is a superkey, with no alternative clause for prime attributes. The dependency Teacher -> Subject fails this test, because Teacher is not a superkey. The relation is therefore not in Boyce-Codd normal form.

The difference between the two normal forms is exactly the clause that third normal form adds and Boyce-Codd normal form removes. Third normal form allows a determinant that is not a superkey provided the attribute it determines is part of some candidate key. That allowance exists because removing such a dependency can cost more than it saves, which is what part (c) shows. Here the dependent, Subject, is prime, so the allowance applies and the relation is in third normal form but not in Boyce-Codd normal form.

(c) The proposed decomposition replaces Enrolment with R1 over {Student, Teacher} and R2 over {Teacher, Subject}.

The decomposition is lossless. A binary decomposition is lossless when the common attribute set determines at least one of the two relations, that is, when the common attributes form a superkey of at least one of them. The common attribute here is Teacher, and Teacher determines Subject, so Teacher is a superkey of R2 over {Teacher, Subject}. The condition holds, so the join of R1 and R2 reproduces exactly the rows of Enrolment, with no spurious rows and no lost rows.

The decomposition is not dependency preserving. A decomposition preserves the dependencies when the union of the dependencies that hold within the separate relations implies every dependency of the original relation. R2 over {Teacher, Subject} carries Teacher -> Subject, so that dependency survives. R1 over {Student, Teacher} carries no non-trivial dependency at all, because neither Student alone nor Teacher alone determines the other in the original relation. The dependency {Student, Subject} -> Teacher has Student and Subject in different relations, since Student appears only in R1 and Subject only in R2, so it cannot be enforced by either relation and cannot be recovered by joining them. That dependency is lost.

The proposal therefore buys Boyce-Codd normal form and losslessness at the price of the dependency that made {Student, Subject} a key. Losing it means the database can no longer prevent a student from being recorded with two different teachers for the same subject, because no single relation in the schema holds enough information to detect it.

(d) The school faces a genuine choice, because no decomposition of this relation is lossless, in Boyce-Codd normal form and dependency preserving at the same time. The proposed decomposition and the original relation each give up one of the three.

Leaving the relation in third normal form keeps the dependency {Student, Subject} -> Teacher enforceable by the relation itself, so the database can still reject a row that gives one student two teachers for one subject. It keeps the update anomaly the school has observed, because Teacher -> Subject is a dependency between two attributes of the same relation, and changing a teacher's subject means changing every row in which that teacher appears. It also keeps the insertion anomaly, because a row is a class and a teacher with no students cannot be represented.

Adopting the decomposition removes both anomalies. R2 over {Teacher, Subject} holds one row per teacher, so a teacher's subject is recorded once and a newly appointed teacher can be entered before any student is assigned, which also removes the insertion anomaly. The cost is that the lost dependency has to be enforced outside the schema, by a constraint or a check in the application that verifies a student has only one teacher per subject.

The better choice is to adopt the decomposition, because both of the problems the school has actually observed are cured by it and the guarantee that is given up can be replaced by a single constraint that is easy to state and cheap to enforce. The anomalies are present today and cause work every time a teacher changes subject; the lost dependency is a guarantee the school can rebuild in one place. A school with a large and changing timetable will feel the anomalies far more often than it will be inconvenienced by the extra constraint. The judgement is a judgement, however, and an answer that keeps the relation in third normal form and argues that an enforceable dependency is worth more than the convenience of one-row updates is defensible, provided the trade is stated.
questions.explanation:
Third normal form and Boyce-Codd normal form are usually presented as a sequence, with the second being a stricter version of the first, and the difference between them is usually reduced to a clause to be memorised. This item makes the difference do work. The relation here satisfies third normal form for a reason that is easy to miss, namely that the attribute on the right of the offending dependency is part of a key, and it fails Boyce-Codd normal form because that reason is not available.

The relation is small, three attributes and two dependencies, and it is deliberately small. With three attributes there is nowhere for the candidate to hide: either the closures are computed and the keys found, or they are not. The two candidate keys are the substance of part (a), and a candidate who finds only one of them will not be able to answer part (b), because the whole argument depends on Subject being prime, and Subject is prime only because it belongs to the key {Student, Subject}. The parts are chained in that way on purpose.

The second half of the item is about the cost of normalisation, which is the part that is usually omitted. Decomposing to Boyce-Codd normal form is presented as an unqualified improvement, and here it is not: the natural decomposition is lossless, so no data is lost, but the dependency that made the pair a key cannot be expressed by either of the two relations, so the schema can no longer prevent a student from being given two teachers for one subject. The candidate has to notice that the price is real and then decide whether it is worth paying.

The final part is an evaluation and has no single right answer, which is why the marking gives no marks for the choice and all three marks for the reasoning. The school has two observed problems and both are cured by the decomposition, which makes adopting it the more natural recommendation, but a candidate who prefers to keep the dependency enforceable and accept the anomalies can take full marks by saying so accurately. What cannot take marks is a recommendation that does not mention what is being given up, because the whole point of the item is that something always is.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.4 Compilation against interpretation on a stated cost model, where the one-off compilation cost is the whole of the decision and the per-run comparison points the wrong way
questions.question:
The engineering team has asked for a recommendation on how to run catcfg, grounded in the costs given in the stimulus. Identify which stage of translation detects each of the three faulty fragments, explain one advantage the compiled form has for this particular workflow, determine when the two approaches cost the same across a sequence of runs, and comment on whether that figure should decide the choice.

(a)

Three faulty fragments of a catcfg script are given below. For each one, identify the stage of translation that detects it -- lexical analysis, syntax analysis or semantic analysis -- and justify your choice.
(i) price + 1@5 (ii) if price > 100 then total = total + price with no closing keyword (iii) pagewidth = priceband * 2 where priceband is a text value and pagewidth is declared as an integer.

[3]

(b)

Explain one advantage that the compiled form has over the interpreted form for this particular workflow, referring to the number of times the script is run and to what changes between runs.

[2]

(c)

Determine the total time in milliseconds taken by each of the two approaches for a single run, and determine the number of executions at which the two totals become equal. Show your working.

[4]

(d)

Comment on whether the equality you found in part (c) should decide the choice, referring to what the workflow does between executions.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a)

(i) 1@5 is lexical: the tokeniser's rules define a number as a run of digits and @ is not a character that can appear in one, so the scanner fails to form a valid token before any grammar is considered (A1). The characters are individually fine; it is the sequence that no token can cover.

(ii) The missing closing keyword is syntax. Every token so far is valid -- if, an identifier, a relation, a number, the keyword then, an assignment -- and it is the arrangement of those tokens that the grammar rejects, because the rule for a conditional requires a terminator (A1). No meaning has been examined yet.

(iii) priceband * 2 with a text operand is semantic. The statement is grammatically well formed and every token is valid; what fails is the check that the types of the operands are compatible with the operator and with the declared type of the target (A1). This check needs the symbol table of declarations, which is why it cannot be done during scanning or parsing.

(b) The compiled form pays the translation cost once and then runs cheaply, and on this workflow the script is executed roughly $260$ times a year -- once each weekday -- against a small number of edits. The number of executions is large and the number of *different* versions is small, so the one-off cost is amortised over many runs (M1).

What changes between runs is normally nothing at all: the environmental data comes from the product database, not from the script. The edit that follows a price-band change is the exception, and it does invalidate the translated form; but even if the script were edited once a month, the translation would be repeated twelve times a year against two hundred and sixty executions (A1).

(c) One run of the interpreter:
$$12\,000\ \text{tokens} \times 1.5\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 18\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 18\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1).$$

One *first* run of the compiled route:
$$12\,000 \times 60\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 720\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 720\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1\text{ for the translation}) ,$$
and each subsequent run costs
$$12\,000 \times 0.25\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 3\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 3\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1).$$

Let $n$ be the number of executions. The interpreted total is $18n$ milliseconds and the compiled total is $720 + 3n$ milliseconds, both measured from the first run and including it. Setting them equal:
$$18n = 720 + 3n, \qquad 15n = 720, \qquad n = 48 \;\; (A1).$$
After $48$ executions both routes have consumed $864\ \mathrm{ms}$. Under the compiled route the script is executed about $260$ times a year, so the crossover is passed in the tenth week of the first year, and the compiled route is decisively cheaper thereafter: at $260$ executions the interpreted total is $4\,680\ \mathrm{ms}$ against $1\,500\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the compiled one, a saving of about $3.2$ seconds a year.

(d) The equality should not decide the choice on its own, because it is derived from a model whose central assumption is that the same script is executed many times unchanged (M1).

The workflow does edit the script: whenever a price band changes, the editor changes the file, and a compiler must then translate the whole thing again at a cost of $720\ \mathrm{ms}$. If the script were edited before every run, the compiled total for $n$ runs would be $n(720 + 3)$ milliseconds against $18n$ for the interpreter, and the compiler would never win. Between the two extremes the answer turns on the edit rate, which the stimulus does not fix. What can be said without that number is that the crossover of $48$ is the edit-free case and therefore the *most favourable* figure the compiler can claim; the real crossover is higher, by $48$ executions for every extra retranslation, and the decision should be taken on a measured edit rate rather than on the model alone (A1).

The model also ignores two things that favour the interpreter: the compiled intermediate form has to be stored and kept in step with its source, which is a real operational cost, and in this workflow the run takes place once a day, so a saving of sixteen milliseconds per run is not visible to anybody. If the only consideration were time, the case for compiling would rest on the tenth week of each year; if the consideration is engineering effort and the risk of a stale translated file, the interpreter may still be the better answer.
questions.explanation:
This is an arithmetic question wearing a systems question's clothes, and the arithmetic is not the difficulty. Multiplying a token count by a per-token cost takes a minute; deciding *what to multiply* is the whole of the item.

The instinct, when asked which of two ways of running a program is faster, is to compare the running times: $18\ \mathrm{ms}$ against $3\ \mathrm{ms}$, a ratio of six. That comparison is correct and it is not the answer, because the compiled route has already spent $720\ \mathrm{ms}$ before any of its cheap runs happen. The candid way to put the question is over how many runs the comparison is made, and the answer is a crossover: for any number of runs below $48$, interpreting is cheaper in total. Part (c) asks for that number explicitly, which removes the ambiguity, but part (b) is where the reasoning has to be supplied before the arithmetic can be trusted, because the number of runs is not a property of the language -- it is a property of the workflow.

That is also why part (d) exists. The crossover of $48$ is computed on the assumption that the script never changes, and the stimulus explicitly says that it does change. Each edit forces a retranslation of the whole script, because the cost model given is a whole-script translation and there is no partial translation. So the honest statement is that $48$ is a lower bound on the crossover and the true figure depends on how often the price bands change, which the question deliberately does not supply. Recognising that a model has one unfixed parameter and saying which one it is, is more valuable than producing a confident number that the model does not support.

Part (a) is a separate lesson attached to the same stimulus, and it is the one that turns up in examinations most often. "The compiler finds the errors" is true and useless: the three stages find different errors for different reasons, and the reason is always that stage's own job. A scanner cannot report an undeclared variable because it has no symbol table; a parser cannot report a type mismatch for the same reason; and a semantic analyser never sees a character that could not be tokenised. The three fragments are chosen so that each has exactly one stage that can catch it and two that cannot, and a candidate who has the stages sorted will be able to say which is which without hesitating.

questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B3.2 Two independent classification axes modelled with inheritance, where the obvious hierarchy multiplies out and the correct design uses composition to keep the two axes separate
questions.question:
The library must decide whether to accept the junior developer's hierarchy. Identify the two axes of classification and the data and operations that belong to each, explain how many concrete classes the proposal contains in use and in full, design an alternative structure that keeps the axes separate, and justify a situation in which the multiplicative hierarchy would nevertheless be the better choice.

(a)

Identify the two axes of classification in this system and, for each, state one piece of data and one operation that depends on it rather than on the other axis.

[3]

(b)

Explain how many concrete classes the proposed hierarchy contains in use and how many it would contain if it covered every possible combination including the one the library has decided never to stock.

[2]

(c)

Design an alternative class structure that keeps the two axes separate, state how many classes it contains, and state what it costs to add the proposed fifth format.

[3]

(d)

Justify a situation in which the junior developer's multiplicative hierarchy would be the better choice despite the larger class count.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) The two axes are format ('Print', 'Audio', 'Video', 'Download') and genre ('Fiction', 'Reference', 'Biography', 'Poetry', 'Periodical') (A1).

A datum that depends on format rather than on genre: the media type stored with a copy, or a play count or an expiry date -- all of these are properties of how the thing is carried, and none of them changes when a biography is reclassified as reference (A1). An operation that depends on format: renew(), which behaves differently for a print copy that can be recalled and a download that expires. A datum that depends on genre: the list of subject headings, or the Dewey-class code. An operation that depends on genre: catalogue(), or suggestSimilar(), which works on subject matter and is indifferent to whether the item is a download or a video (A1).

The test in each case is whether a change on the *other* axis would force a change here. Reclassifying a novel as poetry changes the subject headings and changes nothing about how it is lent; converting the same title from print to audio changes how it is lent and changes nothing about its subject headings.

(b) In use the library holds every combination except 'Download' with 'Periodical', so the proposal needs
$$4 \times 5 - 1 = 19 \ \text{concrete classes} \;\; (A1).$$
It also needs at least one method to differ between them, or the subclasses are empty shells that exist only to carry a name.

Covering every combination gives
$$4 \times 5 = 20 \ \text{concrete classes} \;\; (A1),$$
one more than the number in use. The difference is worth noticing in the other direction: the proposal is already nineteen classes and the library intends to add a fifth format and a sixth genre, which takes the in-use count from nineteen to
$$5 \times 6 - 1 = 29,$$
an addition of ten classes for two changes to the specification.

(c) A design that keeps the axes apart uses two small hierarchies and lets each entry hold one of each:

  • a Format hierarchy with an abstract Format and four subclasses (Print, Audio, Video, Download), each implementing lend() and renew() (A1);
  • a Genre hierarchy with an abstract Genre and five subclasses (Fiction, Reference, Biography, Poetry, Periodical), each implementing headings() (A1);
  • a single MediaEntry class holding a title, a creator, a location, a loan period, one Format object and one Genre object, and delegating the format-specific and genre-specific operations to whichever objects it holds (A1).

The class count is $2$ abstract bases $+\ 4$ formats $+\ 5$ genres $+\ 1$ entry $= 12$ classes in total, of which the two abstract bases carry no instances and the concrete working classes number ten. The library's existing nineteen combinations are expressed as nineteen *objects* of MediaEntry, not as nineteen classes.

Adding Microform means writing one new subclass of Format and changing nothing else: the count of classes goes up by one, no MediaEntry code changes, and the combination of Microform with each of the five genres works immediately. Under the proposal the same change would add five classes, each of which would need its own lend() and renew() implementations even though they would be identical.

(d) The multiplicative hierarchy is the better choice when the two axes do not merely coexist but interact, that is when the behaviour of a combination is not the sum of what the two axes would do separately (A1).

A concrete case from this system: a DownloadPeriodical may be barred from the collection, and a PrintPeriodical must be lent with a shorter period than other print material. If a rule of that kind applies to one cell of the grid and to no other, then the cell has behaviour of its own, and the cleanest place for it is a subclass that exists to hold it. Composition would express the same thing with a conditional inside MediaEntry, and a conditional that tests the pair of axes is exactly a hard-coded combination in a different place (A1).

The general statement is worth giving: composition is preferred when the axes can be combined freely and their behaviour composes; inheritance is preferred when the combinations have their own behaviour. Here nineteen of the twenty cells behave as the composition of their row and column, so composition is right, and a candidate who says so and identifies the one cell that would justify the other design has understood the distinction rather than the rule of thumb.
questions.explanation:
The distinction this item is built on is old and it is still got wrong constantly: inheritance models *what something is*, and composition models *what something has*. The library entry is a print copy and it is a work of fiction, and both statements are true, and neither of them is more fundamental than the other. When a designer picks one of the two axes and hangs inheritance off it, they have quietly decided that the other axis will be handled by something else -- and if there is no plan for that, the other axis gets handled by a class per combination.

That is how the nineteen subclasses appear. Nobody chooses twenty classes for a two-dimensional problem; it happens because the first axis is modelled properly with four subclasses, and then the second axis has nowhere to live, and the path of least resistance is a subclass. The tell is that the subclasses come in groups of five or four with identical bodies, differing only in their name.

Composition removes the multiplication because the two axes become two *objects* held by one class, and objects compose where classes multiply. The entry delegates lend() to its format object and headings() to its genre object, and the number of classes stops depending on the product of the two list lengths. The numbers are small enough here to check by hand: nineteen against twelve, and the addition of a format costs one class against five. That comparison is the argument, and it is why the item asks for the counts rather than for a design principle.

Part (d) is where a candidate who has only memorised "prefer composition" is separated from one who has understood it. There is a real case for the multiplicative hierarchy, and it is not a rare one: when a specific cell of the grid has behaviour that neither axis explains, the cell is an entity and deserves a class. A download periodical that is barred from the collection is such a cell. The point is not that composition is always right; it is that composition is right when the grid's behaviour composes, and a designer who knows which of the two situations they are in has the whole of the answer.

questions.subtopic: B2.4 The same loop taking twelve iterations on one three-digit pair and two on another, and the worst case that has to be derived
questions.question:
The figure shows two traces of the same function, which is written below. Division is integer division and MOD returns the remainder.

FUNCTION f(a, b)
WHILE b > 0 DO
t = a MOD b
a = b
b = t
END WHILE
RETURN a
END FUNCTION

One iteration means one execution of the loop body. For the input a = 377, b = 233 the loop body is executed twelve times and the successive pairs of values are listed in the figure. For the input a = 1000, b = 3 the loop body is executed twice. Both inputs are three-digit numbers, and neither of the two inputs is noticeably harder to read than the other.

(a) State the value returned by the function for the input a = 377, b = 233, and state the value returned for the input a = 1000, b = 3.

(b) Explain what property of the pair (a, b) determines how many iterations the loop performs, and explain why the number of digits in a and b does not determine it.

(c) Determine the largest number of iterations the loop can perform for any input pair with 1 <= b <= a <= 1000, and state a pair of values that achieves it. Justify your answer in terms of the sequence of remainders.

(a)

State the value returned by the function for the input a = 377, b = 233, and state the value returned for the input a = 1000, b = 3.

[2]

(b)

Explain what property of the pair (a, b) determines how many iterations the loop performs, and explain why the number of digits in a and b does not determine it.

[2]

(c)

Determine the largest number of iterations the loop can perform for any input pair with 1 <= b <= a <= 1000, and state a pair of values that achieves it, justifying your answer in terms of the sequence of remainders.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The loop returns the last non-zero value of b before the remainder reaches zero, which is the largest integer that divides both of the original inputs. For a = 377 and b = 233 the figure ends at the pair (1, 0), so the value returned is 1 (A1). For a = 1000 and b = 3 the pairs are (3, 1) and (1, 0), so the value returned is also 1 (A1). Both inputs therefore produce the same answer, and the number of iterations differs by a factor of six.

(b) The number of iterations is set by how quickly the pair of values shrinks, and that is set by the size of the quotient produced at each step. When a is much larger than b the first remainder is small, so the pair collapses in a step or two: at a = 1000, b = 3 the quotient is 333 and the remainder is 1, and the loop is over almost immediately (M1). When a is only slightly larger than b the quotient is 1 and the remainder is a minus b, so the pair (a, b) becomes (b, a minus b) and shrinks by only a small factor each time; in the trace for 377 and 233 every quotient is 1 and the values fall by the golden ratio, 377 to 233 to 144 to 89 and so on, which is the slowest shrinkage the loop can produce (A1). The number of digits is not the governing quantity because it only bounds how many halvings are available, and the actual count is usually far below that bound: two inputs of three digits can need two iterations or twelve, and the deciding factor is the ratio of the two numbers and how close the quotients come to 1, not how large the numbers are.

(c) The largest number of iterations is 14, attained by a = 987 and b = 610 (A1). The justification runs backwards through the loop. If the pair (a, b) with a greater than b takes n iterations, then after one iteration it becomes (b, a MOD b) and that pair takes n minus 1 iterations, so the smallest pair needing n iterations is obtained by making the quotient 1 at every step, which gives the backward recurrence a = b + c where c is the next value in the sequence (M1). Starting from the smallest possible end, the pair (1, 0), and reversing the rule gives (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 2), (5, 3), (8, 5) and so on: the Fibonacci sequence, in which the largest value is 987 at the sixteenth term. If a pair takes 14 iterations then its larger member is at least 987, so any pair with both values at most 1000 that needs 14 iterations must sit exactly at 987 and 610, and 15 iterations would require a larger member of at least 1597, which is above the limit. Checking the two candidates confirms it: the pair (987, 610) takes 14 iterations, while the pair (1000, 999) takes 2 and the pair (233, 144) takes 11 (A1). The same argument explains why the trace in the figure is the slow case for its size: 377 and 233 are the fourteenth and thirteenth Fibonacci numbers, so they are the worst pair below 400, and scaling them up to 987 and 610 keeps them the worst pair below 1000.
questions.explanation:
The trap in this item is a slogan that is true. The loop is logarithmic in the size of its inputs, the syllabus says so, and every candidate will write it down. What the slogan does not do is predict anything about a particular pair, and the figure supplies two pairs of the same size whose costs differ by a factor of six and whose answers are identical. So the candidate has to abandon the slogan and look at what the loop actually does to the numbers.

What it does is replace (a, b) by (b, a MOD b). The size of the second value after one iteration is a MOD b, which is the remainder that is left after removing as many copies of b as will fit. If b is small compared with a the quotient is large and the remainder is small, so the pair drops by a large factor immediately; that is the 1000 and 3 case, where the quotient is 333 and the pair goes straight to (3, 1). If b is close to a the quotient is 1 and the remainder is a minus b, so the pair only slides along by the difference; that is the Fibonacci case, and its slow rate is the golden ratio, which is the slowest rate any pair can achieve. Quoting a logarithm hides all of this because a logarithm is a bound and the question is about actual counts.

The worst case is worth deriving because the derivation is a single reversal of the loop. Ask instead which pair is the smallest that can need a given number of iterations, and the answer is forced: to need many iterations from as small a starting point as possible, every quotient has to be 1, which means each pair is built from the next by adding, which is exactly the Fibonacci recurrence. The worst pair below a limit is therefore the largest pair of consecutive Fibonacci numbers below it, and for 1000 that is 987 and 610. The trace in the figure is the same phenomenon one scale down, which is a useful thing to notice: the answer to a worst-case question about an algorithm is often sitting visibly in the example that was chosen to illustrate the algorithm, if the example is chosen honestly.

There is one further general point. The number of digits is a convenient proxy for the cost of an algorithm when the cost really does depend on magnitude, and it is a misleading one whenever the cost depends on structure instead. Here the three-digit number 999 paired with 1000 costs two iterations and the three-digit pair 987 and 610 costs fourteen. Two inputs of the same length, seven times the work, decided entirely by how the numbers relate to each other rather than by how big they are.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B2.2 A very sparse matrix held in a dense two-dimensional array, where the cost of the representation grows with the square of the order while the data grows linearly, and the unit-test scale is far too small to reveal it
questions.question:
A sparse matrix is held in a dense two-dimensional array, and the same code is used for the unit tests and for production. The matrix, the two scales and the cost of one entry are given in the table. Answer all parts using the figures in the table.

(a)

Calculate the number of entries a dense two-dimensional array stores for each of the two matrices, and state the memory each array occupies in bytes and in gigabytes.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the memory a sparse representation requires if each non-zero entry is stored as an 8-byte value together with a 4-byte row index and a 4-byte column index, and express the result for the production matrix in megabytes.

[3]

(c)

Determine the number of floating-point operations one matrix-vector product performs on the production matrix under each representation, state the time each takes if the processor performs 10^9 operations per second, and hence determine the ratio of the two.

[4]

(d)

Explain why the unit tests give no warning of the problem, and state one property of the data that a designer must check before choosing between the two representations.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) A dense array stores one cell for every pair of row and column indices, whether or not the entry is used. For the unit-test matrix that is
$$1000 \times 1000 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ entries},$$
and at 8 bytes per entry that is $1\,000\,000 \times 8 = 8\,000\,000$ bytes, which is 8 MB (M1)(A1). For the production matrix the same count is
$$200\,000 \times 200\,000 = 4 \times 10^{10} = 40\,000\,000\,000 \text{ entries},$$
and the memory is $4 \times 10^{10} \times 8 = 3.2 \times 10^{11}$ bytes, that is 320 GB (A1). The first array fits comfortably in the 64 GB server and the second one does not fit at all, which is the whole of the difficulty: the two counts differ by a factor of forty thousand because the order differs by a factor of two hundred, and the cost of a dense array goes as the square of the order.

(b) A sparse representation stores one record for each non-zero entry and nothing for the zeros. Each record needs $8 + 4 + 4 = 16$ bytes (M1). For the unit-test matrix that is $10 \times 16 = 160$ bytes, which is negligible (A1). For the production matrix it is
$$400\,000 \times 16 = 6\,400\,000 \text{ bytes} = 6.4 \text{ MB},$$
which is one hundred thousand times smaller than the 320 GB the dense array would need and fits in the server with room to spare (A1). The comparison is worth stating in both directions: the sparse form is not merely smaller, it is smaller by a factor of
$$\frac{3.2 \times 10^{11}}{6.4 \times 10^{6}} = 50\,000,$$
so the two representations are not two ways of doing the same thing. One of them is possible and the other is not.

(c) A dense matrix-vector product performs one multiply and one add for every entry of the array, because the code cannot know which entries are zero without looking at them:
$$200\,000 \times 200\,000 = 4 \times 10^{10} \text{ operations}.$$
At $10^{9}$ operations per second that is 40 seconds for a single multiplication (M1). A sparse product touches only the stored entries, so it performs one multiply and one add per non-zero entry:
$$400\,000 \text{ operations},$$
which at the same rate takes $400\,000 / 10^{9} = 4 \times 10^{-4}$ seconds, that is 0.4 milliseconds (A1). The ratio is
$$\frac{4 \times 10^{10}}{4 \times 10^{5}} = 100\,000,$$
so the sparse product is one hundred thousand times cheaper in arithmetic as well as fifty thousand times cheaper in memory (M1)(A1). The two ratios are not equal because memory is charged per cell while arithmetic is charged per non-zero entry, and the dense form pays the first cost for every cell it holds and the second for every cell it visits.

(d) The unit tests give no warning because the property that makes the dense array unusable is the one property the tests hold fixed. Both matrices have the same density, about 0.001 per cent, and the test matrix is small enough that its dense form is 8 MB and allocates and runs in about a millisecond (M1). Every test therefore passes, and the suite is evidence about the correctness of the indexing arithmetic rather than about the cost of the representation. The property a designer must check is the density, and specifically whether it stays small as the order grows: the decision rule is to compare the number of non-zero entries with the square of the order, and to choose the sparse form whenever the first is much smaller than the second (A1). A useful discipline is to test at the largest order the system will ever see, or at least to assert the density in a test, because a test suite that only exercises the small case cannot distinguish a representation that scales from one that does not.
questions.explanation:
This item is about the difference between a cost that grows with the size of the container and a cost that grows with the size of the contents. A dense array is a container: its cost is set by the number of rows and columns, and it is the same whether the matrix holds four hundred thousand values or none at all. A sparse representation is a record of contents: its cost is set by the number of values that are actually there. When the two are compared at a fixed density, the container's cost grows with the square of the order and the contents' cost grows linearly, so the gap between them grows without bound and the choice between them stops being a matter of taste.

The reason this is worth a question is that the arithmetic is trivial and the decision is not. Every number in the item is a multiplication. What the candidate has to supply is the recognition that the two multiplications are measuring different things, one a capacity and one an occupancy, and that a test suite run at a small scale cannot distinguish them because both are small. The unit-test matrix is eight megabytes, which is nothing; the production matrix is three hundred and twenty gigabytes, which is five times the memory of the machine it is deployed to. Nothing happens between those two figures except that the order changed, and the order enters one of them twice.

The density is the same in both rows of the table, and that is the deliberate part of the design. A candidate might reasonably think that the test is unrepresentative because the test matrix is sparse in a different way from the production matrix, and the table forecloses that: the two densities agree to three significant figures. What differs is the scale, and the scale is exactly the variable that a dense representation is sensitive to. So the test suite is not merely unrepresentative, it is unrepresentative in the one direction that matters, which is why the failure appears only at deployment.

The two ratios, fifty thousand in memory and one hundred thousand in arithmetic, are worth separating. Memory is charged per cell stored, so the ratio is the ratio of the cell count to the entry count. Arithmetic is charged per cell visited, and a dense routine visits every cell while a sparse one visits only the stored entries, so the same comparison applies. The factor of two between them comes from the 16 bytes a sparse record costs against the 8 bytes a dense cell costs. A candidate who reports a single ratio for both has not noticed that the two costs are charged on different quantities, and that is a real and common confusion about asymptotic arguments.

The item is claimed at difficulty 3 because it has one lever. A candidate who sees that the representation must match the density has everything else the item needs, and the remaining work is three multiplications and a division. There is no second idea in it: the numbers are clean, the two representations are both familiar, and the only thing the question asks the candidate to notice is that a container and a record are not the same kind of thing.

It is worth being clear about what the remedy is, because the item invites the wrong one. Buying more memory does not repair the design, it postpones the failure: at order two hundred thousand the dense array is already five times the size of the machine, and the next increase in the order doubles that ratio. The representation has to change, and the change is small, which is what makes the wrong choice expensive rather than merely unfortunate. The cost of the mistake is not the memory that was wasted, it is the deployment that could not be made.
